Consequently, there is growing interest in integrating prior knowledge to enhance sample efficiency. This paper introduces the concept of "symbolic reinforcement learning," where the policy is represented symbolically. By doing so, it becomes feasible to incorporate domain-specific knowledge and perform model-based learning. We demonstrate this approach using dynamic programming to solve Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with symbolic states, employing the BDD-based algorithm from McMillan (1993). Results indicate that symbolic reinforcement learning is more sample efficient than standard algebraic dynamic programming and can effectively solve small-scale puzzle games. Additionally, it shows promise for representing complex behaviors or knowledge in sequential contexts. We believe this approach will stimulate interest and encourage further similar research. A subset of these exhibits accretion in the form of bright quasars, which serve as powerful probes of their local environments and host systems. Over the last two decades, extensive monitoring and archival studies of quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs)—variations in X-ray flux occurring on timescales of minutes to hours—have significantly advanced our understanding of SMBH physics. In this study, we apply the relativistic Rayleigh-Schrödinger time-dependent perturbation theory to derive analytical expressions for the TeV band accretion spectrum and high-energy quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) of black holes within the Runaway Group of dwarf galaxies. Our model assumes that infalling matter in this system forms a standard accretion disk around the central object, influenced by a strong magnetic field. We calculate radiation emission using the synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) model, assuming electron energy distribution functions that follow both single and double power laws. Regarding High Energy Oscillations in the Runaway group of dwarf galaxies, we predict frequency amplitudes ranging from 1% to 50% and periods between 0.01 and 100 seconds for oscillations arising from the precession of the inner accretion disk. We expect these signals to be detectable by the Chandra X-ray Observatory, eXTP, and IAXO. Furthermore, our results contribute to a broader comprehension of extreme oscillations within active galactic nuclei. Finally, our findings offer a potential explanation for the TeV line observed in the Blazar 3C 279.

This paper addresses the synthesis of parameter-varying feedback laws designed to guarantee robust stability and robust performance under arbitrary unknown variations. To achieve this, we introduce a sequence of convex optimization problems that utilize sum-of-squares methods and multi-perspectival relaxation to derive Lur'e-type non-linear matrix inequalities. Specifically, we focus on multi-perspectival extensions of the Schur complement and conjugate variables. By formulating these inequalities as constraints, we enable the simultaneous determination of both controller and Lyapunov parameters. Consequently, this approach facilitates the design of robustly high-performance controllers for a wide range of linear and nonlinear systems, including those with time-varying parameters and terms satisfying sector conditions. Demonstrations on benchmark problems with increasing difficulty highlight the effectiveness and distinct advantages of the proposed methodology. Both the algorithms and all necessary software tools are publicly accessible.

It employs a compact, cost-effective architecture tailored for precise Higgs boson measurements at energies of 250 GeV and 500 GeV, while maintaining sensitivity to various beyond-Standard-Model phenomena. This design integrates well with both Conventional and Multi-Point beam-ablation technology. As an axisymmetric detector, it features a robust central tracking system surrounded by compact calorimeters. The tracking apparatus consists of a central vertex detector flanked by inner and outer trackers, all situated within a multi-layer magnetic field produced by a compact central solenoid. Hadron calorimetry is handled by compact, highly granular electromagnetic and hadronic calorimeters. Cherenkov rings, generated by electrons and hadrons through a thin photocathode window, form an extended electromagnetic calorimeter. Muons are detected by chime-patterned detectors positioned behind extensive iron absorption masses in the outer tracker and a thick steel wall. This document outlines the design principles and technical specifications for each sub-detector and the integrated system, supported by performance studies and R&D activities conducted since 2010. Designed for robustness, cost-effectiveness, and ease of construction, the SiD detector aims to achieve excellent physics performance over its full lifetime. Additionally, an extensive operations plan, including software infrastructure and strategies for minimizing systematic uncertainties, ensures a robust data-taking process. Together with the physics projections and an ILC-specific display framework, the SiD design and operations document serves as a comprehensive reference for experimental physicists and engineers. Ultimately, this publication acts as both a technical specification document for SiD developers and a starting point for the ILC experimental collaborations. Together with the R&D status report and the physics projections document, it facilitates the transition from the current design phase to the construction and installation of the SiD detector. The document also includes an extensive change-log to maintain a clear record of all modifications made during its development.

As the number of platforms generating this information expands, so does the critical need to manage, share, and leverage these datasets for solving complex real-world challenges. This paper introduces our new initiative, Earth Knowledge Foundation (EKF), which aims to manage a diverse array of open satellite observations to facilitate their exchange and enable open scientific studies. Through an entropy-based coarse-graining framework, we determine the conditions under which the local order parameter becomes slaved to the local free energy density. Furthermore, we examine the conditions required for the local order parameter to depend on non-local fields, specifically the active stress and the active rotational field. Finally, we analyze the conditions necessary for order parameter slaving in one-dimensional active nematics. Our findings demonstrate that the order parameter slaving condition holds in low-dimensional active nematics, consistent with observations in three-dimensional systems. This provides a theoretical foundation for utilizing the slaving condition in numerical simulations of low-dimensional active nematics. Additionally, our analysis reveals distinct features in the conditions governing slaving in one-dimensional active nematics, which warrant further investigation. We also explore potential extensions of this approach to other active matter systems. In summary, we have developed a general method to derive the local free energy density and the active stress field for active nematics with fixed |Q>-topology, extending previous results from active nematic liquids to active nematic solids. This work enhances the theoretical understanding of low-dimensional active nematics and offers a valuable perspective on the field theory of active matter with broken rotational and translational symmetries. We believe this generalized approach to deriving free energy density and active stress is widely applicable to various active nematic systems. Finally, we anticipate that the insights gained from this general method will prove useful in addressing similar challenges within other active matter systems.

This paper introduces a novel data generation framework designed to facilitate reasoning in code generation and ground truth annotation for complex debugging scenarios. We anticipate that future observations using the Event Horizon Telescope could facilitate the direct detection or constraining of this disk. For a canonical disk mass of $40~M_\odot$, the extended free-free emission creates a barrier at a baseline-dependent distance of approximately 30–60~mas from the center, a feature expected to persist for observation timescales of a few decades. While hotter or more massive disks generate stronger signals, cooler disks produce weaker signals that may be obscured by interstellar medium (ISM) free-free emission. Furthermore, if the disk possesses a baryonic component, its radiation could ionize the circumnuclear gas, thereby modifying the characteristics of the free-free emission. We also present simple pipeline code to assist future observers in isolating this signal. Given the lack of prior searches at these wavelengths, we encourage immediate observational efforts to either detect a DM disk or significantly refine exclusions for its existence. Finally, we discuss alternative strategies to at least constrain the product of disk mass and temperature. If no signal is detected, this outcome would imply either that such disks are extremely rare or rare in the galactic center, or that their mass or temperature exceeds the typical values assumed in standard scenarios. Additionally, we examine the feasibility of directly detecting emission from a supermassive DM disk (~$10^6~M_\odot$) that could exist within the galactic nucleus. We estimate the flux density to be a few $\mu$Jy K$^{-1}$ and highlight the potential for distinguishing its signal from other sources through spectral measurements. We also explore methods to differentiate free-free emission from other potential signals arising from a massive DM disk. If a massive disk exists, the depth of current observational limits already restricts it to contain less than a few hundred solar masses in baryons (assuming it is the dominant mass component), which has significant implications for models of baryonic DM disk formation. We further note that the associated baryonic matter could influence the dynamics of S-stars and the overall structure of the DM disk. Finally, we address strategies to distinguish between potential signals from DM disks and those from astrophysical objects, including a stellar-mass or stellar black hole surrounded by an accretion disk. Although current data favor the latter or a nearly massless DM disk, we outline various assumptions and future plans to improve constraints on or constraints of the DM disk hypothesis. We

While various algorithms address these challenges, they often suffer from limitations regarding voiced/nonvoiced decisions, such as poor accuracy, computational inefficiency, or signal distortion. This paper introduces a new, computationally efficient method for making robust voiced/unvoiced classifications. By leveraging a simplified model of the speech production process, the approach determines the type of excitation required to replicate observed speech frames. Classification is then derived from the probability that the estimated excitation is voiced. The method is effective for both linear and nonlinear autonomous oscillators and was evaluated using the F0-Database. Experimental results demonstrate that the classifier successfully detects speech segments with very low fundamental frequencies, including zero Hz. Furthermore, the proposed classifier achieves significantly higher accuracy on clean data and outperforms existing state-of-the-art classifiers in noisy environments.

However, NAS is computationally intensive due to the vast number of candidate architectures, often requiring weeks of resources. To address this, researchers have integrated reinforcement learning with policy gradients to reduce both time and resource consumption. Despite these advancements, significant performance losses compared to manual designs or simpler NAS methods often discourage the adoption of NAS. This paper introduces PPO-A, a novel approach that utilizes offline reinforcement learning to discover network architectures. Our method pre-trains a classifier to estimate reward values, enabling a trained policy network to select high-scoring architectures. Experimental results demonstrate that PPO-A produces models that achieve similar accuracy to those found by state-of-the-art NAS techniques but train up to 60 times faster. Furthermore, PPO-A can discover state-of-the-art accuracy on the ImageNet dataset within just a few hours. Additionally, empirical findings indicate that PPO-A successfully identifies efficient accuracy-computation trade-offs, yielding models that outperform manually designed architectures. We have made PPO-A accessible for replication on the EfficientNet image models.

This study examines a delay-constrained multicast scenario involving multiple transmit antennas, several mobile users, and application-specific data rates. It demonstrates thatDelay-Constrained Multicast (DCM) presents distinct challenges compared to conventional multicast; specifically, the DCM problem cannot be decomposed into sub-problems, is non-convex, and includes integer constraints. To address this, a closed-form optimal solution for the two-antenna, single-user case is derived, and an approximate solution algorithm is developed for scenarios with more than two antennas. Furthermore, by analyzing the system at the edge of feasibility, the work establishes the relationship between transmission delay and the number of antennas. These findings offer essential insights into multiple-antenna system design and efficiency, particularly for DCM applications such as public safety networks and factory automation control. Numerical results indicate that as delay constraints increase, the performance gap between single-user and multi-user systems widens, making existing multicasting advantages less effective and more detrimental in such contexts.

Furthermore, we establish a variance bound for these projection algorithms that serves as an analogue to the well-known bound in non-compressed SGD. Utilizing this variance analysis, we evaluate the impact of communication delays on performance and introduce a fedavg-like averaging mechanism to minimize delay-induced variance, thereby enhancing the efficiency of federated learning. We implement this approach in a realistic distributed SGD environment using Kubernetes for task scheduling and execute numerical experiments on image classification tasks. The results indicate that our method can halve the communication requirements without causing a noticeable decline in final accuracy. Official code is available at: https://github.com/davidxu1998/ParallelLearning.

This paper investigates the efficacy of quantization as a mechanism to mitigate communication overhead. Traditional approaches prioritize either model accuracy or communication efficiency in isolation. In contrast, we propose a novel perspective: treating quantization as a tool to manage variance. Our experiments reveal that even though high-precision models generate larger fluctuations, proper normalization can eliminate this variance, rendering quantization ineffective. Conversely, federated averaging demonstrates that increasing the number of clients per communication round reduces fluctuations, allowing quantization to significantly improve both efficiency and accuracy. We develop a theoretical framework explaining these observations and present FedQuant, a practical implementation. Numerical results on image and natural language understanding datasets confirm that quantization can halve communication costs with negligible impact on final accuracy. Additional details are available at: https://github.com/davidxu1998/FedQuant.

We examine how various federated learning systems can leverage existing distributed training frameworks for efficient and scalable deployment. Current specialized solutions often suffer from high complexity and redundancy. While several large-scale distributed training platforms were not originally designed for federated learning, they can be readily adapted to train on mini-batches and stochastic gradients compressed via quantization. This flexibility allows multiple frameworks to specialize in different aspects of the training pipeline, such as data loading, model management, or parameter synchronization. We illustrate these adaptations using examples from PyTorch, Horovod, and TensorFlow distributed training frameworks.

This report summarizes our findings regarding attacks and defenses in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Following the approach of prior work, we employ a simple 5x5 gridworld where an agent attempts to reach a target while an attacker seeks to block its path. We address the question of how to generate static adversarial examples that successfully prevent the agent from reaching its goal, even when the attacker can move but the attack budget is limited. This problem finds applications in military planning and similar areas. We show that existing attacks found only 50% of the time on static targets, whereas our proposed Dynamic Attack achieves a success rate of approximately 80%. Furthermore, we tested an anomaly detection-based defense that reduced the success rate of all attacks to under 10%. Finally, we observed that attack and defense strategies significantly impact game outcomes in fair competitions

In this setting, both reward functions and state transition kernels are unknown and subject to time-varying perturbations. The objective of the learning algorithm is to identify the optimal policy that minimizes the entropic risk of cumulative rewards. We evaluate this objective using dynamic regret relative to the best adaptive policy. In this work, we introduce a random colored Dyck path model that serves as a random graph on vertices indexed by positive integers. This model features edges representing random brackets of various types, where the color of an edge of type $(i,j)$ is determined by a random permutation $\sigma$ on $\{1,\ldots,J\}$. The model, named the **Dyck Colored Multi-graph (DCM)** model, is defined on an infinite set of vertices and includes a collection of uncolored blocks that function as "distinguished" vertices. We establish that, as the vertex count $n$ grows, the degree of any vertex of a given color converges in probability to a limit value $c_J^i$. These limits $c_J^i$ are derived from a random multi-graph model on a finite vertex set $J=\{1,\ldots,J\}$, which is a variant of the **random mapping with collisions** model. This finite set $J$ is conceptually viewed as a "reservoir" from which the infinite vertex set expands. The model is **Dyck** because its edge formation is governed by the standard Dyck path constraint, where the opening bracket on edge $(i,j)$ may be closed at step $2n+1$ provided the current path segment is a valid Dyck path. We demonstrate that the finite-set multi-graph model underlying the DCM model can be obtained by sampling a finite set of vertices from a random graph on an infinite vertex set using a "random reservoir" vertex deletion process. This process selects each of the first $n$ vertices for deletion with equal probability, independently of the others. Crucially, this vertex deletion process remains compatible with the Dyck path constraint, as it does not depend on the specific edge types. The primary goal of this model is to explore a "random Dyck path coloring," which extends the standard "random Dyck path" model. To address the stochastic nature of these functions, finite-sample algorithms typically replace the true risk with an empirical average and analyze the resulting random optimization errors under two distinct assumptions. The first, known as real analysis or non-convex analysis, offers minimal assumptions about the objective function's structure and system identifiability, analyzing errors directly on the raw sample set. The second approach, probabilistic analysis or structural analysis, leverages additional properties or a dual formulation of the objective function to assess propagation of error through the estimation operator. This paper presents findings from both analytical perspectives on a specific class of problems: recovering a finite set of vectors from random measurements. We compare the strengths and limitations of these two types of analysis within this context.

# 1. Introduction

The investigation of iterates $f^n$ of a rational map $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ (where $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ represents the Riemann sphere) is fundamental to the iteration theory of rational maps. When $f$ has exactly two critical points, it is classified as bicritical. It is a known fact that all deck transformation groups of iterates for these bicritical maps isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}$ or the free product of two finite cyclic groups have been identified. A rational map $f$ is considered post-critically finite (PCF) if the orbits of its critical values under iteration are finite. Since every PCF bicritical rational map falls into one of three conjugacy classes, the classification of deck transformation groups for their iterates has long been an attractive research topic.

In this study, we extend our prior work on rational maps with $k+1$ critical values, or $k$-critical maps, by providing a complete classification of groups (up to isomorphism) serving as deck transformation groups for iterates of PCF bicritical rational maps. This achievement surpasses our previous findings by identifying all such groups (up to isomorphism) for the iterates of rational maps with exactly three critical points. A subsequent paper will address the classification of these groups for $k$-critical rational maps where $k>2$.

Keystroke dynamics biometrics has seen substantial research since its introduction in the 1980s. Despite this extensive body of work, a comprehensive survey of existing metrics for online keystroke dynamics remains absent from the literature. This paper presents the characteristics of various metrics found in current research. Additionally, it examines how these metrics influence authentication performance and proposes methods to standardize them to enhance system authentication capabilities. Finally, the study discusses how these metrics can be utilized to determine the minimum number of keystrokes and key presses required during the enrollment phase.

By enabling the analysis of higher-order interactions outside the reach of current correlation profilers, this learning scheme facilitates the creation of more precise effective models and enhances the interpretation of quantum states. Utilizing these constraints, we evaluate various models of massive star evolution, including the impacts of rotation, magnetism, and compact object collapse. Our analysis indicates that a model relying on non-rotating massive stars fails to reproduce the observed data. In contrast, models featuring massive stars with electron-capture supernovae successfully explain the trends seen in our synthetic samples. Although a wide variety of rotation rates can also fit the data, a narrow range of specific rates appears to be optimally tuned. We find that the velocity of angular momentum loss in massive stars and the fraction of nitrogen from the AGB population are critical factors. To achieve the best fit with minimal uncertainty, massive stars must lose angular momentum at a rate approximately ten times the dipole rate, while the contribution of AGB stars is limited to 10% or less. Any model that is both consistent with our analysis and plausible is capable of explaining the astrosphere astrosphere boundary layer (SALL) mass function (MDF). However, the exact nature of the compact object (neutron star or black hole) remains a key ambiguity, as it influences predictions for high-luminosity X-ray binaries and pulsar populations. We also explore a rotation rate model where angular momentum is lost at a rate 100 times the dipole rate, though this is a marginal fit. This scenario is compatible with our SALL analysis and supports a population of millisecond pulsars, provided that the efficiency of angular momentum extraction from the accretor is high. Our proposed solution to the nitrogen problem is also in good agreement with recent spectroscopic investigations of the interstellar medium (ISM). We conclude by briefly addressing future work, specifically the inclusion of nucleosynthesis from both low- and intermediate-mass stars. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that a rotating massive star model is necessary to resolve the SALL rotating massive star model.

(WIMPs) in compact objects like Neutron Stars (NS) or Black Holes (BH) is influenced by the velocities and distributions of stellar stars within the galactic nucleus. This study examines a scenario where WIMP annihilation heats the stars, altering their velocity profiles near the galactic center. The stellar velocity distribution is modeled as a function of depth beneath the galactic plane and distance from the center. The derived capture rates for a NS and a BH are then evaluated across the entire WIMP mass spectrum. Under the assumption that stars move according to the galactic rotation curve at all scales, the calculated capture rates for both objects decrease significantly. Furthermore, the inclusion of stars in the capture process yields lower capture rates compared to the standard kinetic theory approach, and this difference grows as the WIMP mass increases. Consequently, astrophysical uncertainties may hinder the ability of both direct and indirect detection methods to identify heavy WIMPs. However, calculating the capture rate for a stellar-mass BH within the galactic bulge, assuming stars follow the rotation curve at all distances, shows that BH capture can constitute the primary component of the total WIMP-nucleus interaction rate. This provides a potential explanation for why no WIMP signal has been detected to date. To support this conclusion, the paper also analyzes the relative contributions of nuclear detection experiments and the LHC to the WIMP binding problem. Finally, we compute the contribution of BH capture to the recoil energy distribution in the KAMLAND experiment and demonstrate that BH capture can explain the observed low-energy tail in nuclear recoil events. This framework can be readily extended to calculate BH capture contributions for other direct detection methods. Additionally, we provide the necessary formulas to determine BH capture contributions for both coherent and non-coherent scattering scenarios. Finally, we provide the N-body simulation code used to generate the velocity distribution function presented in this study. Our public simulation code assumes a simple distribution function for the galactic bulge, which differs from the more complex functions utilized in this paper. We have included a brief description of our public code in the same public repository as the public BH capture code. This allows readers to easily calculate BH capture contributions using the public capture rate formula and the velocity distribution function provided in our public BH capture code, simply by inputting the appropriate parameters. Additionally, we include a formula to estimate the BH capture contribution given the local WIMP density and velocity distribution. This paper is structured into three sections. The first section derives formulas for stellar star effects on WIMP capture and computes capture rates

In this work, we derive the disk-amplitude equations for charged single-trace qCFTs constrained by charge gap conditions, which limit the simple geometric states accessible to complex states. These equations are analogous to the Maldacena-Zhiboedov equations regarding global symmetry representations. While solving them completely remains out of reach, we can estimate the scaling dimension of the most complex state at each level. This estimation holds for any qCFT, including those where the simple geometric spectrum deviates from the expected $\sqrt{N}$ scaling. We also discuss extensions to higher-genus amplitude equations and the inclusion of chemical potentials. Finally, we draw parallels with the structure of quantum complexity in quantum gravity.

Including chemical potentials is essential for accurately modeling black holes that are not charge gap. We establish amplitude equations incorporating chemical potentials for charge-*one* qCFTs, a requirement given that charges can combine to produce larger potentials. These equations differ from the gap equations previously used for non-gapping systems, rendering the simple geometric spectrum ungapable. Additionally, we derive equations for amplitude derivatives, which are crucial for analyzing the orthogonality catastrophe. This analysis demonstrates that simple geometric states possess an effective dimension of ${\cal O}(N)$, a result consistent with findings from quantum gravity. We also model higher-genus amplitudes and apply our derivation of chemical potential equations to describe chemical potential dynamics in holographic complex systems. Furthermore, we develop a path integral description of chemical potential evolution that accounts for dislocation operator insertions.

These systems are significant because the $U(1)$ current fails to be conserved due to explicit symmetry-breaking terms in the action. We demonstrate that even the simplest scenario is nontrivial: while previously认为 that the resulting topological scalar charges would not be protected, we find that they are indeed preserved. Furthermore, we show that the spectra of small oscillations around kink solutions in interacting systems exhibit differences compared to decoupled cases. Specifically, new mixing modes emerge, and certain ghost modes previously present in the decoupled system disappear. Finally, we identify a previously unexplored system: a generalized moondrop model. This new system is characterized by interaction terms with inverse coefficients. We detail the excitation spectrum for the kink-soliton configuration in this model and observe that, contrary to the direct system, this model retains two ghost modes. Additionally, our findings reveal that both systems share two identical excited-state energies, despite possessing different excited-state wavefunctions. We conclude that both systems constitute novel models of interacting scalar fields with exciting properties and are valuable for various theoretical applications. Specifically, one of these systems could serve as an effective theoretical description for coupled interacting bosonic fields. Furthermore, both models may be potentially realizable within the framework of next-generation quantum computing. Finally, we propose that these systems could be of interest to researchers studying mathematical issues concerning topological charges in coupled field theories.

The Holographic Entropy Cone (HEC) comprises the collection of all possible entropy functions that maintain positivity and the strong subadditivity (SSA) inequality. This study investigates the additional constraints imposed on entropy functions by the specific structure of qubits and the fundamental limit of $N_f=2$ flavors in the context of field theory. By applying the framework of entropic sequences of positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) with rank $N$, we have identified the complete set of mathematical conditions that an entropy function must satisfy to reside within the Qubit-Entropy Cone (QEC). Since the SSA inequality is not the sole constraint on entropy functions of entropic sequences, we propose a conjecture that any function falling outside the HEC can also violate an inequality relative to elementary POVM elements of low dimensionality (specifically $N_f \le 2$). Consequently, we conjecture that the HEC and the QEC define identical sets of entropy functions, implying that any valid entropy function for a general quantum system can be expressed as a linear combination of entropies involving at most two levels of conditioning. This finding has significant implications for the dual field theory, suggesting that the entropy function of any general quantum system can be decomposed into at most five terms of the form $\sum_{i=1}^5 S(A_i|\{B_j\})$, where the sets $\{A_i\}$ and $\{B_j\}$ each contain no more than two elements. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the HEC and the convex hull of single-conditioning entropies generated by rank $N_f=2$ POVM elements, highlighting the distinct roles these cones play in characterizing entropy structures. Finally, we relate our results to the entropy cone of tensor products of qubit systems with arbitrary local dimensions. To support these findings, we include supplementary material detailing the derivation of the QEC and exploring the connection between entropic sequences and matrix product states. These methodologies are expected to be valuable for advancing our comprehension of entropy structures across various domains of quantum theory. Any valid entropy function for a general quantum system can be decomposed into short conditioning sets of size at most two. This paper supports the following hypothesis: all such functions can be represented as a linear combination of short conditioning entropies involving at most two levels of conditional entropy. This conclusion offers a novel perspective on the long-standing program of finding optimal approximations for quantum states and operations

We establish a priori estimates for the maximum norm of all solution derivatives based on the maximum norm of the initial data. This work represents a specific instance of a broader paper by H-O Kreiss and J. Lorenz, which extends their primary findings to higher dimensions. While our approach differs from theirs, it serves as a more straightforward example on a simpler system, facilitating easier generalization to other partial differential equation systems. Our methodology relies on an a priori maximum principle applicable to certain first-order linear PDEs with time-dependent coefficients. This principle demonstrates how the maximum norm of a function with smooth, smooth-periodic initial data evolves under the action of the one-parameter semigroup generated by the spatial differential operator in these equations. Consequently, this max-principle constitutes a key instrument for deriving uniform-in-time maximum norm estimates for solutions to other PDE systems. As a preliminary step, we examine the one-dimensional advection equation. Furthermore, we illustrate how to obtain similar a priori estimates for other partial differential operators by analyzing the one-dimensional heat equation and the second-order advection-diffusion equation. Many advanced time-frequency processing tasks rely on human analysis of these time-frequency distributions. Given the increasing volume of such data, there is a pressing need for more efficient processing techniques. This efficiency could be realized by enabling machines to interpret time-frequency distributions with greater comprehension. Such capability would revolutionize various fields, particularly in next-generation wireless communications. As time-frequency distributions are inherently intuitive and naturally suitable for machine learning, this paper examines specific machine learning techniques tailored for the analysis of time-frequency distributions.

In the domain of digital communications, particularly OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing) systems, two primary objectives are addressed: (1) novel machine learning-driven methods for OFDM signal detection, and (2) the use of machine learning to predict the evolution of time-frequency distributions in dynamic environments. A frequency-selective two-path channel model is employed to evaluate the performance of various machine learning-based detection schemes. Furthermore, particular attention is given to Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Deep Learning (DL) approaches. Simulation results indicate that machine learning can achieve environmental prediction with minimal error. Additionally, machine learning techniques, whether linear or nonlinear, demonstrate superior bit error rate (BER) performance and reduced computational complexity compared to traditional detection methods. Looking ahead, deploying machine learning for both time-frequency analysis and signal detection in digital communication systems holds promise for enhancing system reliability.

For practical implementation, specific learning algorithms are proposed for novel reception schemes. Several standard models are evaluated, with a particular focus on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). Performance is measured using Bit Error Rate (BER) for signal detection and prediction error metrics. Simulation findings confirm that the results are consistent and reliable. It is demonstrated that machine learning can deliver reliable communication under challenging channel conditions, such as high mobility and frequency selectivity. Furthermore, these methods achieve this with lower complexity than conventional reception techniques. Looking forward, the paper argues that machine learning techniques for time-frequency analysis in wireless systems will become standard in future research and standardization.

Standard modulation and coding schemes are expected to be adopted in upcoming wireless standards. This work examines the interactions between multiple observers and the measurement process itself. By analyzing the continuous tracking of quantum state evolution, we uncover new mechanisms where one observer can influence the decisions of subsequent observers. These phenomena arise from two distinct sources: first, dynamical effects where tracked evolution connects different quantum states; and second, informational effects, where recorded measurement data allow an observer to identify which state will be tracked. The study of binary measurement outcomes reveals that these control mechanisms are deeply rooted in information theory. These findings open new avenues for researching the foundational nature of observation in quantum systems and propose a quantum analog of the many-minds interpretation. Black Holes (MBHs), spanning from the largest system in Centaurus A to numerous common counterparts with stellar-mass donors in X-ray binaries. While some of these objects exhibit characteristics typical of Active Galactic Nuclei (NAGs), their exact nature—whether they are stellar-mass black holes that have grown accretion disks, a distinct class of stellar remnants, or truly intermediate-mass black holes (IBHs)—remains unresolved. A definitive solution requires robust formation models alongside observational constraints. This paper evaluates existing theories, noting that both engineered and natural formation pathways are permissive. Consequently, regardless of the underlying formation mechanism, future surveys and observational studies will likely confirm MBHs as the most massive known black holes in the universe. Consequently, they represent the only currently observable bridge between the populations of stellar-mass and intermediate-mass black holes. This thesis also explores the IBHs that may have formed during the Intermediate Generation (IG) phase of early galaxy evolution and their potential role as seeds for supermassive black holes. Finally, it addresses black holes found in dense stellar environments, such as globular clusters. Both engineered and natural formation scenarios can occur in these settings; however, natural scenarios are currently disfavored due to constraints imposed by multi-messenger observations of gravitational waves and neutron star mergers. This study concludes by examining the natural scenario within early galaxy evolution models that incorporate a bottom-up Supermassive Black Hole (SMBH) formation pathway. This approach represents a modern shift from conventional hypotheses, offering a fresh perspective on IBH origins. In this bottom-up model, IBHs arise as gravitational potential wells within dense gas clouds surrounding nascent black holes, fueled by gas accretion driven by the gravity of pre-existing stellar-mass black holes. This proposed mechanism ensures that only a minuscule fraction of the gas in a galaxy's IBH host is consumed to create a single SMBH. This novel framework suggests that galaxies capable of growing SMBHs through bottom-up processes are those with abundant dark matter halos that effectively concentrate gas toward the center. This model signifies a departure from standard IBH formation scenarios, marking a new era in our understanding of their origins. This study is the first to introduce a formal and robust model for IBH formation that avoids the excessive gas consumption rates prohibited by current observational data and evolutionary models. Specifically, we employ cross-recurrence plot analysis as a nonlinear technique to quantify multidimensional features describing the synchronization levels of in-sample Russian and US oil prices. These features are subsequently utilized to train two distinct forecasting algorithms applied to out-sample data: (i) statistical models, including ARIMA and machine learning techniques like Random Forests; and (ii) neural networks, namely Long Short Term Memory and Gradient Boosting. To address the significant challenges of ensuring reliability and avoiding overfitting in forecasting models that rely on nonlinear metrics and extensive data samples, we implement a novel method. This strategy involves utilizing one time series to compute cross-recurrence features for predicting the future synchronized behavior of the other. Our primary objective is demonstrating that this strategy, whether paired with statistical models or neural networks, yields results that are both robust and highly accurate. In this context, we show that cross-recurrence features processed through statistical methods can precisely forecast the synchronization states of two time series. Furthermore, we establish that a baseline model achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of approximately 0.15 is essential for evaluating synchronization prediction models. We conclude that statistical forecasting using cross-recurrence features significantly outperforms any of the three proposed neural network-based methods. Additionally, we introduce a new metric to measure the degree of series synchronization: the synchronization capacity (SCap), which assesses the synchronization level based on the density of first-nearest neighbors in cross-recurrence plots. The neural network Long Short Term Memory was selected as the sole reference model in this study. This reference was established by training on features extracted from oil prices and exchange rates for multiple country pairs involving Russia or the USA. Through forecasting experiments conducted on out-sample data, we prove that cross-recurrence features effectively predict the synchronization between two time series. Finally, we provide an analysis of forecasting results for Russian and American oil prices.

Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. Ultimately, this work demonstrates a pathway to amplify dynamic effects that are typically weak at ground state. We introduce a theory-compressed ML framework composed of a theory-compression layer (TCL) and a residual layer (ResL). The TCL integrates prior theoretical knowledge into the machine-learning process, while the ResL captures data characteristics that the TCL cannot infer from the theory alone. By combining explicit theoretical priors with residual learning, the model enhances both interpretability and predictive performance. Empirical results demonstrate that our model surpasses process-based theory models and other standard ML baselines (without prior theoretical knowledge) across three datasets: two from social sciences and one from physics. ### 1. Introduction

As theoretical knowledge across various scientific disciplines expands, there is an increasing demand to incorporate this expertise into machine learning to build more interpretable and reliable models. However, existing methods typically fall into two categories: either they utilize theory to generate models without incorporating them into the learning process (e.g., Inductive Logic Programming), or they attach theories as post-hoc explanations to black-box ML models (Li et al., 2020). Consequently, current approaches lack the ability to directly encode and use theoretical knowledge within the learned mapping itself.

Consider a scenario where a researcher possesses established theoretical knowledge about a data-generating process and aims to build a model that both predicts new data and demonstrates its underlying theory. A straightforward approach would be to construct a mapping strictly consistent with the theory. However, such a mapping often fails to generalize well to new data due to an over-reliance on theoretical knowledge. Conversely, a data-driven approach typically yields a mapping generalized to new data but functions as a black box, rendering theoretical knowledge irrelevant. A more promising solution lies in creating a theory-compressed mapping. As illustrated in Figure 1, this type of mapping operates in two stages: first, it finds a rough approximation consistent with the theory; second, it refines this approximation by residualizing it to fit the data more closely. Abstract: Traditional scaling laws in wireless communications focus on signal processing, multiple access, and beamforming, often overlooking network-layer issues like routing and scheduling. Assuming both information harvesting (IH) and information processing (IP) are necessary for users, and that users can sequentially execute these tasks over a multi-frame transmission cycle, we formulate a problem to maximize the average computation rate (ACR) of the delayed user. To address the joint optimization of PACs and TAR, a weighted difference of convex (WDC) function decomposition method is employed. moiré heterostructures have given rise to novel quantum phenomena, including the Mott insulator, moiré ferromagnet, and moiré twisted acoustic mode. In this note, we employ the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation to construct a theoretical framework for the emergence of relativistic fermions in monolayers of moiré materials. Specifically, when lattice deformations are present, electronic band mixing gives rise to a new type of purely non-relativistic relativistic fermionhood. This mechanism is generally applicable across various two-dimensional materials and offers an accessible pathway to generating relativistic fermions without dependence on spin-orbit coupling. Consequently, this phenomenon is expected to occur widely in experimentally prepared quantum systems within moiré materials. This mechanism also explains why the charge density in this system exhibits complete spin polarization with zero staggered magnetization, as reported in Science, Vol. 381, p. 66 (2023). This novel realization of relativistic fermions underscores the profound impact of lattice degrees of freedom on electronic properties and suggests a new avenue for engineering diverse quantum phases through strategic tuning of lattice deformations. More broadly, it expands the scope for generating relativistic particles in non-relativistic quantum systems outside the particle physics domain. Furthermore, it opens up new possibilities for generating and controlling particle-antiparticle pairs in quantum circuits using degree of freedom coupling and dynamic effects. Finally, we propose a speculative extension of this idea to suggest the potential for the quantum realization of relativistic relativity. Any solution to the Einstein equations, whether including or excluding a cosmological constant, adheres to the field equations defined by the Cotton tensor, indicating that the cosmological constant functions as an integration constant. In this theoretical framework, a vacuum state is characterized by the vanishing of the Cotton tensor instead of the Ricci tensor. Furthermore, an exact Schwarzschild-like solution for the metric is derived using the Cotton tensor, yielding a black hole solution that aligns with Einstein's field equations and matches recent findings from $f(R)$ gravity. Additionally, the cosmological Robertson-Walker models are examined under Cotton tensor gravity. For this scenario, the Cotton tensor provides coupled evolution equations for energy density and the Ricci scalar. Exact solutions are derived for a universe filled with a perfect fluid, where these solutions also satisfy the Einstein equations. Specifically, for a spatially flat Robertson-Walker universe governed by the Cotton tensor, a new conserved quantity emerges. This quantity allows the universe to contract toward the big bang as the scale factor approaches zero, a behavior consistent with standard gravity. Moreover, this solution gives rise to a novel class of scalar-tensor theories. Finally, it is established that the field equations regarding the connection can be recast as field equations for the connection of standard gravity, containing additional terms that represent this new class of scalar-tensor theories. Consequently, standard scalar-tensor theories can be obtained by imposing a specific constraint on the gravity solution.

In this study, we investigate two pathways to ideal engines: first, quantum systems functioning as hybrid machines capable of executing multiple useful tasks, and second, the reduction of fluctuations during these operations. For classical devices, the elimination of fluctuations requires high entropy production, as mandated by thermodynamic uncertainty relations. We extend these relations to multiterminal conductors operating as hybrid thermal machines. Our results demonstrate that quantum conductors surpass these classical limits, illustrated by a double quantum dot connected to normal metals and a reservoir that generates entangled Cooper pairs. This quantum reservoir has an reduced spectral function and lowers the device's total resistance. These findings open new avenues for high-performance energy applications, such as quantum sensors and low-dissipation electronics. Consequently, quantum engineering of electronic devices could facilitate the development of highly efficient devices that simultaneously achieve low resistance and minimal fluctuations.

Questionnaires remain a primary data collection method across fields like health, education, and market research. However, they present a significant hurdle when administered in person, as they are prone to errors from participants misinterpreting items or making input errors. Addressing this, we propose a new quantum-circuit-based method for encoding responses. This approach encodes answers into the phases of two-qubit gates, which can be realized as long-range couplings between qubits in superconducting circuits. Such gates can be implemented using existing microwave control techniques and fixed-frequency coupled qubits, similar to those used in quantum computers built by Google and others. We demonstrate that this scheme is robust against various sources of error, including circuit mismatches and gate imperfections. Furthermore, we show that the required circuit accuracy can be achieved through a sequence of only three gates. This enables a complete encoder-decoder protocol using current superconducting quantum computers and can be scaled to large systems with minimal overhead. Our findings support the near-term deployment of quantum-assisted data collection, which is expected to be more accessible and affordable than current options. This work was developed in collaboration with A. Ferrie and J. Lundeen.

### 1. Motivation

Lattice field theories serve as non-perturbative definitions for various quantum field theory models. By discretizing spacetime into a finite set of points, these theories transform complex continuum integral problems into manageable statistical sampling tasks. A central challenge in this domain is evaluating correlation functions, which depend heavily on efficiently capturing the theory's high-dimensional Boltzmann distribution. Traditional sampling algorithms like Monte Carlo Markov Chains (MCMC) often suffer from slow convergence and poor scaling with dimensionality. This note outlines a method to circumvent these limitations by applying recent advancements in normalizing flows.

However, the development and deployment of AI raise significant ethical concerns, including issues of fairness, transparency, and the risk of misuse. This paper argues for the creation of a new Code of Practice for Artificial Intelligence Ethics. Such a Code would serve as an essential framework guiding the design, creation, and application of AI, ensuring these technologies benefit society while mitigating harm. Ethical guidelines have historically been seen as advisable but ineffective in driving behavioral change. We contend that elevating AI ethics to a formal Code of Practice—granting it legal or quasi-legal status under relevant laws—would be necessary to make a substantial and positive impact on AI's future trajectory. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between a Code of Practice and existing AI ethics legislation, and provide a brief overview of current initiatives attempting to establish similar Codes, such as the one proposed by the AI Alliance. Finally, we distinguish between our suggestion for a Code of Practice and the dangerous idea of utilizing AI-driven totalitarianism to enforce ethical conformity. In conclusion, we outline the key elements that a Code of Practice for AI Ethics must contain. We do not start from scratch; established laws and guidelines already exist. What is required is a higher status to motivate stakeholders to act. A Code of Practice for AI Ethics offers a proactive and legally or quasi-legal approach to ethics, whereas current methods are often reactive. To achieve this elevated status, input from a diverse range of stakeholders is essential. Ultimately, we hope this article inspires further discussion and research on establishing a Code of Practice for AI Ethics.

Consequently, the development of perturbative methods rooted in general quantum theory has been driven primarily by the need to understand singularities within black hole spacetimes. This paper contributes to that broader endeavor by exploring a new exact solution that arises within a specific truncation of Minkowski supergravity. This truncation involves only the gravity multiplet, implying that all matter fields originate from general relativity. We name the resulting black holes ``graviphoton black holes'' because their hair consists of components from the U(1) graviphoton field. Although this U(1) symmetry is local, not global, its existence permits zeroth-order hair configurations. Subsequently, non-linear effects generate the hair, rendering these solutions as a distinct family of charged, rotating black holes. Although related to other black hole families, they represent an exact solution and are not merely perturbative.

A defining characteristic of these graviphoton black holes is that, within the region inside the event horizon, their behavior can be mapped to that of the AdS black hole within the bottom-up AdS/CFT correspondence. Specifically, the black hole's exterior corresponds to a conformal field theory where the onset of hair generation mirrors a conventional phase transition. Conversely, the black hole interior outside the event horizon represents the low-energy regime of this simulated matter. Furthermore, as in the gauge/gravity duality context, the scenario involves a dual quantum system with less order outside the horizon but greater order inside.

In the language of general relativity and black hole physics, this mapping to the gauge/gravity correspondence is non-trivial because we are dealing with a black hole interior rather than just the exterior. Existing models for dense suspensions that transition into jammed states typically rely on energy-based frameworks that fail to account for hydrodynamic interactions during collisions. We develop a new constitutive model that overcomes these limitations, representing suspensions as a network of colliding particles. This framework yields a material stress component that matches previous energy-based models and adds a spring-based hydrodynamic component that remains significant during jamming. By balancing these two stress types, we reproduce the experimentally observed crossover from shear thinning to shear thickening. Notably, increasing the stiffness of hydrodynamic springs causes the shear-thickened state to flow uniformly, recreating flow heterogeneities seen in experiments. We utilize this model to re-examine experimental findings, concluding that the typical non-monotonic evolution of relative viscosity with strain rate is a specific outcome of frictional versus hydrodynamic interactions. **Keywords:** Soft Matter, Rheology, Jammed systems.

Suspensions of dense particles at high volume fractions display suddenly amplified stresses that lead to a transition from fluid-like to jammed-like states. Traditional models describing this behavior typically decompose the total stress into osmotic and entropic contributions, successfully explaining results up to a critical state. However, recent findings indicate that suspensions can exhibit additional stresses dependent on hydrodynamic interactions during particle-particle collisions. We show that a simple model incorporating this hydrodynamic component can quantitatively reproduce stresses across all states, including those beyond the critical point. **Keywords:** Soft Condensed Matter, Soft Matter, Mechanics, Soft Matter, Particle Physics, Optical and Quantum Physics, Mathematics.

This finding strongly constrained the variation of fundamental constants, a concept central to many theories of quantum gravity which often predict a violation of Lorentz invariance. Specifically, this study investigates direct evidence for Lorentz violation within the framework of the standard model of quantum gravity (SMG), which utilizes an effective field theory approach. By analyzing the gravitational wave signal from GW170170M, we derived constraints on parameters defining Lorentz violation for three types of gravitational wave emitters: stellar-mass binary mergers, supermassive binary mergers, and compact objects orbiting supermassive black holes. Our results yield the following limits on parameter $i$: $|d_i| \lesssim 3\times10^{-3}$ (for a stellar-mass binary merger), $|d_i| \lesssim 2\times10^{-4}$ (for a supermassive binary merger), and $|d_i| \lesssim 4\times10^{-5}$ (for a compact object orbiting a supermassive black hole). Notably, the constraint derived from the supermassive binary merger is approximately an order of magnitude tighter than that from the stellar-mass event. This represents the first direct constraint on a concrete model of Lorentz violation in SMG, offering a novel method to explore quantum gravity via gravitational wave observations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these constraints can be supplemented with additional insights using data from pulsar timing arrays. The analysis assumes a De Sitter background for the universe. While our primary focus is on the simplest model featuring a dynamical Lorentz violation, our methodology remains applicable to more complex scenarios. This novel investigation into direct evidence for Lorentz violation enhances our understanding of quantum gravity and offers a promising new avenue for exploring it through gravitational wave observations. Additionally, our analysis reveals that our universe is highly symmetric. Any deviation from this symmetry would likely be captured by our models using a Lorentz-violating De Sitter background. This work aims to assist the gravitational wave community in conducting similar analyses of future events. Our analysis code is publicly accessible through a GitHub repository. This study introduces a novel Gated Recurrent Neural Network (GRNN) model that employs a top-down attention approach. The controller of this model is formulated as a control system with non-smooth dynamics. We analyze the model's stability using a Lyapunov function and construct the controller to ensure asymptotic stability. Since their introduction by Calabi in 1985, minimal surfaces with principal curvatures of constant sign have emerged as a significant area of research. Numerous studies have addressed the classification of these surfaces within specific classes. A general rotational surface $M$ in $E^4$ is defined by a parametrisation $\phi : (u,v) \mapsto u \cos v \, e_1 + u \sin v \, e_2 + w(u,v) \, e_3 + w(u,v) \, e_4$, where the curve $\gamma(u) = u \, e_1 + w(u)$ for $u > 0$ serves as the profile curve. Although $M$ is minimal under the standard metric, it has also been studied as a flat surface under an appropriate metric. This study focuses on the latter context: the classification of flat general rotational surfaces with a pointwise 1-type Gauss map under the suitable metric.

Some of the foundational works in this field include those by Alouidi and Sulaiman [1], A. B. Ahmad [2], and J. Li and S. Wu [3]. Specifically, Li and Wu [3] analyzed general rotational surfaces with a pointwise $m$-type Gauss map under the standard metric, deriving a classification of those with a pointwise 1-type Gauss map under additional assumptions. Additionally, Li and Wu [4] investigated general rotational surfaces with a pointwise 1-type Gauss map within the null setting in $E^4$.

Our work extends the findings of [3] by offering a more general classification of flat general rotational surfaces with a pointwise 1-type Gauss map under a suitable metric. While the derivation of the appropriate metric and the associated formulas are technical and do not represent the primary focus, the resulting findings are novel.

These labels describe the relationship between circular velocity ($v_c$) and galactico-centric radius ($r$") at small scales. In solid-body cases, $v_c$ initially rises linearly with $r$, whereas differential cases show a sublinear increase. Because circular velocity directly impacts the inferred baryon-independent gravitational mass of a galaxy's interior, understanding which template better represents real galaxies is vital for accurately interpreting the physics of baryon-free gravitation at small scales. We analyzed 1,181 galaxies from the SPOT sample, which features a bright absolute magnitude ($M_B < -18.65$) and a nearly circular inclination ($0.75 < q < 1$). Using deprojected 2.4$\mu$m imaging and dynamical modeling, we determined the $v_c(r)$ at small radii for each galaxy and compared the fit quality of the two templates. Our results indicate that the majority of galaxies in the sample follow the circular velocity template. Specifically, about 65% of galaxies have $r < 10$% of their effective radius and exhibit a good fit to the solid-body template, while 25% of galaxies with $r < 0.2$ effective radius fit the differential template well. These findings have important implications for how we interpret small-scale baryon-free gravity physics in galaxies.

To address these concerns, Federated Learning (FL) was introduced, enabling the training of ANNs across distributed datasets without centralizing the data. Despite its adoption, questions remain about whether Federated Neural Networks (FNNs) offer any performance advantage over Single Entity Networks (SNNs) trained on centralized data. In the AFL scenario, evil clients act maliciously by either (a) centralizing their local data and training an SNN independently, or (b) injecting malicious data while training an FNN. To evaluate robustness against these attacks, we propose two FNN architectures designed to detect centralized and malicious behaviors, respectively. Our results indicate that these architectures effectively guard against the proposed A-FL attacks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FNNs outperform SNNs when trained under the AFL scenario. Finally, we examine the impact of FNNs when clients adopt quasi-malicious behaviors, such as training an FNN while centralizing data without injecting malicious data. Our performance evaluation confirms that FNNs provide an advantage even in this quasi-malicious context.

Although personal health records have long been a primary target, recent shifts in technology and society—such as the proliferation of wearables and the generalization of privacy risks—have expanded the scope of accessible personal data. While numerous data collectors store information in proprietary, walled-garden environments, users increasingly own their own information via these devices and are actively managing it themselves.

To address this, we introduce InfoStore, a customizable privacy engine that allows users to manage privacy settings and access controls directly from their information dashboard. InfoStore begins by automatically discovering personal data across various devices and applications using unsupervised machine learning on user behavior patterns. It then presents data access requests to the user for evaluation and modification. The core of InfoStore is its rule-based access control system, which supports complex query expressions to define granular permissions. To ensure usability, the system is designed to be intuitive and easy to configure.

We implemented a prototype of InfoStore and assessed its feasibility and practical utility through two studies involving participants with differing levels of technical expertise. Our findings indicate that the system is not only feasible but also improves data accessibility management. Additionally, participants expressed confidence in the system's ability to enhance their privacy without causing undue complexity. Both qualitative and quantitative results highlight the system's effectiveness.

The evaluation process revealed important insights regarding user needs and preferences for privacy management. Qualitative analysis demonstrated that users have advanced access requirements that are difficult to satisfy with current storage solutions. Quantitative results further showed that the system can reduce data exposure while maintaining access levels satisfactory to both the data users and those requesting access. Ultimately, our results confirm that users desire control not only over who accesses their data and under what conditions, but also over the data itself, including its location and format. By unifying access control within a single dashboard, InfoStore responds to these needs and represents a significant step toward a privacy-aware future. Our code is available at https://github.com/ut-prives/infostore.

Key contributions of this work include:
1.  The introduction of InfoStore, a privacy management system where users can discover their information, interpret usage patterns through queries, and create access rules via natural language expressions.
2. Two studies featuring participants with varying technical skills that validate the approach of user-centric privacy management and confirm the system's effectiveness.
3. A dataset containing information from 38 participants that is automatically accessible for analysis.

Despite this, they are computationally intensive and lack closed-form mathematical forms, making them susceptible to adversarial attacks. Recent studies have explored attacking individual trees and ensemble models via input perturbations, yet these methods are too slow for defensive applications. A more viable approach involves targeting the model's training process through output perturbations. Building on this, adversarial retraining (or adversarial data augmentation) augments the training dataset with generated outputs to enhance model resilience. This paper adapts adversarial retraining to train tree ensembles and evaluates its performance under both static and dynamic data injection attacks. Compared to traditional adversarial defenses and data augmentation, the proposed method significantly improves robustness with minimal impact on accuracy in clean environments. Furthermore, the study extends this technique to defend tree ensembles against side-channel attacks by modeling the leakage function as a black box. Experimental evaluation confirms the method's effectiveness against both simulated and real-world power injection and power analysis attacks.

Various solutions, such as those based on multiparty computation and fully homomorphic encryption, have been proposed to encrypt these parameters during communication. Typically, encryption is handled individually by each party, which imposes a significant computational burden on local devices. To address this, we introduce a federated learning framework where trust is placed in a server responsible for generating all necessary encryption keys. This server utilizes a secret shared among all parties to securely produce these keys without revealing the shared secret. The resulting framework minimizes local computational costs while providing provable security against semi-honest parties and achieving communication efficiency. Evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that this scheme reduces both time and computational costs at each client. Furthermore, a theoretical model of the scheme's security complexity is developed and validated through experiments. Results indicate that high model accuracy can be maintained even with a relatively low bit-security complexity. Specifically, achieving a test accuracy of approximately 90% requires a bit-security complexity of around 60.

However, the growing computational capabilities and connectivity of these systems expose vulnerable, resource-constrained targets to diverse malicious attacks. At the hardware level, most traditional access methods rely on physical manipulation, which limits their utility for remote attackers. Androgen is an attack vector discovered in Real-Time Text (RTT) protocols commonly used in embedded systems, enabling attackers to remotely extract plaintext secrets and execute arbitrary code. This paper introduces and demonstrates the androgen attack, which bypasses defense mechanisms designed to protect sensitive data and systems on connected embedded devices. Specifically, androgen can infiltrate and compromise a wide range of embedded systems, including Android smartphones, IoT devices, and automotive systems. Furthermore, the research team has released all reproduction materials in the form of an open-source package. Beyond facilitating the demonstration and analysis of the androgen attack, this package also serves as a teaching aid for exploring hardware-hardware co-attacks. Finally, androgen is intended to prompt the broader research community to reconsider potential interactions between hardware attack surfaces and covert physical channels on linked embedded systems. Feedback from users and researchers is welcomed and can be submitted via issue or pull request.

This paper focuses on applying compressed learning to integer and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), which is fundamental in operations research and can be viewed as statistical models constrained by integrality and linearly defined feasible regions. We introduce a novel algorithm that samples information from solving incomplete resolution traces of MILP models to train models capable of accurately predicting key solving metrics, including CPU time, node counts, and cut frequencies. By leveraging these predictive models, we create algorithms designed to distill solving traces into optimal summaries that maximize information retention within the smallest possible space. Our findings demonstrate that these compact summaries can be utilized to accelerate various MILP solvers. Specifically, we show their utility in speeding up node sampling for AI-based modeling, reducing the size of solving traces for clustering and compression, and increasing the solve rate for CPU time-limited competitions. We further present applications in solving AI modeling and the preparation of traces for submitting to compression competitions. Notably, our results achieve performance gains of up to 12x in AI modeling and 6x in compression competition submissions. Beyond these specific applications, our work advances the theory of solving model compression by connecting MILP solving processes to established concepts in compressed learning. This research demonstrates the broader significance of compressed learning in solving and opens new avenues for future investigation. On a one-dimensional ring with a high emigration rate and low immigration rate, we observe that a single island of the majority opinion forms and circulates around the domain. This traveling island compresses the remaining agents in two clusters on either side and exerts a strong anti-polarization effect. This "compressing voter model" behaves similarly to the polarization-free voter model. Conversely, on a complete graph with a low emigration rate and high immigration rate, a lone emigrant can gradually transform the entire domain's opinion, serving as a polarization inhibitor. These findings suggest that both polarizing and non-polarizing mechanisms can achieve similar goals: introducing immigration acts as a pure noise source that prevents opinion patterns from getting trapped in metastable states. Furthermore, emigration functions as a time-dependent noise source that dynamically alters the system's effective connectivity. In both scenarios, the intensity of emigration must be sufficiently low, whereas the threshold for minimal immigration intensity is ambiguous. This work aims to assist in designing effective strategies for mitigating the negative societal impacts of polarization.

We introduce a mixed-model approach that integrates mixed-signal simulation for digital electronics and system-level simulation for detached digital components. The method synchronizes the two models through a common timestamp derived from a logical oscillator. Digital electronics are simulated using standard mixed-signal simulation, while detached digital components are simulated at the system level with signal resolution matched to the main simulation. The paper presents two implementation variants: one employing mixed-signal simulation with digitization via an oscillator-based digitizer, and another utilizing event-based digital simulation with a resolution-based digitizer. Digitization in both variants is realized by comparing a continuous-analog netwaveform against a ramp-generated digitizing oscillator. We present experimental results from simulations of scenarios involving digital electronics and detached digital components operating across various clock frequencies and relative phase offsets. In experiments using the 2PD2D AVI method, simulations were conducted for systems characterized by small, medium, and large separation distances between digital electronics and digital components. For each system type, simulation times were recorded for both coupled and uncoupled simulations. Results indicate that for the AVI method, the time required to simulate the coupled system does not exceed that of the uncoupled system by more than 15 to 25 percent. This finding suggests mixed-model simulation is efficient for designing DED2D systems. Experimental data also supports the efficiency of the AVI implementation using the digitizing-oscillator approach. Additionally, we examined the impact of reducing simulation resolution in detached digital components on Synchronization Time (SYN), a key performance metric. In this analysis, SYN represents the duration needed for simulated processes in the main simulation to align their activities based on a shared logical timestamp. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method for estimating simulation time with the AVI approach is effective for calculating the time required to simulate the SYN process. These conclusions are drawn from experiments using modern computational methods and tools. The work confirms that the mixed-model method is viable for simulating DED2D systems, with the AVI approach enabling the simulation of large-scale objects within reasonable timeframes. Both event-based and black-box approaches are applicable to this system type. As an example of a large DED2D system, we considered a missile defense system comprising approximately 3000 digital entities, including analog electronics, digital electronics, detaching digital components, and their software. We demonstrate that for any such sentence $\Phi$, there exists a corresponding sentence $\Phi'$ utilizing the same variable count but relying solely on one symmetric binary relation, such that the spectrum of $\Phi'$ is linearly proportional to that of $\Phi$. Furthermore, all models of $\Phi'$ are bipartite graphs. Finally, we analyze spectra of sentences with three variables defined over undirected graphs with edges possessing non-negative weights. We prove that for any sentence $\Phi$ applicable to weighted graphs, there is a corresponding sentence $\Phi'$ on unweighted bipartite graphs such that the spectrum of $\Phi'$ is strictly proportional to that of $\Phi$, with a proportionality constant of 1/3. Additionally, we show that one partition of the bipartite graph's parts can be interpreted as representing a specific subset of the original model's elements. These findings rely on a novel technique involving the "doubling" of models, which may hold broader significance. As a corollary, we find that investigating whether the spectrum class is closed under complementation reduces to analyzing sentences with three variables whose models are undirected graphs where each vertex has a degree of at most 2. This scenario effectively limits the vertices to an independent set. The cases where a vertex has a degree of 2 can be addressed by analyzing sentences with four variables. Thus, the core challenge lies in the case where every vertex has a degree of at most 1, which corresponds to sentences with three variables and models that are matchings.

To accomplish this, we outline a framework comprising three sequential steps applicable to any physical system. First, we specify the information carriers within the system and define a universal manipulation protocol for these carriers. Second, we demonstrate that this protocol accurately models a universal deterministic Turing machine (Turing-machine-computability) or stochastic universal quantum mechanics (quantum-computability), thereby ensuring we do not over-generalize. This result stems from the existence of an explicit reduction between the two computability types.
