This study derives a semi-analytical formula for the dynamical density-density linear response function (correlation function, LCDF) of noninteracting massless Dirac fermions at finite temperature and DC field within the $q \rightarrow 0$ limit. This result is derived using the thermodynamic relation linking the LCDF to the spectral function. Crucially, this formula incorporates effects from DC fields and thermal populations of low-energy quasiparticles, elements absent in prior research. We demonstrate that these specific effects become significant when $\omega_F > |E_g/2 + \mu|$, where $\omega_F$ represents the Fermi energy, $\mu$ is the DC field, and $E_g$ denotes the doping-induced gap. Additionally, we calculate the weight of these effects across the entire frequency spectrum and analyze how they vary with DC field and temperature. Since the derived formula relies solely on single-particle properties, it lacks any leading-order interaction effects; therefore, these effects can be incorporated via standard many-body techniques like the random phase approximation. Finally, we apply our formula to examine how these quasiparticle population effects influence the soft-mode behavior and stability of the Dirac fermion system. Our findings indicate that DC field and temperature stabilize the otherwise unstable soft mode by increasing its wave vector, a result that aligns with established literature.

to adversarial examples, which can deceive even structurally distinct models. This paper introduces a novel class of adversarial inputs known as "cyclic" adversarial images. These images are valid natural photographs of objects or scenes that can be easily identified by human observers. However, when presented to certain DNN architectures, they are misclassified. Uniquely, these adversarial examples function only in a target-specific manner: misclassification occurs exclusively against a pre-defined target class. We provide an extensive analysis of the characteristics of these adversarial samples and establish a proven lower bound demonstrating their target-specific nature. Furthermore, we develop effective attack methods capable of generating high success-rate cyclic adversarial images even with limited training data. Finally, we investigate various defense strategies and evaluate their effectiveness against this previously unstudied threat. Since cyclic adversarial images offer a new dimension to attacks, we argue they pose a serious real-world risk, particularly for applications involving image authentication and privacy. Consequently, we recommend that DNN robustness evaluations and defense implementations should incorporate cyclic adversarial examples.

A promising solution involves developing a new type of event-based event-driven spiking neural network (SNN) sensor that directly intently processes event streams, serving as an event-driven interface between an event-driven SNN and an event-driven deep neural network. This approach minimally reduces unnecessary event computation and maximizes energy efficiency when interacting with dynamic environments. To my knowledge, no research has yet explored applying event-driven SNNs to event-stream processing. This study introduces MEME, an event-driven Event-stream Spiking Neural Network consisting of two layers: an event-based Convolutional Neural Network and an event-based Fully Connected Neural Network. MEME was trained on synthetic data to detect events within an event stream and was subsequently evaluated on two real-world datasets: TUD-Mobility and SURREY event streams. Specifically, MEME attempts to identify events involving moving objects (event detection) and analyze the internal states and behaviors of mobile entities (event introspection). The performance results indicate that MEME effectively identifies events, performs self-introspection, and generalizes well on event streams. Furthermore, the system achieves significant energy savings by generating fewer events when interacting with dynamic environments compared to its performance on static scenes. The source code for MEME can be accessed at https://github.com/meme-snn/meme. The efficacy of this event-driven Event-stream SNN for event detection and mobile object introspection establishes a new foundation for event-stream processing using event-stream SNNs. This research opens up new possibilities for energy-efficient, real-time event-stream sensing and event-processing systems. The results are thus significant for dynamic object tracking, as well as for a broad range of event-driven event-stream event-processing applications.

These events exhibit intensity fluctuations over microseconds and are characterized by right-circular (R) or left-circular (L) polarization. Although the physical mechanisms behind this polarization and the evolution of the magnetic field domain driving the storm have garnered significant interest, recent observations have offered only a fragmentary view. This study presents an unusually complete set of observations of a R-type noise storm, incorporating ground-based radio data and X-ray/OUV imaging from the Extreme Solar Sounder Imager (ESSSI) and Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACT) array. During the event, ESSOI and IACT detected hard X-ray bremsstrahlung at wavelengths of ~10–50 pg, driven by electrons accelerated in active region loops. We identified both compact and extended emission sources correlated with the noise storm; the latter suggests particle precipitation within a magnetized plasma sheet. While radio emission was consistently R-polarized, a fraction of IACT data revealed circularity levels fluctuating between ~0.1 and ~0.4, with no evidence of depolarization. We propose that high electron beam energies caused by micro- or mini-flares result in reduced circularity. Furthermore, we suggest that the magnetic field responsible for the noise storm underwent complete reconfiguration via the contraction of a magnetic flux rope. This study marks the first application of ESSOI and IACT instrumentation to investigate R-type solar radio noise. A future focus will be a comparative analysis of R- and L-type polarization across multiple noises events. This methodology represents a cutting-edge approach for exploring solar magnetic fields. Both ESSOI and IACT are operational and accessible for data collection; we intend to apply this methodology to additional noises events in upcoming publications. Our findings indicate that analyzing noises events using this ground-based and near-space instrumentation can yield insights into solar magnetic fields at an unprecedented level. The noises source is linked to magnetic energy release, and its study may aid in predicting strong solar flares and CMEs that impact the near-Earth environment. Keywords: Solar magnetic fields; Solar noises; Solar particles; Solar Flares; Solar flares prediction.

**1. Introduction** The MOT is one of the most widely used devices in atomic physics for confining and cooling atoms to temperatures as low as millikelvins. These ultra-cold atoms find applications in atomic clocks, Bragg diffraction, quantum information, and the study of quantum gases. Despite its importance, the standard theoretical framework for MOTs, which relies on rate equations, fails to offer essential details necessary for high-density applications. Recent advancements in simulation tools, supported by rising computational power, enable the analysis of atomic systems through the distribution function. However, existing advanced techniques for calculating the distribution function within a MOT remain incomplete. In contrast, the method described here provides exact solutions to the Fokker-Planck equation for a MOT. **Figure 1. This work introduces a novel class of line waves formed by combining mirror symmetry with spatial inversion, both featuring a phase variation of $\pi$ across a $2D$ unit cell. The resulting line wave modes exhibit unique properties, including polarization independence and the ability to propagate without a phase shift progression, thereby enabling highly efficient energy confinement and control. As proof of concept, we designed class $C_{6h}$ line waveguides using graphene metasurfaces that support multiple polarization-independent line wave modes. These modes demonstrate extraordinary propagation within extremely narrow transverse confines of approximately $0.02\mu m$ at terahertz frequencies, providing an innovative platform for ultra-compact passive and active spatial control of light. Additionally, we demonstrated that introducing a linear phase variation to the metasurface generates twisted beam modes with controllable topological charges. We further proposed a second harmonic generation example, offering an efficient method to achieve this phenomenon in line waveguides. Finally, we proposed an analogy between our class of line waves and topological surface states found in class $D$ fermionic systems. This research represents the first demonstration of polarization-independent, exceptionally confined line waves under class $C_{6h}$ metasurfaces and introduces a new framework for line wave guidance, offering diverse applications in active and nonlinear nanophotonics, as well as vector and topological beam propagation.

Temperature-dependent susceptibility measurements indicate that the ground state of this system is accessible at approximately 160 K. Below 140 K, Ru3+ ions (spin 5/2) adopt a collinear antiferromagnetic order. Notably, the easy-axis magnetic anisotropy of 7f-Tb (7f-J=6) necessitates field-cooling to achieve long-range magnetic order. Conversely, in Nd3RuO7, 4d-Ru ions exhibit antiferromagnetic ordering with a propagation vector of k = 1/2 along the b-axis at a slightly lower temperature of 128 K. Above 140 K, long-range magnetic order emerges in 4f-Nd ions, characterized by an easy-plane anisotropy configuration. Ronney et al. proposed a theoretical framework for 7f-Tb collinear ordering involving alternating-bond spin-1 chains. Consistent with this proposal, we observed that long-range magnetic order in Tb3RuO7 is established only under field-cooling within specific external magnetic field orientations. Additionally, we detected local magnetic ordering of 7f-Tb spins near the Ru long-range ordering temperature. The ordering temperatures of the 4f-Nd and 4d-Ru interactions in Nd3RuO7 are governed by intermetal exchange interactions mediated by overlapping 4f and 4d electron orbitals, as well as the relative strength of Russell-Saunders exchange coupling within each ion type. Furthermore, we investigated the influence of transition-metal valence on the magnetic properties of 4d-Ru ions. While both compounds share similar structural features, Nd3RuO7 contains more overlapping 4d-electron orbitals compared to Tb3RuO7. This difference in electronic structure explains why the magnetic anisotropy of 4d-Ru in Nd3RuO7 deviates from the collinear order predicted by the Arbuzov-Khomskii effect for alternating-bond spin-1 chains. These findings clarify the mechanisms responsible for the magnetic behaviors observed in these two compounds. This research was conducted at the J-PARC Center.

By utilizing a simplified body model that treats segments as rigid rods, the method calculates gait parameters through the evaluation of degree of freedom (DOF) coordinates. To manage computational efficiency and data complexity, a dimensionality reduction technique is applied to the resulting feature vectors. While principal component analysis has been a standard approach, this study evaluates it against two machine learning-based alternatives: autoencoders and ts2vec. The analysis utilizes 15 gait features, including those related to speed, alongside DOF values. DOF are selected for their robustness to transformations such as translation, rotation, and scaling. The efficacy of each analysis is determined by training classifiers to identify abnormalities based on specific gait features. Using a dataset comprising healthy and "abnormal" (simulated) gaits, classifiers trained with DOF-based vectors achieved the highest F1 score of 0.82 with a logistic regression classifier. Switching to machine learning-derived feature vectors improved performance, yielding an F1 score of 0.85 using an autoencoder and 0.86 using ts2vec. These findings are corroborated by the lower classification error rates. Furthermore, these learning-based vectors demonstrated superior performance in distinguishing between specific types of abnormalities. The paper also examines the anisotropy of these vectors to guide future feature extraction strategies. Overall, the study illustrates a highly efficient method for automatic gait analysis that requires only a small number of skeletal joints. These highly discriminative and compact feature vectors hold significant potential for applications in anomaly detection and classification. BigScience's 1.3-billion-parameter pretrained multilingual model, which initially supports 13 languages. This study examines the elements influencing the model's language adaptability and analyzes the trade-offs between computational expenses and anticipated performance. Our results indicate that language adaptation can be achieved at low cost—using only task-specific examples—without necessitating a larger parameter count. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the language adaptability of small multilingual models can be quantified through minimal computational investment. have revealed jet cores in the millimeter wavelength band for the microquasar GRS 1915+105, confirming their existence in accreting binary systems for the first time. Historically regarded as the most intrinsically powerful stellar-mass mass-ejecting structures ever observed, these jets may exhibit even greater power at radio frequencies. Our latest mm-core measurements indicate a re-brightening phase during 2013, which aligns with the system's most active period across all wavelengths. During this interval, the jet's dynamical scales can be measured with mm precision. Furthermore, this data represents the most extensive and precise collection of mm-wave time-series observations from an active stellar-mass black hole to date, enabling the measurement of jet properties at micro-dynamical levels. Future datasets are anticipated to facilitate the direct confirmation of jet velocities via Doppler measurements and will allow for the constraint of the jet's magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) nature through core spectral indices. Additionally, these observations will help determine the size of the magnetosphere surrounding the black hole. The interaction between the mm jet and this region is governed by the same fundamental physical mechanisms that regulate supermassive jet activity on kiloparsec scales. Both systems are fundamentally defined by the magnetosphere size relative to the overall scale; thus, these mm-wave data may help resolve the debated question of why some systems produce jets while others do not. Our findings will be published in the special issue of Astro-physics in 2014, commemorating 20 years of monitoring GRS 1915+105.

Although many organizations attempt to gauge opinion on Twitter, they often rely on manual sampling or rely entirely on available sentiment analysis APIs. the Coulomb interaction influences electronic phases and properties within the square lattice half-filled Hubbard model. We introduce a non-local constraint that restricts the inter-orbital Coulomb repulsion $U'$ to short ranges, then analyze the resulting effects as this restriction tightens. Our results indicate that in the limit of half-filling and vanishing $U'$, the low-energy two-dimensional ($d=2$) system's physics is governed by a Fermi surface with a square-like shape. As the range restriction on $U'$ is relaxed, we observe the emergence of charge ordering and antiferromagnetic ordering, alongside significant modifications to the magnetic spin correlation length and spectral functions. These variations are consistently interpreted using Landau and strong-coupling theories, respectively. Consequently, our findings suggest that limiting the Coulomb interaction to short ranges generates ordered phases and alters electronic properties in a manner comparable to enhancing the effective Coulomb interaction $U$ in conventional Hubbard models. These observations have broad implications for understanding correlated electronic systems where Coulomb interaction ranges are shortened, either intrinsically or extrinsically.

The Noisy Student (NS) training technique addresses this by leveraging high-confidence labels from larger models to create extensive training datasets for smaller networks. Although this model distillation strategy enhances network efficiency, it depends on a more accurate student model. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the use of larger, slower master models during the NS process, allowing smaller noisy student models to train in parallel. Additionally, on edge devices constrained by computational resources, generating large volumes of student data may be impractical. To resolve these issues, we propose a novel method called the Quiet Student (QS) approach, wherein small models train independently on their own limited data. Experimental results on MAX76000 FPGA-based edge devices show that our QS method requires less computing efficiency and approximately 60% less effective training data than traditional NS. Specifically, training an YOLOv3-based object detector on the CC3200 development board demonstrates that our proposed method produces more efficient networks capable of accurate object detection on limited hardware. We have open-sourced the source code at https://github.com/SMARTEdges/SmartsObjectDetector. This work will be presented at EMBC 2022.

To address this lack of clarity, we introduced a meta-model of NFPA 99 in a prior work, formalizing key concepts and their relationships in a manner that is user-friendly and accessible. In this paper, we take the standard one step further by constructing a meta-meta-model of the meta-model. This meta-meta-model reveals the structural "shape" of NFPA 99, illustrating how the standard is organized and how its content is arranged, without necessarily explaining the content itself. Under equilibrium conditions defined by room temperature and a dc current of 0.1 A/cm$^2$, the equilibrium carrier density is $n_{eq} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$ and the carrier scattering time is $\tau_{eq} \approx 150$ ps. Non-equilibrium states are achieved by delivering short current pulses with a peak density of $j_p = 10^7$ A/cm$^2$ and duration $t_p$ ranging from 2 to 10 ns, which momentarily increase the carrier density by $\delta n \approx -4 n_{eq}$. Following each pulse, the system relaxes to its initial state. We analyze the recovery dynamics of the modified parameters—$\delta n$, $\tau$, and the room-temperature dc Hall resistivity change—immediately after the pulses. The observed non-equilibrium states are best explained by the plasmonic heating of carriers via non-equilibrium carrier-plasmon decay. This model accounts for the initial fast decay with a time constant of $\delta \tau = 10$ ps, followed by a slower decay characterized by a time constant $|t_p/t_{eq}|^{-1}$. Furthermore, we discuss how this mechanism relates to the "cold plasmon" model previously suggested for superconducting nanowires. Background: Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely recognized for its effectiveness in solving sequential decision-making tasks, yet it often fails to generalize well to tasks or environments not encountered during training. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed various approaches, including utilizing multiple similar tasks, assuming unmodeled dynamics, employing generative models, and employing coreference attention mechanisms. These methods aim to enhance RL representation power, enable efficient generation of simulated tasks, or facilitate reasoning about them. Our proposed framework differs by focusing on dynamic weighting of signal types and on-policy learning to simultaneously address both challenges. Results: We find that only one type of signal should be assigned a positive weight at a time, specifically when that signal is informative. Using this framework, we successfully learned a task using a sparse uninformative signal that would be impossible to learn with sparse informative signals of equivalent density. More broadly, we show that this framework enables agents to learn tasks that do not transfer to new environments, a capability that is unattainable with other signal combinations. Finally, we extend this approach to a large-scale Atari domain, achieving superior results on tasks that were previously unsolvable or unscored using other signals. Conclusion: We conclude that our framework provides a theoretically and practically effective solution for a broad range of problems, particularly those involving sparse uninformative rewards. This approach can be modeled as performing Bayesian inference over an unknown reward function within a specific prior distribution. By adjusting the parameters of this prior, one can control the relative likelihood of different signal types and their conditional expectations given those signals. This framework also has applications in coreference attention and improved policy evaluation. Code: https://github.com/alexeiap/apexlearn.

a causal parameter typically involves a two-step process: first, modeling the treatment and outcome while accounting for potential confounders; second, utilizing these predictions in ATE estimators like the Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) method. In a setting where an adversary can arbitrarily alter an $\epsilon$ fraction of the state-action-reward-next-state tuples in a batch dataset, the learner's objective is to derive a near-optimal policy from the corrupted data. We first establish that for linear MDPs of dimension $d$, a worst-case optimality gap of $\Omega(d\epsilon)$ is inevitable, even when corruption is limited to the reward component alone. Consequently, we argue that focusing on linear MDPs and pursuing high sample efficiency algorithms are critical avenues for improvement. To advance this goal, we introduce nearly optimal algorithms across various model classes: linear bandits and linear quadratic control. For linearity assumptions, we consider $\epsilon$ and $p$-corruption models; specifically, data is $\epsilon$-corrupted if at least an $\epsilon$ fraction of tuples differ, or $\p$-corrupted if at least an $\epsilon$ fraction of tuple elements differ. Our primary contributions are as follows:

*   **Efficient Policy Evaluation.** We present a provably efficient algorithm for linear control problems under $\epsilon$ and $p$ corruption. This method recovers the standard optimal value function (up to small additive errors) in both linear quadratic and general MDP contexts, requiring only $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^2})$ and $\tilde{O}(\frac{d}{(1-\gamma)^3})$ samples, respectively. Notably, these sample complexities are independent of the corruption fraction.

*   **Adversarially Robust Policy Improvement.** We propose the first black-box, efficient policy evaluation and improvement algorithms for linear MDPs under corruption. Specifically, we develop an online algorithm with $d$-optimal robustness guarantees that necessitates $\tilde{O}(\frac{d^3}{(1-\gamma)^4})$ samples and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\frac{d}{(1-\gamma)^5}})$ episodes, again sample-complexity-wise optimal vs. prior work.

*   **First Adaptively Robust Off-Policy Learning.** We present the first adaptation algorithm with strong robustness guarantees. This approach achieves an optimality gap of $\tilde{O}(\epsilon (\log(d/\delta)+B))$ using $\tilde{O}(\text{cond}^2(d))$ samples and $\tilde{O(\text{cond}(d))}$ episodes

Leveraging internal energy sources to drive unidirectional rotation at the molecular scale represents a fundamental challenge in nanotechnology. This study demonstrates the design and simulation of a molecular assembly incorporating a molecular motor that can self-propel and push an attached cargo. The system comprises two components: a three-legged, source-powered motor (five atoms) and a square-shaped cargo (five atoms). We analyzed their dynamics by solving the equations of motion for their atomic spheres using the time-marching method across various temperature conditions. Our modeling of the shape-dependent interaction between the motor and cargo aligns with the common assumption of an retentive surface between adjacent organic molecules. The simulation results indicate that a motor operating at the leading edge of the cargo induces rotation of the entire assembly in one direction, meaning the motor both propels the system and locks the motor and cargo together. We further show that the angular velocity of the assembly depends on the mass distribution between the motor and the cargo. Furthermore, the system's rotational ability is significantly influenced by the spatial arrangement of the motor's legs; specifically, a motor with an odd number of legs exhibits higher angular velocities compared to those with an even number. Finally, the angular velocity is also affected by the number of atoms in the cargo. These numerical simulations of a molecular motor pushing a cargo hold significant potential for transporting objects in chemical environments. Additionally, this work contributes to the development of source-powered organic machines capable of performing tasks other than object transport.

## 1. Introduction

Many natural systems comprise interacting entities that exhibit complex collective behaviors, a phenomenon well-documented in ecological models involving animal populations (e.g., prey-predator systems) and chemical models displaying non-linear kinetics. This study investigates general conditions under which ecological systems sustain complex states of matter characterized by spatially heterogeneous patterns. These patterns represent a specific type of self-organization, where long-range forces or many-body interactions drive the spontaneous emergence of spatially structured states in closed systems.

To date, analytical and numerical work on this topic has primarily utilized mathematical models describing two species with direct pairwise (binary) interactions. However, in recent years, research has turned toward the challenge of modeling biological and chemical processes involving group interactions. Consequently, new classes of models have been developed to capture phenomena driven by collective behavior, allowing for the representation of interactions between animal groups of varying sizes. Similarly, chemical reactions occurring in confined spaces can exhibit many-body kinetics, as seen in ozone decomposition. It is therefore crucial to develop theoretical frameworks capable of representing such higher-order interactions.

Following the analysis of specific models, this paper presents a general approach to analyzing systems of reaction-diffusion equations on a d-dimensional domain $\Omega$, incorporating terms for many-body interactions. This scheme is applied to analyze ecological systems based on graph interactions. The study addresses stability issues, focusing on scenarios where mean field interactions produce effective forces acting on system populations. The resulting analysis yields new mathematical insights into pattern formation dynamics.

Recent molecular dynamics (MD) studies have modeled the formation of $\alpha$-matter using two distinct $ \alpha$-liquid drops: an inner sphere drop and an outer shell drop. This study applies the density functional method (DFM) to investigate the ground-state structure of seven $\alpha$-particles organized in this double-layer $\alpha$-liquid drop configuration.

**Method:** The study employs a new tabulated functional from the SLy family of symmetric nuclear matter, modified to accurately represent nuclear matter composed exclusively of $\alpha$-particles. This functional is well-suited for calculating the equation of state (EOS) relevant to the equation governing the double-layer $\alpha$-liquid drop structure.

**Results:** The calculated ground state energy of the seven $\alpha$-particle system is 55.52 MeV, which aligns closely with experimental data at 55.84 MeV. The ground state root mean square charge radius is calculated as 3.33 fm, compared to the experimental value of 3.30 fm. Furthermore, the excitation energy for the 0$^+$ state at 2.13 MeV matches the experimental 2.14 MeV.

**Conclusions:** The results indicate that the properties of the $\alpha$-liquid drop structure are well-reproduced in the ground state of the seven $\alpha$-particle system. Additionally, the energy spectrum of the 7 $\alpha$-particle system is well-described. Consequently, it is concluded that the correlation between the two $\alpha$-liquid drops (inner and outer shell) is essential for explaining both the energy spectrum and the formation mechanism of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$. Finally, an excited state with $T=1$ at 18.15 MeV in the 7 $\alpha$-particle system is predicted.

in Quantum Mechanics (QM). We review several prominent arguments found in the literature that justify the necessity of complex formalism and offer additional insights by introducing alternative perspectives. Our goal is to reinforce the challenging pedagogical task of explaining why Quantum Mechanics requires complex numbers. In particular, we present a quantum system model with a formal structure analogous to standard formalism but utilizing the framework of quaternions. Next, we clarify that the equivalence between quaternion-based and complex-based quantum systems stems from the fact that the maximal subalgebras of a quaternion algebra are isomorphic to complex algebras. Finally, we describe a complex-based quantum system using an algebra constructed from matrices with entries in the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$, where $p$ is a prime number; this system is equivalent to a quaternionic quantum system with a larger parameter value. This demonstrates that complex numbers are not inherently required to define a quantum system and can even be replaced by rational or integer numbers. Since no existing proposal exists that demonstrates a physical necessity for complex numbers in physics, we suggest that one of the primary challenges for foundational research is developing an explicitly real formulation of quantum theory and a corresponding experimentally feasible model system to illustrate it. Such a challenge could potentially find a solution by extending our final example to a continuous field $\mathbb{F}_q$ where $q$ is an power of a prime number. While this does not imply that complex numbers are unphysical, it suggests that key foundational questions in Quantum Mechanics are those driving quantum theory research most closely aligned with key questions in mathematics.

This paper presents Indecision Trees, an enhanced version of Decision Trees capable of learning and performing inference under conditions of uncertainty. Furthermore, they generate a robust distribution of potential labels and can be decomposed into logical arguments suitable for integration with other reasoning systems. We have implemented Indecision Trees in Prolog, but the method is also compatible with other languages, facilitating easy deployment and hybrid system construction. While Decision Trees are widely used and effective for classification, Indecision Trees offer greater flexibility and can interface with other reasoning systems. Their use of many-valued logic naturally handles uncertainty, while the ability to represent distributions of labels makes them suitable for interfacing with Bayesian reasoning. Their Prolog implementation ensures learnability and fast inference, with a simplified verbal description available for non-technical users. We believe Indecision Trees complement other tree-based methods like Random Forests and Support Vector Machines. They are particularly valuable where Bayesian or logical reasoning is already present, enabling seamless integration without performance loss. This includes scenarios involving logical deduction, such as diagnosing faults from observations using rule-based systems, or quantifying uncertainty like calculating the likelihood that a patient has a specific disease based on their symptoms.

However, in practice, CPs often refuse to pay for content distribution, citing the difficulty of identifying which specific users are accessing their content and the associated privacy concerns. This paper introduces a new stateless Cryptographic Distributed Ledger (CDL) that eliminates the privacy issues inherent in current tracking methods. We demonstrate, through a comprehensive privacy analysis, that our system enables a nearly equal cost-sharing split between CPs and ISPs without revealing any private information from either party.

Our contributions are threefold:
- We present a new CDL-based Cryptographic Distributed Ledger (CDL) distributed across isomorphic graphs to ensure high content availability.
- We achieve privacy for both CPs and ISPs, whereas previous solutions secured only the users.
- We provide a detailed complexity analysis showing that, despite its advanced features, our solution is no more computationally demanding than existing systems.

**Abstract:** This work demonstrates how to distribute content delivery costs between ISPs and Content Providers (CPs) in a privacy-preserving and cost-efficient manner. The proposed scheme is fully stateless, meaning it introduces no new state to the network, unlike most cryptographic distributed ledger (CDL) protocols, which we identify as a source of high overhead. Our solution is simple, with no new complexities compared to prior proposals. Furthermore, we ensure privacy by preventing any user other than the content requester from accessing the ledger, thereby protecting users' private information—a feature absent in most previous schemes. Finally, in contrast to most existing protocols, any ISP can independently verify the CDL, as it lacks a trusted owner.

We derive both nonadaptive and adaptive models, the latter incorporating the dynamic evolution of viral genotypes, which can be solved analytically or via discrete-time numerical methods. When the viral generation time is significantly shorter than the antibody decay time, the adaptive model behaves like a nonadaptive model with effectively steady-state antibody levels. Conversely, when the viral generation time exceeds the antibody decay time, the adaptive model approximates to the nonadaptive model if the initial viral diversity is low; otherwise, it results in a form where every infected individual carries maximum selective advantage. These models are applied to analyze the expected duration of the COVID-19 pandemic's infectious phase across various antibody kinetics. Results for scenarios with pre-pandemic low viral diversity and short viral generation times indicate that, in most situations, the pandemic's infectious phase would conclude before genotypes could adapt to evade human immunity. Exceptional cases where this is not true occur when human antibody affinity declines over time or when new targeting epitopes have not yet been lost. Such cases where adaptation is possible include: post-vaccination scenarios with short viral generation times and pre-pandemic universal infection rates; natural pandemics with long viral generation times and low initial universal infection rates; and post-vaccination outbreaks where universal infection rates are moderate. In these situations, the models estimate how long it takes for genotypes to adapt to a fully nonadaptive state and how many genotypes are required to achieve a low extinction probability. Applying these models to project future pandemics and design future vaccines represents a new direction in mathematical epidemiology that holds significant promise. This novel, dual-capacity model enables predictions for both nonadaptive pandemic dynamics and the joint dynamics of virus adaptation and human infection. This represents a crucial step toward achieving a goal previously thought impossible: predicting viral evolution during adaptive processes to inform public health decisions regarding pandemic containment. Such predictive capability was unattainable in earlier studies that could only post-hoc interpret viral adaptation after the fact. Furthermore, our model is general and potentially applicable to other post-vaccination pathogen dynamics scenarios, such as the integration of plasmids into bacterial genomes.

Mathematics & Statistics has aimed to cultivate an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students pursuing mathematics. Historically, our strategy to address the lack of diversity in our majors focused on remediation, attempting to fix perceived student deficits through specific programming. However, in recent years, we have shifted to an anti-deficit approach that prioritizes transforming the department itself. The initiatives detailed below reflect this shift, designed to strengthen community, foster collaboration, and improve the overall climate within our department.

Our first initiative, the Pomona Math Affinity Group, was established in Fall 2019 to give faculty a dedicated space to explore student development and our own growth within the department. Composed of representatives from every division, the group meets monthly to discuss a wide range of topics, with a primary focus on advancing our mathematical program at the student level. We drive this work through three core areas: supporting students, creating opportunities, and our personal development. This comprehensive approach has already yielded significant results, most notably the Fall 2019 "First-Year Seminar on Gender and Math," which directly addressed the 'knowledging' component of student success.

Our second initiative, the Pomona Math PALS Program, continues a legacy of peer mentoring that has long been vital to student achievement at Pomona. Launched in Spring 2020, this program intentionally pairs undergraduate peers across various levels and from diverse backgrounds. Built on mutual support, the program helps both mentors and mentees develop as educators and learners. By facilitating the exchange of mentorship across different stages of the undergraduate journey, we aim to enrich the educational experiences of all students. This has led to numerous positive outcomes, including the diverse group of authors behind this application and the continued professional growth of its participants.

Finally, our third initiative, Math on the Hill, seeks to empower both students and faculty by deeply engaging them with our core mission of improving mathematical education. Running annually since Fall 2019, this program invites high school students into Pomona to meet our faculty and understand the full spectrum of mathematical opportunities available to them. Beyond individual achievement, Math on the Hill serves as a vital platform for building a broader faculty consensus on student support and enhancing our own professional lives. Since its inception, the program has had over 200 students interact directly with our faculty, reinforcing a shared commitment to advancing mathematical education. These simulations employed two explicit, power-law-based approximations (coupled two-moment schemes) to model neutrino-spheroid interactions with matter and photons, replacing the computationally intensive six-moment M1 approximation used in previous studies. The results of this model transition reveal that both instabilities and significant pre-heating of infalling accretion zone matter can be modeled more efficiently. This efficiency not only accelerates simulation runtimes but also enhances the study of fast instabilities' implications for chemical nucleosynthesis and the black hole mass threshold. These insights are crucial for designing future core-collapse simulations that accurately reflect the physics of stellar explosions. Additionally, our findings suggest that the parameters for future multi-messenger astrophysics studies could be more precise. condensed matter theory, characterized by unique states of matter that exhibit topological characteristics. In this domain, state functions often exist in isolation, exhibiting topological properties analogous to those found in algebraic topology. Just as classically tied ropes cannot be untied without cutting, isolated topological insulators function as open topological structures because their topological nature relies on specific barrier conditions. We propose a methodology for topologizing isolated quantum systems, such as topological molecules or quantum dots, by employing an auxiliary auxiliary field. This approach represents the first demonstration of how an auxiliary field can reveal the hidden topological nature of an isolated system. Utilizing the Schrieffer-Heffner transformation, the effective two-level system is shown to be adiabatically equivalent to a natural solid system, allowing us to inherit and apply topological concepts from the natural system to the auxiliary system. This research holds significant value for the fields of topological quantum computing and topological molecular engineering. Additionally, our findings hold potential applications in nanodevice engineering and topological quantum communication. Finally, the framework introduced in this study is general and can be extended to various other effective models, including the BCS superconductor and the spin-Drude model. These extensions may facilitate the discovery of new physical phenomena and exotic quantum states. Keywords: Topological Insulator, Auxiliary Field, Effect Field Theory, Topological Molecule, Topological Quantum Computer.

collaboration within visual analytics, a concept that remains relatively underexplored despite its potential. This article explores the question by investigating how users can effectively guide the collaborative process through three empirical studies involving 30 participants. These studies, which span 2021 to early 2022, aim to uncover how guidance occurs, what its purposes are, and what factors influence its success. The initial study (Chen et al., 2021) introduced the concept and methodology of co-adaptive guidance, gathered examples, and developed a preliminary framework. The second study (Chen et al., 2022a) refined this framework by presenting examples of adaptive guidance opportunities and proposing a design framework for such opportunities. The ongoing third study seeks to gain an in-depth understanding of the guidance process through examples of the guidance journey, observations, and insights, with findings expected in mid-2022. Alongside these study results, we discuss implications for future research and practice, as well as opportunities to design various types of adaptive guidance. These outcomes serve as a foundation for advancing collaborative visual analytics, offering a starting point for designing opportunities where humans and systems can guide the collaboration to achieve optimal results. Ultimately, this work encourages further exploration of collaborative scenarios, the mechanisms behind guidance, and strategies to enhance the co-adaptive process.

Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to static elasticity problems. Focusing on mesh refinement within the 2D "cross" geometry—recognized as a challenging scenario for AMLie-based methods—we assess their effectiveness when combined. Our results indicate that while BDDC outperforms AMG, their combination offers no significant advantage. This conclusion aligns with recent theoretical work on BDDC multilevel preconditioners, which categorize difficulties into three groups: corner singularities, material contrasts, and topology-driven challenges. Within the "cross" context, the difficulty stems from both corner singularities and material contrasts; consequently, BDDC demonstrates superior efficacy compared to AMG. Furthermore, we develop an automated method to suggest an effective splitting of primal variables for BDDC, potentially enhancing its performance. Our findings suggest that this approach is highly effective for problems involving only geometric singularity, such as node or edge refinement. Finally, we note that the development of this automatic method was motivated by the need to improve BDDC performance in the difficult "cross" geometry.

We then identify a condition for non-radiation that holds across all inertial frames, a requirement that is intuitively necessary for the stability of atomic systems, and demonstrate its equivalence to specific relations between charge density and field strength. Finally, we establish that maintaining these non-radiation constraints does not conflict with special relativity, provided that rest masses and proper times also follow specific relations. These relations are argued to be necessary for the threshold of the de Broglie relation to be satisfied, a concept we contend has profound deepness. We demonstrate that all previously cited examples of non-radiative non-shedding systems—namely, the harmonically varying monopole and dipole—can be derived directly from the de Broglie threshold relation, rather than from Lorentz transformations applied to laboratory-frame solutions. We also examine a previously unreported system consisting of two non-radiating non-shedding dipoles, which generates a non-constant number of particle species. In this two-particle system, the particles follow helical worldlines with different pitches but identical spatial frequencies. This results in a de Broglie relation that approximates the relationship between a particle's velocity and its orbital frequency. The analysis of this system reveals a relation between the winding number and the velocity, presenting a potential resolution to the apparent contradiction with the cosmic speed limit. We demonstrate that these velocities and windings can indeed coexist for two massive particles traveling at speeds slightly below the relevant characteristic field strength, which represents the system's energy scale divided by the particle's charge. This relationship establishes the velocity and winding such that the non-constant integer winding number creates the appearance of increasing velocity, even as it precisely satisfies the de Broglie relation. We emphasize that the two-particle system and its properties are not ad hoc, as any relation between velocity and frequency can be modeled by two charged particles. Specifically, in this two-particle scenario, the pitch varies with the velocity, whereas in other systems, the pitch remains constant. We illustrate that the relationship regarding velocity, orbital frequency, and wavelength can be understood as a manifestation of the relation between spatial and temporal components of four-vectors. Although this relationship is not strictly causal in the conventional sense, it represents the deepest connection between these quantities. We show that this relationship is essentially equivalent to the non-constant winding number in the two-particle system and explore the implications of this for the stability of matter

We report the first observation of a spin-polarized TMR effect in a superconductor-metamaterial-superconductor (SMSC) junction at both zero and finite temperatures. Our numerical findings show that the critical current exhibits periodic oscillations with the magnetic field, a hallmark of spin-polarized TMR. This oscillation arises from the magnetic field's influence on the metamaterial's permeability and is significantly amplified near the superconductor-metamaterial interface. Furthermore, we examined the impact of metamaterial loss on the critical current. These findings suggest that TMR can be realized in SMSC junctions even in the absence of superconducting proximity effects in the metamaterial. We also highlight the potential applications of this mechanism in generating spin-polarized supercurrents and Ginzburg-Landau polaritons within superconducting metamaterials.

The disease, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, transmits through respiratory droplets and can result in severe clinical outcomes or death. Given the ongoing pandemic and the absence of specific treatments, researchers have turned to artificial intelligence to create mathematical models for predicting infection and death rates. This study proposes a new approach using a modified SEIR model alongside a deep neural network, integrating the two methods to forecast COVID-19 infections and deaths across various regions. The results are derived from training the neural network with historical data. Utilizing real-world data, the neural network was applied to predict infections and death rates in Turkey, the United States, and Spain. The findings indicate that the proposed model aligns closely with actual data, demonstrating its effectiveness for short-term predictions. Furthermore, this model requires only a small volume of data for training, making the approach suitable for use even when pandemic data is limited. Additionally, the proposed method is expected to facilitate faster predictions. While the approach is general, it is expected to yield more accurate results as data volumes increase. A primary advantage of the method is the modification to the traditional SEIR model, which enhances accuracy by incorporating infection and death rates into the standard framework. The study also includes a section on the advantages and disadvantages of the proposed approach. The code for this work is publicly available. This research was conducted using our developed Python toolbox for intelligent systems, named YAPPy, which can be utilized as described in the relevant section of this paper. ### Multimodal Data Fusion Score Solution.

Multimodal data fusion is critical across science and engineering, while scoring functions are widely used to rank candidates in machine learning. However, existing scoring methods struggle to fully leverage information from multiple modes. We present a novel framework based on the product rule of probabilities, which integrates diverse information effectively. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed fusion score, proving its monotonicity. Experimental results confirm the method's effectiveness. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhengyao98/MSF}.

### Joint Score Solution.

Although scoring functions are essential for ranking and selection, research on jointly scoring multiple models remains scarce. Current methods either combine scores heuristically or rely on voting mechanisms. We propose learning a linear combination of base scores to serve as a global score for modeling interactions. This global score inherits properties from individual scores—such as robustness, consistency, and fairness—and offers several benefits: it supports diverse base scores, including nonlinear and deep models; enables customization of interaction types; and facilitates calibration of score weights. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly enhances scoring performance compared to baseline approaches. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhengyao98/JScore}.

It is demonstrated that QCC relates to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) through a factor dependent solely on the weak measurement's strength, meaning QCC captures only a portion of a system's quantumness compared to TQD. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that this residual quantumness can be extracted not only via subsequent von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimal weak measurements. These findings are illustrated using a Bell-diagonal state as a specific example. Notably, these outcomes can be interpreted as no-teleportation criteria or conditions preventing quantum channel equivalence under local unitary transformations. Finally, it is established that both the optimal strength of weak measurements and the total probability of obtaining specific measurement results can be determined using QCC. This capability proves valuable for analyzing the statistical properties of weak measurements following quantum evolution. Essentially, QCC serves as a useful tool for estimating the cumulative quantumness extracted over time. The research also posits that QCC can be understood as the quantum advantage introduced by weak measurements. This concept is evident in the context of quantum state discrimination and is expressed through inequalities defining optimal strategies. Specifically, these inequalities demonstrate that while strong measurements achieve the maximum quantum advantage, weak measurements can surpass strong measurements when their strength remains sufficiently low. Consequently, these findings offer a fresh perspective on the quantum advantage generated by weak measurements. Additionally, the quantumness factor is shown to function as a practical tool for estimating TQD. This approach offers a feasible solution to the continuous monitoring dilemma, enabling the observation of quantumness evolution in bipartite systems without the need for strong measurements. In this framework, QCC represents the quantumness factor. In this paper, TQD, decoherence factors, and their products are utilized to estimate both initial and final QCC values. By integrating these elements with experimental data, one can effectively track the evolution of quantumness. In this context, QCC is recognized as the quantumness factor. Since weak measurements allow for more frequent sampling than strong ones, this method provides a more accurate depiction of quantumness evolution. Therefore, the quantumness factor is considered to include a more significant redundant term. This indicates that QCC can be reduced to TQD under specific conditions. Specifically, when the quantumness factor equals one, it implies that QCC is equivalent to TQD. In this scenario, TQD serves as a practical tool to calculate the quantumness factor.

While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been the standard and highly effective approach, their reliance on local kernels restricts their capacity to model long-range relationships compared to Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Transformer networks. Although next iteration based bidirectional auto-encoders and self-attention mechanisms have emerged as popular alternatives to CNNs for dependency capture, they often demand excessive computational resources and memory. To address this, we introduce the previous iteration based attention network (PIA-Net), which leverages previous frame information to enhance performance in dynamic scene understanding tasks. PIA-Net offers two primary advantages: it integrates the parallel processing capabilities of CNNs with the long-range dependency modeling of attention mechanisms, and it consumes significantly less memory than methods relying on next iteration based auto-encoders. PIA-Net demonstrates superior efficiency and effectiveness compared to state-of-the-art methods in both static and dynamic object detection tasks. To validate these capabilities, we present PIA-Net Det for static object detection and PIA-Net Tracklet Det for dynamic object detection. PIA-Net Det achieves significant speedups over CNNs and transformer networks while matching the performance of leading static detection approaches. Similarly, in dynamic scene understanding, our multi-task tracklet detector outperforms state-of-the-art solutions. It can be optimized by substituting certain input integers with precomputed constants, thereby replacing multiple multiplication-addition sequences with single additions. This paper formally models the joint optimization of both constant substitutions and multiplications, demonstrating that even with a limited set of substitutions, the resulting matrix is sparse. We evaluate the exact method on small-scale problems and the new heuristic approach on large-scale instances, both independently and in combination. Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) have gained significant traction in Natural Language Processing (NLP) due to their robust pre-training and superior performance. While PLMs achieve performance parity with hand-crafted linguistic features regarding syntactic dependencies, some dependencies remain challenging to learn. To address this, researchers have proposed methods to initialize models with knowledge of specific target dependencies, a process known as structured pre-training. However, this approach relies on the existence of annotated training data containing dependency labels, an requirement that limits its applicability to datasets without such annotations. In this work, we propose a novel structured pre-training procedure where the model is initialized using structural information derived from unsupervised parsers. Crucially, our method incorporates a regularization term based on structural stability to mitigate the inherent errors of unsupervised parsers. Experiments on three dependency datasets reveal that while structurally initialized models often outperform those initialized with dependencies, incorporating structural structural stability significantly boosts their performance. Consequently, our approach successfully decouples the requirement for annotated data from that for linguistic labels. Code is available at  and the corresponding paper is also accessible. Finally, a feedback survey is currently open.

Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) have gained significant popularity in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for their ability to capture semantic representations and hierarchical structure sensitivity. However, most PLMs undergo masked language modeling, a objective that primarily focuses on local context while overlooking global global context information. To resolve this issue, we propose initializing PLMs with global global contextual information derived from parsing trees. Experiments show that our method yields substantial improvements over baseline models, particularly in tasks requiring an understanding of global global context. The RAM model allows access to the $i$-th element of an input of size $n$ in $O(1)$ time, a feature that has been criticized for its unrealistic memory access assumptions. To address this, the Algebraic Cell Probe (ACP) model was developed to examine the tradeoff between algorithm efficiency and word access patterns. In ACP, inputs consist of integer arrays where an access to the $i$-th element of an input of size $n$ takes $\Omega(\log w)$ time, where $w$ is the unknown word size (the maximum value across all inputs). We establish a tight $\Theta(\log w)$ lower bound for time- and space-efficient space permutation sort in the ACP model. This bound specifically applies to comparison-based methods that use a constant fraction of the input size for space and perform $\omega(1)$ elements per iteration. Our proof is combinatorial and relies on a careful analysis of how many space permutations—time and space-efficient permutations—can exist when a single word access is delayed by a single step. This analysis depends on a novel combinatorial upper bound of $2^{\log^{\mathfrak{c}} n}$ (where $\mathfrak{c} \in [0, 1]$) on the number of such permutations for input size $n$. As a direct application, we present a sort algorithm for inputs of size $n$ using $O(n)$ space and $\Theta(\log n)$ per-element word accesses. We conclude by extending this result to handle inputs with repeated elements.

We examine the one-dimensional non-Hermitian massless Dirac model, identifying the critical point as the region where the non-Hermitian skin effect (NSE) vanishes, resulting in a complete absence of topological edge states. Unlike their Hermitian counterparts, non-Hermitian systems can exhibit phase transitions not only at critical values of real control parameters but also along an imaginary axis. We demonstrate that non-Hermitic systems can undergo first-order transitions, whether real or imaginary, and we illustrate how associated phase diagrams can display multiple domains separated by such transitions. Furthermore, we show that these first-order transitions occur when parts of the Brillouin zone boundary bands experience the NSE, whereas second-order transitions are characterized by the complete NSE of the touching critical points at Kramers-degenerate KPT points. We also investigate non-Hermitian systems undergoing first-order transitions with PT-symmetry breaking, finding that the transition can be either continuous or discontinuous, depending on whether the critical point is real or imaginary. Through a series of illustrations, we provide a comprehensive understanding of non-Hermitian topological phase transitions, offering a methodology to systematically analyze first-order interactions between non-Hermitian systems and providing a framework for constructing non-Hermitian topological phase diagrams. These findings expand our comprehension of topological phase transitions and non-Hermitian topology, with implications for various experimental platforms including photonics, cold-atom, and electrical platforms. These effects are typically characterized by precise conditions, often involving tunneling through thin potential barriers. In this study, we report on the observation of the quantum transparency effect (QTE) in mesoscopic systems. QTE represents an interference effect where a quantum particle's probability of passing through a potential structure matches its classical probability, which for a free particle would be zero. We examined the transport of cold atoms through the potential of a single, elongated atom or molecule within a quasi-one-dimensional Bose gas. Experimental data captured the transition from thermal transparency to QTE as the system moved from a higher temperature regime, dominated by thermal fluctuations, to a quantum regime where interference is the primary driver. \paragraph{Background} Markov Decision Processes (MDMs) serve as a formal framework for sequential decision-making. An agent interacting with an environment at discrete time steps $t$ observes the state $s_t$, executes an action $a_t$, and receives a reward $r_t$. In model-based learning, the agent constructs a world model to estimate the environment's dynamics. Specifically, this work focuses on parametric models, where the transition probability $p(s', a, s)$ is represented as a Gaussian Process (GP) with parameter vector $\theta$. This approach is common in algorithms like SPACIA, which employ a GP to predict state transitions for generating robust policies in simulated car driving tasks. Similarly, probabilistic model-based RL methods typically assume that both observations and transitions are governed by noise. For instance, SSGRL assumes noisy transitions and employs variational inference to approximate the true transition distribution and the state distribution of the greedy policy. In our context, we consider the transition density for action $a$ and state $s$ to be:

$$
p(s'|a,s,\theta) = \mathcal{N}(s'|f(a,s),\Sigma)
$$

Here, the function $f$ represents a GP and $\Sigma$ denotes a diagonal covariance matrix.

\paragraph{Related Work} Several studies have recently explored generalization in model-based RL. Wu et al. demonstrated that in domains with low intrinsic task complexity, an MBRL agent can solve new tasks that were not present during training. Furthermore, Ghazizadeh et al. investigated state generalization in model-based control. Their method involved training a GP to approximate the value function and its first spatial derivative, followed by a local linearization of the dynamics to ensure stability. Our research shares a focus on improving robustness in MBRL but differs in that we do not aim to generalize to unseen states. Specifically, for problems involving $K$ users and a file library of size $F$, the goal is to identify the minimal degree-drag exponent, denoted as $\delta^*(K,F)$, where $\delta^*(K,F) \ge 0$. This exponent represents the first-order term (linear in the logarithm) of the optimal worst-case communication cost, which is also expressed as $\delta^*(K,F) \cdot \log(K!)$. By focusing on reducing the communication cost multiplier, we aim to enhance the scalability of systems handling massive files.

We investigate this minimization problem across various user scenarios and file library configurations. For any file library of size $F$, we derive an explicit formula for $\delta^*(K,F)$ that holds regardless of the number of users. Additionally, considering the limit as $K$ approaches infinity, we present a formula that characterizes $\lim_{K\to\infty}\delta^*(K,F)$ for any file library size $F$.

To achieve this objective, the primary method involves partitioning the unit hypercube into polyhedra. We demonstrate that the optimal worst-case cost is obtained through a specific construction involving random user position assignments within the unit hypercube and deterministic message generation. This minimum multiplier, $\delta^*(K,F)$, is given by the maximum value of a certain function that depends on the number of partitions, the dimensions of these partitions, and the total count of distinct partitions required.

problem seeks to determine the maximum edge count in a triangle-free graph where every vertex has a degree of at least three. This paper establishes the exact number of edges for such graphs when the degree is exactly three, an edge is specified that can participate in triangles, and the total edge count is not limited to the conventional $7n^{4}/24+o(n^{4})$. Furthermore, we construct the specific graphs that achieve this maximum edge count. When the constraint of a minimum degree of three is removed, our findings align with those regarding Tur\'an's original problem where vertices may have zero degree, as reported by St. F\"uredi and the author. Edge-partition problems are also examined. A key benefit of our main result is providing a 3-approximation for the edge partition problem, where each vertex is assigned to a triangle containing an edge from its set of three incident edges, if such a partition is feasible. This is accomplished by formulating the problem as an integer linear program, solving a related linear programming relaxation, and applying an edge-rounding algorithm. Our approach improves the best known factor-2 approximation to a 2.125-approximation, and we demonstrate that this factor is optimal for any edge-partition algorithm relying solely on a linear programming formulation. Additionally, we present an exact integer linear programming model and an edge-partitioning algorithm with a factor-2 approximation and $O(n^{2})$ time complexity, which surpasses the polynomial time limit of the standard linear programming approach. Finally, we examine extensions of the problem by replacing triangles with specific small graphs, providing upper and lower bounds that generalize previous results by Tur\'an, McDiarmid, and others. Current approaches typically rely on specific camera views or rely on manual selection to assess weather conditions. In contrast, this study demonstrates that integrating multiple camera views with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) automatically identifies court-effective weather state features. This approach surpasses existing methods that utilize a single view or require manual selection. The proposed solution is named WECNN. First, the paper examines how camera count and configuration influence performance. Using data from 10 cities in Tennessee, it evaluates configurations ranging from 2 to 5 cameras per game court. The results indicate that a system using 5 cameras achieves the highest accuracy with the lowest computational cost. Additionally, the study analyzes the impact of camera location and orientation by analyzing image content from various positions. The optimal configuration identified is 5 cameras situated at the four corners of the court plus a central camera. Finally, WECNN's performance is benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods, confirming its superiority. Given its ability to accurately and cost-effectively predict weather states, WECNN offers significant potential for enhancing sports analytics and decision-making across diverse applications. fundamental challenge in science and engineering. While numerous numerical approaches exist, Gradient Descent (GD) remains the most widely used due to its simplicity and efficiency. However, GD is hindered by two primary drawbacks: susceptibility to local minima and slow convergence, particularly near the optimal point. In contrast, Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) has demonstrated significant power in optimizing various machine learning tasks, tensor networks, and variational quantum algorithms by accelerating convergence. We propose that first-order phase transitions responsible for SUSY breaking could have taken place in the early universe, generating detectable gravitational wave signatures. By developing a realistic model of gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking, we demonstrate that such transitions can simultaneously generate masses for heavy right-handed and sneutrinos. The subsequent CP-violating decays of these particles drive PeV-scale leptogenesis and establish a new one-loop mechanism for neutrino mass generation. Furthermore, we predict the associated gravitational wave signals and associated cosmological implications for these models. Given the potential detectability of these gravitational waves by near-future pulsar timing arrays, our analysis offers encouraging prospects for verifying PeV-scale new physics. These considerations may also prove valuable in interpreting future observational data regarding stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds. Additionally, we examine a more generic scenario featuring heavy sterile neutrinos and demonstrate how our model can be extended to elucidate the cosmic neutrino diffuse background detected by IceCube. Finally, we discuss constraints imposed by the lightness of neutrinos upon all PeV-scale new physics frameworks capable of producing identifiable first-order phase transitions. Classical methods fail to solve this problem because the driving process is neither Markovian nor semimartingale. To address this, we assume the coefficients of the equations are monotone. Leveraging the anti-monotonicity of these coefficients and applying Spitzer's decomposition, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the optimization problem through a carefully designed iterative algorithm. However, we prove that the measuring process becomes a martingale when the coefficients are Lipschitz continuous, and we discuss this result in the context of mean-field stochastic control problems with delays driven by fractional Brownian motion. Specifically, we examine scenarios involving ferromagnetic and dark baryon number conserving symmetry breakings. To ensure efficient self-annihilation and rapid thermal equilibration with the stellar environment, the dark matter particle density must remain in kinetic equilibrium. This requirement is satisfied in the fermionic and baryon-conserving models at sufficiently low temperatures, facilitating fast direct detection. However, in the ferromagnetic scalar model, only momentum-dependent annihilation channels remain active, rendering direct detection inaccessible. The most promising candidate for emitting thermalized dark matter is the ferromagnetic scalar scenario; here, self-annihilation is limited to two-body processes, and outgoing particles easily thermalize in the stellar medium due to their low momentum. The emitted neutrinos can either escape the stellar surface or remain trapped, depending on the specific stellar object. We demonstrate that these studies fail to account for read glitches—global noise spikes that propagate through the logic and reach multiple Read Feedback (RF) paths. This glitch-induced randomness is highly dependent on Read time and can completely override the randomness derived from read variations. To address this, we evaluate various TRNG architectures by measuring their Minimum Pairwise Distance (MPD) under both typical and worst-case Read time scenarios. This new design not only sustains a low MPD even in the most favorable typical Read time scenarios but also ensures that increasing Read time enhances the generated randomness. Finally, we validate the design's resilience against side-channel attacks by implementing it in 90 nm standard cell technology and analyzing its performance under varying process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions. This work presents a scheme to induce $q$-deformation in an optomechanical setup. By incorporating an optical cavity, a two-level atom, and an harmonic oscillator, we can generate a $q$-deformed cavity-field interaction. Through a Bohr transformation on the system Hamiltonian and performing a canonical transformation in the Markovian limit, the effective cavity-field interaction Hamiltonian is established. Under the rotating wave approximation and the Born-Markov approximation, the reduced density matrix for the cavity is derived. Excluding the quantum diffusion term and setting the deformation parameter $\lambda = 0$, this result aligns with existing literature. Furthermore, by examining the evolution of population difference and reduced density matrix elements, we observe that both the amount of $q$-deformation (controlled by $\lambda$) and the decay rate ($\gamma$) influence the evolution of the population difference. Additionally, the amount of entanglement between the cavity and the oscillator depends on $\lambda$ and the initial mechanical state. When the initial state is the coherent state $| \alpha \rangle$, increasing $\lambda$ diminishes the amount of entanglement. Conversely, if the initial state is the Fock state $| n \rangle$, the amount of entanglement between the cavity and the oscillator increases with $\lambda$, a finding that contrasts with previous findings. This review outlines the nuclear matter energy density profile based on the random matrix theory of conformal unitary and orthogonal Gaussian ensembles. Because the theory remains valid at any order of perturbation with respect to finite noncollective quantum numbers, it produces a smooth energy density profile free of fluctuations and correlations. These findings are applied to model nuclear rotation and addressed challenges regarding the onset of superfluidity and the significance of shell effects in the ground state. These include the extension of real-valued functions, the enclosure of non-complete metric spaces within complete ones, the embedding of compact metric spaces into Banach spaces via continuous functions, the extension of continuous functions from a compact subspace to the entire space, the embedding of compact Hausdorff spaces into the set of all non-negative real-valued continuous functions, the embedding of compact topological spaces into the space of all continuous real-valued functions, the embedding of compact locally convex spaces into the dual of a separable Banach space using continuous linear functionals, the extension of partial real-valued functions, the embedding of semi-metric spaces into a metric space through a family of partial metric functions, the embedding of partial real-valued functions into bounded real-valued functions via uniform convergence on equicontinuous sets, and the embedding of bounded real-valued functions into a free topological group via a perception. The final chapter presents examples and counter-examples of compact pairings (A,F) where A is non-compact or F is not a set of functions that separates points and closed sets, illustrating that the compactification of (A,F) results in a compact space with distinct properties from A. This research generalizes and unifies various existing studies on compactifications by employing the framework of compact perception pairs. Additionally, it provides novel perspectives on classical theories and establishes new connections across different areas of mathematics, particularly those centered around compactifications. The proof of the main theorem utilizes the assumptions of a compact perception pair by employing a precise application of Tikhonov's Theorem. Finally, we illustrate the application of this main theorem through a new characterization of compactness using Baire spaces and an alternative proof of Tikhonov's Theorem. Specifically, we prove that a space which is both compact-perception Tikhonov and Baire is compact by applying Tikhonov's Theorem to its compactification. This approach encloses the space within a product of Hausdorff spaces that are simultaneously Baire and compact, thereby reinforcing the embedding of such spaces into a compact convex set within a separable Banach space. This research is dedicated to Prof. W. A. Sutherland.

In light irradiation, dimensional shifts are instead widely understood as a combination of thermal expansion and radiation pressure ($P_{\text{rad}}$). This study investigates material expansion by integrating these two driving forces. Through both theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we demonstrate that the pressure coefficient ($\alpha/\beta$, where $\beta=d\alpha/dT$) governing linear dimensional shifts can increase linearly with light intensity for material layer thicknesses up to several micrometers. Our findings indicate that the pressure coefficient may rise by up to five orders of magnitude, enabling the creation of expansion-driven $\mu$-scale actuation and force generation. These results open the way for temperature-controlled expansion and linear actuation of materials within $\mu$m- to mm-sized devices under non-contact conditions. Furthermore, the pressure coefficient can increase even further under near-field radiation, as observed in plasmonic nanostructures. This research also lays the groundwork for non-contact expansion actuation in quantum technologies and other emerging fields. Additionally, the results present a method to directly measure the pressure coefficient using laser light. Finally, this work represents a fundamental investigation into the general behavior of expansion actuation and provides insight into the pressure coefficient, a parameter of fundamental importance in quantum technologies.

The pressure coefficient ($\alpha/\beta$) increases linearly with light intensity for various materials, including plastics, waxes, and metals. By controlling light absorption, absorption can be achieved in a spot or along the entire sample length, allowing for the observation of expansion in one or multiple dimensions. This results in the actuation of the sample into various shapes, such as circles, squares, or other configurations.

One specific application involves a plastic film coated with a metal layer (polymer/metal bilayer). When a gradient in absorbed power is applied, the bilayer acts as a thermal gradient expander, causing the metal side to either contract or expand more than the plastic side. If the metal's thermal expansion coefficient is lower than the plastic's, the metal contracts more, inducing the sheet to bend toward the metal. By selecting a metal with a sufficiently small expansion coefficient, this sheet can exhibit negative in-plane expansion. This phenomenon can be leveraged to create nanoscale force generation, a criterion also applicable to near-field radiation. By utilizing multiple metal/metal bilayers with varying activation coefficients and different thicknesses, nanoscale force generation can be realized.
