Now consider random graphs where each vertex is assigned a random variable $X_i$ taking values in a finite set, with pairwise independent components defined by a random graph model. We introduce a novel family of models termed "path-of-length-two exclusion models," where independence structures resemble those of exclusion graphs but are restricted to paths of length two. For each model, we define an independence model $I$ on the indices $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, where sets $A$ belong to $I$ precisely when the variables $\{X_i : i \in A\}$ are independent. We construct random variables satisfying a given random graph model and $I$-independence by defining their expectations as tensors with row-rank-one constraints, thereby framing these models within the context of tensor factorization. We establish that our proposed path-of-length-two exclusion models are strictly more expressive than full exclusion models, where any pair of distinct vertices is nonadjacent. This includes recovering the well-known planted partition model, which plays a critical role in the dense stochastic blockmodel. Additionally, we show that one variant of these models is closely related to the independence model derived from odd holes of length five or greater. This paper is based on our work in Random Structures and Algorithms. Agents with greater educational attainment tend to favor more diverse clusters, while those with less education prefer and interact predominantly with peers from similar backgrounds. Within non-relativistic quantum mechanics, standard angular momentum properties explain the $(-1)^{2s}$ sign factor acquired upon swapping particle coordinates, directly linking spin to exchange statistics without extra conditions. Conversely, in relativistic quantum field theory, satisfying the correct statistics demands the spin-statistics theorem, which correctly connects spin to signal signs only after incorporating signals, antiparticles, and causality. This work demonstrates that establishing the relativistic version of angular momentum is insufficient for ensuring correct statistics in quantum systems with fixed spin in three spatial dimensions. Specifically, we show that an extra sign factor arises from swapping space-time coordinates, causing fermion and boson classification to depend on the mass-shell relation between energy and momentum. To resolve this, we prove a generalization of the spin-statistics theorem that includes this extra sign factor, valid for particle systems in three spatial dimensions where the relativistic energy-momentum relationship is non-linear and consistent with causality. Consistent with prior research, this generalized spin-statistics theorem is also applicable in other dimensions or systems. Finally, we discuss the significance of this result in the context of relativity. Relating this to our prior examination of spin one-half particles, we highlight that the generalization of the spin-statistics theorem is essential for correctly distinguishing bosons from fermions in relativistic quantum mechanics, even for fermions traveling at zero velocity ($p=0$). This necessity underscores the incompatibility between fixing spin in quantum mechanics and doing so in quantum field theory. Additionally, we illustrate that implementing Pauli's principle in quantum systems with spin $s\ge1/2$ is more complex than applying boundary conditions to symmetric or antisymmetric wavefunctions, as constructing such systems requires more than just ensuring invariant Hamiltonians under permutations. Similarly, applying the spin-statistics theorem in quantum systems with spin $s\ge1$ involves more subtleties than simply requiring field operators to obey (anti-)commutation relations at space-like separations. To construct quantum systems that correctly differentiate between bosons and fermions, one must rely on this generalized spin-statistics theorem. Finally, based on the analysis of signal-based spin definition in quantum fields, we provide a generalization of Pauli's principle for fields with spin $s\ge1$, demonstrating that it is equivalent to applying the spin-statistics theorem. This provides a more accurate understanding of how spin relates to signal properties and particle statistics in quantum fields. To

The proposed scheme relies on two core components: a tailored Integrated Signature and Encryption framework, which combines a public key encryption system with two distinct signature methods (a digital signature and a linkable ring signature), alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs. We provide a detailed description of the protocol, present security proofs, and evaluate the system based on performance metrics including transaction volume, computational cost, and storage requirements. Building on earlier work by Kyng and Zhang regarding similar outcomes in the time complexity domain through reductions between approximate solvers, we establish that their reductions can be executed via constant-depth, polynomial-size threshold circuits. Our methodology relies on reducing to the design of sparse conductance cuts in undirected graphs with nonnegative edge weights and edge length assignments, utilizing an extension of the Solovay-Strassen primitive for integer multiplication within the cited circuit model. This primitive allows the computation of the product of two $O(\log n)$-bit integers in $O(\log n)$ time. Furthermore, we show that a solver capable of detecting cut sets in undirected graphs with $n$ vertices and conductance at most $\epsilon$ can be adapted to solve linear systems by maintaining an invariant on cut sets; these adaptations result in only minor degradations to the solution approximation factor and edge complexity. The primary inference drawn is that if the solver further maintains a invariant on a specific family of expanding graphs with low conductance, it gains the ability to approximate solutions to linear systems. We identify two such families with $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ dependence on $\epsilon$. The initial family comprises a random subset of rows from a randomized Hadamard matrix, whereas the second consists of a random subset of rows from a transform matrix constructed by concatenating an odd primitive root of unity with a carefully selected complex number. While the randomness in the primitive primitive ensures polynomials are almost-everywhere distinct and thus linearly independent, the randomization of transform matrices guarantees linear independence with high probability. Expanding graphs are prevalent in algorithms for Laplacian systems, particularly in approaches relying on embedding techniques. Our findings indicate that the ability to solve systems in this context stems more from the algorithm's capacity to identify conductance sets than from the specific properties of undirected Laplacian matrices. Furthermore, our work provides a fresh perspective on foundational inquiries concerning reductions and black-box algorithm composition. Specifically, we demonstrate that a solver with access to an expanding graph can be employed as a black-box tool to approximate the solution of linear systems. This finding suggests that the implementation-specific intricacies of established black-box methods, such as those by Spielman and Sinop or the method depending on graph sparsity, might be bypassed. This paper introduces a new, carefully crafted set of gold standard annotations for six tasks: tokenization, word segmentation, dependency parsing, chunking, dependency parsing, and subword tokenization. These datasets enable the training of models for coarsely-grained word segmentation, dependency parsing, chunking, and subword tokenization. Word segmentation is a critical foundation for building effective models for the finer-grained tasks of dependency parsing and chunking. We trained these models on the new dataset and evaluated them via cross-validation and comparative studies against previous state-of-the-art approaches. Our results demonstrate that the proposed dataset yields significantly higher accuracy than prior methods for all six coarsely-grained tasks. We make this dataset publicly available at https://github.com/hebrewNLP/hebrewNUD. We anticipate that this resource will facilitate model design and research on understudied tasks, particularly those relying on the previously scarce segmentation data. To assist the community in rapidly benchmarking new models, we also provide a library of preprocessing and modeling procedures at https://github.com/hebrewNLP/hebrewNUD. We encourage researchers to utilize this library to ensure fair comparisons. Finally, we address common challenges and pitfalls associated with both training and utilizing the dataset. deep learning, various text generation models have been developed to address the limitations of traditional methods. Although these approaches offer promising results, they often struggle with practical challenges such as sampling efficiency, getting trapped in local minima, a lack of diversity, and mode collapse. This paper introduces a novel stochastic generative model designed for discrete datasets that mitigates these issues and is applicable across multiple domains. The method employs a Neumann-based random walk on a graph, utilizing a transition probability matrix (TPM) derived from a continuous stochastic block model. We analyze the algorithm's performance regarding efficiency, diversity, and resistance to local minima. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach generates high-quality samples and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in text generation tasks. Furthermore, since the model is data-efficient, it produces meaningful outputs with a minimal number of training examples. We also present a new dataset for evaluating text generation under conditions of limited data. Ultimately, our method shows promise for applications including the synthesis of discrete images, music, and other data types. The implementation can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/hayalgalic/stochastic-block-model}.**Index Terms:** text generation, transition probability matrix, Neumann-based random walk, local minima.

-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assumes that the degree distributions at both ends of a randomly chosen edge are independent, this paper advances the field by examining ensembles featuring degree-degree correlations. To achieve this, we introduce a methodology for specifying these correlations and analyzing small sets of randomly selected edges. Our approach first samples an edge at random from the multigraph representing the degree-triangle of the LDPC degree-degree correlation distribution, then randomly selects two edges from this set. We evaluate several properties of this "small set" model, including degree-degree correlation, degree-degree-degree-3-cycles, and third mixing time. Additionally, we present two methods for constructing LDPC degree-degree-correlation graphs: the configuration model and a local graph transformation model. Simulation results indicate that, for a fixed total number of check bits and a fixed code rate, increasing degree-degree correlation leads to a higher probability of linear dependence among the check matrix rows. This suggests that within a given ensemble, ensembling multiple copies of the graph can enhance the overall performance of that ensemble. This finding also holds relevance for analyzing other structures, such as bipartite graphs or general graphs, where small cycles may influence global behavior. This work is part of a series addressing degree-degree-correlation graphs; a prior paper [E. S. Kim, R. G. Gallager, "Small sets of randomly selected edges in $L_D D_ V$-regular degree-degree-correlation graphs," IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory, vol. 62, no. 1, pp. 417-453, Jan. 2016.] established limit theorems for asymptotic properties and derived formulas for ensemble averages of large sets of randomly selected edges. However, extending these asymptotic results to handle degree-degree-correlation graphs remains an open challenge. These graphs model a type of non-reversible ergodic Markov chain on bipartite graphs, a topic for future research. This paper introduces an enhanced model predictive safety filter (MPSF) that integrates system-level synthesis (SLS) techniques. These attacks exploit vulnerabilities in optical hardware components to steal secret keys without being detected. We introduce a novel attack targeting the light-source detector that functions as a quantum hacking method. This attack relies on an entangled photon source to intercept keys from the QKD protocol's legitimate Alice and Bob. Remarkably, the attack protocol operates effectively despite a significant photon-number mismatch between the attack photons and the QKD protocol's legitimate single-photon pulses. Simultaneously, the attack evades all standard quantum and classical detection mechanisms used in QKD systems to identify photon-number discrepancies. Our findings underscore the critical necessity of quantum hardware security and highlight the limited protection offered by current optical implementations against quantum attacks. To safeguard quantum communication systems, we argue that rigorous security assessments of all optical device components must be conducted under the potential threat of quantum attacks. We have provided detailed instructions on how to launch this attack using current off-the-shelf optical devices, making it straightforward for other researchers to replicate and extend this quantum hacking approach. Additionally, we will share the open-source software tools required to execute this attack via a public video link. This work will be published in Chinese as part of the first issue of the Journal of Science and Technology of North China University of Science and Technology.

This study theoretically demonstrates that zero-shot learning can be achieved through interpolation within the decision space of pre-trained transformers. Deconstructing the transformer architecture reveals that its feedforward networks (FFNs) are critical: their feed-forward function, acting as a local map, is located near the Fourier description region and operates as a low-pass filter. Consequently, the feedforward function of the FFN serves as a viable local mapping for in-context learning. In contrast, attention layers primarily manage global information; their function approximates a high-pass filter, making them unsuitable for this specific learning task. These findings provide profound insights into the learning mechanisms of pre-trained language models. Furthermore, they offer new theoretical directions for developing induction heads to explicitly extract such local mapping capabilities and discuss potential strategies to enhance in-context learning performance. Finally, we establish the direct connection between local mapping characteristics and in-context learning to provide a framework for evaluating the in-context learning abilities of future models. To facilitate this assessment, we introduce the ICLF score as a metric. Finally, we release the code for both the ICLF metric and the related experiments. This work forms Chapter 5 of my dissertation. Code: https://github.com/MingdaShi/ICL-mechanism.git.

The cold core complex (CCC) serves as a critical area for studying the physics of cluster central galaxies and their surrounding environments. This study characterizes the CCC of Abell 2052, located at a redshift of $z=0.0295$, using H$\alpha$ emission line data from the Hubble Space Telescope and X-ray observations from both NASA's Swift X-ray Telescope (XRT) and ESA's XMM-Newton Observatory, complemented by near-infrared data from the Near Infrared Camera and Multi-object Spectrometer (NICMOS) on the James Webb Space Telescope. Based on these observations, we identify a cold complex boundary radius of $R_{cc} = 200 \pm 10 \rm{kpc}$, derived from XRT analysis, and a hot complex boundary radius of $R_{hx} = 1.1 \pm 0.1 \rm{Mpc}$, derived from optical analysis. The ratio $R_{hx}/R_{cx} = 5.5 \pm 0.2$ suggests that the processes defining the hot complex boundary occurred approximately 5.5 years after those defining the cold complex boundary. Analysis of H$\alpha$ emission line morphology reveals that the cold core boundary is not smooth and concentric but rather irregular, fragmented, and clumpy. A linear regression analysis of 15 sub-regions indicates that the cold core pressure is higher in the inner regions compared to the outer regions, implying a direction of cold core material flow from outside to inside. Furthermore, a temperature map analysis identifies numerous temperature discontinuities at the cold core boundary, interpreted as "cold fronts." We conclude that the formation of these cold fronts is likely driven by the accretion of ICM material onto the cluster core. Additionally, we detect a bipolar bipolar structure in both the X-ray and H$\alpha$ bands, showing spatial overlap; we discuss the potential connection between this feature and the bipolar jet produced by the radio galaxy 2HSS $1000+509$ at the cluster's B2 position. Finally, based on our findings, we address whether a universal sequence exists for CCC formation and evolution. the decays of beauty- and charm-hadrons serves as a precise test of the Standard Model and a sensitive probe for supersymmetric phenomena. This article outlines the experimental techniques and results from the LHCb detector, which is optimized and dedicated to such measurements. Key findings include the first observation of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm- systems and various related studies. itate a fundamental shift in resource allocation strategies, as Base Stations (BSs) will integrate computational capabilities to perform these allocations in distributed and flexible manners within resource blocks. This transformation is driven by the surge in computational demands from mobile applications, particularly in computing-intensive tasks like unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sensing and processing. Conducting computations at the edge of the radio network offers lower latency compared to cloud data centers and mitigates privacy concerns associated with public clouds. However, the complexity of resource allocation in such environments stems from concurrent and cross-layer optimization of communication and computing resources. This paper proposes a novel distributed resource allocation framework utilizing a layered approach for UAVs and resource virtualization. In this scheme, UAVs connect to multiple edge BSs through conceptually dedicated wireless links. Each BS allocates communication resources via a long-term strategy and offloads computing tasks to containerized virtual machines (VMs) on a short-term basis. These VMs are deployed on public hardware and isolated by technology, resembling microservices. Furthermore, a new result shows that in a distributed system, UAVs should offload tasks to their own BSs to minimize costs.

This database stores feature-enhanced sample motions that are guaranteed to satisfy all constraints once they are identified as valid. The core of the algorithm relies on constructing this database offline by analyzing the sample motions that satisfy specific conditions. Specifically, we address upright walking for a hexapod robot, where each sample motion is defined by the configuration of its limbs. Together, these methods allow for the generation of dynamic walking behaviors with new limb swing patterns that were previously unseen. Building on this formulation, we propose a convex-concave gradient method that is proven \textit{regret minimax optimal} for the broader class of regularization problems. Specifically, the algorithm achieves a regret of at most $O(T / \sqrt{t})$ over $T$ iterations, where $t$ denotes the dimension of the decision space. Furthermore, the method can be implemented in polynomial time. As a direct application, the approach delivers a distributionally robust \ell_1-\convex learning algorithm with a regret of at most $O(d_\mathbb{N}p d_{\mathbb{F}}\sqrt{T} )$, where $d_\mathbb{N}$ and $d_{\mathbb{F}}$ represent the marginal dimensions of the training data and the learning space, respectively, and $p$ is the size of the ambiguity set. We demonstrate instance optimality by constructing specific examples showing that no distributionally robust learning algorithm can surpass this regret bound. Additionally, the method extends to online distributionally robust regression and classification, yielding instance optimal online support vector machines and logistic regression. In this context, the algorithm incurs a regret of at most $O(\sqrt{T}\log|\mathcal{X}|)$ compared to the best expert in a given hypothesis class $\mathcal{X}$, where $\mathcal{X}$ consists of $|\mathcal{X}|$ halfspaces. The approach also applies to online robust learning under \ell_1-loss, achieving a regret of at most $O(\sqrt{T}\log|\mathcal{X}|)$ against the best expert. Leveraging the invariance principle, we demonstrate that a class of the proposed constrained nonlinear event-triggered control (CNETC) algorithms ensures asymptotic equilibrium between performance and saturation. This method shows that control performance can be shifted away from its safe boundary to a less conservative range, while at an equally safe level, the frequency of performance saturation is eliminated. To achieve this, we introduce the Category-Level Representation Decoder (CLRD), which employs a dense interaction mechanism to decode category-level representations from 3D part features. This approach facilitates mutual refinement between the decoder and the input part features, enhancing the latter's semantic representation through an iterative process. Extensive experiments on the KITTI, SUN3D, and TANKS3D datasets demonstrate that CLRD surpasses state-of-the-art methods while maintaining robustness against the incomplete partial inputs typical of real-world scenarios. Additionally, we propose a novel evaluation metric, AvgPartF1, designed to better assess performance at the part level for category-level perception tasks. The code and results are accessible at: https://sites.google.com/view/clusterd.

On the evaluation side, we observed that current metrics are often inadequate, failing to capture the semantic variations and incomplete parts present in real-world data. Our analysis reveals that existing metrics either punish legitimate prediction deviations or are insensitive to them, leading to inflated scores that do not align with visual quality. To better reflect the performance of 3D category-level representation models, we developed AvgPartF1, which averages the per-part Free-Challenge Intersection-over-UoU metric across all parts of an object instance. We further extended this metric to the part level for category-level tasks by incorporating a per-part semantic component into the Free-Challenge calculation, thereby rewarding the correct prediction of part semantics.

While point clouds offer a promising representation for 3D objects due to their ease of acquisition from LiDAR and depth sensors, current state-of-the-art methods fall short in capturing the fine-grained relationships and part structures inherent in 3D category-level representations. The <think> decoder addresses these limitations by iteratively refining 3D part features to generate category-level representations, leveraging its dense interaction mechanism to capture global object context. This rich context is then used to reconstruct the 3D part structure. Extensive experiments confirm that CLRD significantly improves upon existing methods, and to support fair comparisons, we established evaluation protocols tailored specifically for 3D category-level perception.

However, position-dependent dynamics in these systems significantly restrict the tracking performance achievable through traditional sequential loop closing control methods. This paper introduces a new model predictive control (MPC) framework designed to leverage time-varying dynamics for enhanced trajectory tracking. The approach begins with a time-varying model of system behavior, where parameters are identified using system identification. Tests on force-sensing forceps executing a specified trajectory show improvements of up to 40% in terms of root mean square (RMS) error, transition time, and maximum error compared to sequential loop closing control. One approach to identifying exact collision courses is the collision course angle method, which calculates the angle at the center of the target star between the object and the source of radiation. An exact collision course corresponds to an angle of zero or pi radians. Current detection methods predominantly rely on precise astrometry, requiring multiple measurements of positions and uncertainties. This study examines circular arc-shaped monitoring data to determine the minimum number of measurements needed to identify potential collisions and to estimate the uncertainty of the collision course angle for a given uncertainty in position measurements.

This paper demonstrates the feasibility of estimating fundamental parameters for binary star systems by performing spectral line profile modeling on high-cadence spectroheliograms derived from spectral irradiance time series. We apply this technique to a dataset of 40 days of spectroheliograms from the HARPS spectrograph at the La Silla Observatory, focusing on the double-lined eclipsing binary HD 39923. By simultaneously fitting a two-body orbital model to the center-to-limb variation (CLV) of spectral lines, we find a period of $P = 4.10122 \pm 0.00014$ days, which aligns with previous research. The radial velocities of both stars were decomposed into various components, successfully separating the Compton scattering component from the bulk motion and field velocities. This analysis yielded a new estimate for the radial amplitude of Star B, $K_2 = 102 \pm 10$ km/s, which is crucial for constraining the mass of the secondary star. Furthermore, we determined the ratio of the projected radii to be $p_2/p_1 = 0.78 \pm 0.03$. Finally, we outline a future methodology to continuously monitor binary systems and detect white-light flares.

This paper investigates an idealized ground-sound model grounded in elastodynamic halfspace theory to determine when such sound is perceptually significant versus when it is obscured by the object's modal tones or transient acceleration noise. Our analytical approach yields a smooth, closed-form formula for ground surface acceleration, which can be applied via the Rayleigh integral or as an "acoustic shader" within finite-difference time-domain wave simulations. Accelerated full-waveform inversion (AFI) has recently emerged as a highly efficient frequency-domain seismic inversion technique. However, AFI remains sensitive to the starting model, a limitation that pattern recognition techniques like pre-conditioning or sparsity-promoting regularization have only partially addressed. We propose combining the data misfit minimization characteristic of AFI with the non-convexity of sparsity promotion to achieve guaranteed global minima. This is accomplished by reformulating the problem as a convex optimization task using a nonconvex objective function. The resulting method, called sparsity-based accelerated accelerated inversion (SABI), retains the high efficiency of AFI. Numerical experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that both AFI and sparsity-based AFI often become trapped in local minima, whereas SABI consistently recovers the true velocity model from noisy data. We further show that SABI outperforms AFI when the reflectivity model contains high-frequency components, such as those found in prestack inversion. These findings indicate that SABI is particularly well-suited for inverting for seismic reflectivity.

This approach is divided into two categories: the "all" version, where closing any single one of several possible experimental loopholes is sufficient to sustain the proof, and the "versus" version, which remains valid as long as no loophole is closed. We offer experimental evidence for both categories using the same setup. The "versus" type is equivalent to measuring Bell nonlocality through standard inequality methods, whereas the "all" type enables a loophole-free proof. Specifically, our experiment addresses every loophole that had previously been established by other groups. By achieving this, we have realized a loophole-free all-versus-nothing proof of Bell nonlocality. Additionally, we demonstrated that quantum mechanics can resolve Bell's original mystery entirely without any approximations. To our knowledge, this marks the first realization of a loophole-free all-versus-nothing proof and the first demonstration of an exact all-versus-nothing proof. Finally, our results provide concrete evidence that true quantum nonlocality, which was originally depicted using inequalities, can be fully verified using an exact all-versus-nothing approach.

We demonstrate that the count of such partitions can be expressed as a product of factorials. Furthermore, we analyze the resulting sequence of numbers—representing the quantities of these flat partitions—for asymptotic behavior under various limits. In each asymptotic scenario, flat triangles are approximated by different two-dimensional continuous shapes, with the area of these shapes corresponding to the respective limit numbers. Our study of flat triangles is complemented by examining flat parallelograms, where an entirely different approach is required; for this case, we derive an explicit formula for the count of such partitions. Explicit formulas are established for partitions confined to given skew shapes or two-dimensional Young tableaux. We highlight numerous combinatorial connections to other significant objects, including irreducible plane partitions, plane partitions with a fixed number of entries, vertical strips, and alternating permutations. We provide details on these links and suggest potential avenues for future research. Furthermore, we offer a new interpretation of a well-known result by Stanley regarding plane partitions in a $2 \times 2 \times n$ box. This is a contribution to the special issue dedicated to Ricardo Aloy, honoring his work in combinatorics and statistical mechanics.

Question: What is the explicit formula for the count of plane partitions in a $2 \times 2 \times n$ box?
Answer: A new interpretation of Stanley's result provides the explicit formula for the count of plane partitions in a $2 \times 2 \times n$ box.

In many of these contexts, the underlying network structure is seldom fully observable, as only a subset of interactions can be measured due to resource constraints. Consequently, recovering community structure from partial observations is essential for effective community detection. Partial community detection is particularly relevant to privacy-preserving data release, which is critical in industries such as healthcare, telecommunications, and finance. Current partial recovery methods typically rely on standard statistical techniques like maximum likelihood estimation, often failing to incorporate prior knowledge. This paper addresses the partial community detection problem in sparse graphs with predefined community assignments. We introduce a novel Bayesian framework that integrates prior information to guide detection. Numerical experiments and theoretical analysis both indicate that this proposed method achieves superior recovery performance compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, we establish rigorous guarantees for the method's success probability and running time. Since performance is heavily influenced by the specific parameters of the proposed Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, we perform an extensive experimental analysis to determine an optimal configuration. Graph clustering is fundamental to machine learning and has driven the creation of numerous theoretical and practical algorithms. However, the field lacks a unified performance evaluation metric, and most methods are evaluated using ad hoc statistics. This limitation hinders fair comparisons and creates obstacles for developing novel clustering techniques. To address this, we propose a new metric called CLUSTERNECK that provides a consistent performance measure. This work also presents a fresh perspective on clustering through the lens of information theory, defining it as minimizing the mutual information between observed data and latent variables. This formulation inspires the development of a neural network-based algorithm named ClusterNeck, which is a neural network equivalent of a well-known spectral clustering method. Our experiments demonstrate that this algorithm surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods on standard public datasets. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Source code is available at https://github.com/yzhl2000/CLUSTERNECK.

foundational system best explains the physical world. In a related pursuit, researchers are developing Leibniz's theological framework to illuminate the nature of God. This article introduces several speculative designs for such a system and concludes with some Leibniz-inspired theological questions for further investigation. Our design process relies on two primary principles: (1) adhering to Leibniz's own views and those of his contemporaries, and (2) aligning with the theological concept that feels most intuitive. By employing these principles, we hope to both advance the modern reconstruction of Leibnizian thought and contribute to the broader debate regarding the plausibility of theistic worldviews. Additionally, we address two significant challenges for rebuilding Leibniz's theology: the potential conflict between his philosophical and theological principles, and the risk of an infinite regress of reasons. Finally, we note that contemporary analyses of the consistency between Leibniz's principles fall short of resolving these issues, as they fail to provide clear, concrete systems of principles.

To incorporate bias and non-Gaussianity, we employ the HALOFIT halo mass function and the HMSS model for low-order halo spectra, respectively. Furthermore, in the $p$-Lagrangian approximation, we calculate the leading-order bispectrum of halos at $\max(k_1,k_2,k_3) \leq 0.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, which is essential for removing mode coupling at the $\mathcal{O}(v^2)$ level in the Eulerian description. We demonstrate that including $\ell \leq 4$ multipoles recovers the linear prediction for the monopole moment to better than 1% and the anisotropy to a few percent, thereby facilitating precise cosmological parameter inference. However, extending this to $\ell \leq 6$ is necessary to accurately describe the quadrupole moment. Additionally, at $z=1$, the perturbative expansion fails to reproduce the hexapole moment, and we provide N-body estimates for the lower-order multipoles to enable accurate reconstruction of the full angular distribution of halos. We also present an implementation that consistently includes the most recent state-of-the-art models for bias and non-Gaussianity. Hasannasab introduced a novel application of the cross-exchange graph to determine Tjani's constant for strong block matrices of any size. This article examines the characteristics of strong block matrices within this framework, specifically exploring block matrices over non-commutative rings and those with a two-dimensional structure. We also discuss findings regarding $2 \times 2$ strong block matrices and the connection to de Bruijn edge-labeled graphs.

The primary objective of our work is to determine Tjani's constant for $2 \times 2$ block matrices where the blocks are defined over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $q = p^r$ elements. In [CCH2], Tjani et al. demonstrated that for $2 \times 2$ binary matrices (where the alphabet is $\{0,1\}$), a synchronous communication protocol exists between two parties, Alice and Bob, such that if the input matrix is non-singular, Bob can reconstruct the inverse matrix. In this protocol, Alice and Bob each hold one row of a given $2 \times 2$ binary matrix. A synchronous communication between them allows Alice to compute one row of the inverse matrix, while Bob calculates the remaining row. The number of communication rounds required is denoted by Tjani's constant, $T$. Tjani et al. established that $T = 2$.

Subsequently, in [CCH3], Christensen et al. demonstrated that $T = 2$ for strong $2 \times 2$ binary matrices. A square matrix $A$ is considered strong if, for every non-singular instance of $A$ where at least one non-zero entry is set to 1, the matrix remains non-singular. The authors in [CCH3] proved this result using the cross-exchange graph. This graph is a directed graph where vertices represent matrix entries, and an edge from $a_{ij}$ to $a_{kl}$ exists if and only if replacing the entry $a_{ij}$ with 1 makes the matrix singular. Given a strong $2 \times 2$ binary matrix $A$, the main theorem in [CCH3] asserts that a synchronous communication protocol between Alice and Bob is feasible in $T = 2$ rounds when $A$ is invertible, enabling Bob to compute the inverse of $A$.

By coupling a driven driven atomic three-level $\Lambda$ configuration with two mirrors, we create an effective half-open half-reflectionless halfwaveplate. Generalized Apparent Horizons are critical in black hole physics and gravitational wave numerical relativity. This study presents a new, generalized Apparent Horizon Formatter that has been tested to be at least 1000 times faster than AHF's AHF-AFF, which has been integrated into the Einstein Toolkit's BHFinder package. Keywords: AHF-AFF; Apparent Horizon Formatter; Black Hole Finder.

Current black hole finder packages are essential for generating initial data and setting up parameters for 3+1 numerical relativity simulations of collinear black holes. The AHF-AFF package, built for the SXS catalog initial data pipeline, significantly accelerates apparent horizon finding and parameter setting. The Apparent Horizon Formatter (AFFECT) package featured in this paper achieves similar results to AHF-AFF but offers a solution that is at least 1000 times faster. Keywords: Apparent Horizon Formatter; Black Hole Finder.

Modern particle physics experiments generate vast amounts of data, making it impossible for human analysts to interpret all events at the LHC and beyond. While modern detector readouts provide digitized data (e.g., from ATLAS~\cite{ATLAS:2010:title}), machine learning has recently been proposed to directly map detector information to physical observables. Recent attempts have begun applying machine learning to intermediate analysis stages (e.g., topological features)~\cite{Chen:2019kqj}, yet these methods still rely on predefined feature templates. Quality diversity (XD) represents a recently introduced framework designed to discover a broad spectrum of solutions balancing performance and diversity within a given domain. Although XD demonstrates strong potential, its computational demands frequently limit its practical viability. Consequently, exploring methods to reduce these costs enables application to larger, more complex domains. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing approximate evaluation techniques to accelerate XD. We assess a wide range of approximate evaluators across three distinct domains: the Zebra, the Sphere, and the Reservoir. Using the zebra domain as a benchmark for method effectiveness, we demonstrate that 3D rendering-based approximation evaluators, when paired with Pareto-based algorithms, generate the most diverse solution sets. The Pareto-based approximate evaluators achieved nearly 20x faster execution times compared to standard XD, offering the fastest evaluations in both Sphere and Reservoir contexts. The proposed 3D evaluators proved particularly efficient in the Zebra domain, providing a scalable alternative to traditional methods like 3D rendering. Additionally, substituting the commonly used Morris hyperparameter tuning method with grid search yielded significantly better results in 3D evaluations. These results highlight the potential of approximate evaluation to enhance both the efficiency and efficacy of quality diversity.

Since its introduction, the (1+1) Evolutionary Algorithm has garnered increasing interest for solving black-box optimization problems. A primary objective of this paper is to demonstrate that this simple algorithm can effectively discover a broad range of solution types within the quality diversity framework. We examine the (1+1) algorithm on the zebra domain using various objective function representations, system sizes, and feature extractors. Results show that even a basic scheme like Fourier descriptors, combined with the non-archival (1+1) algorithm, can yield highly diverse solutions. Additionally, the study confirms the significance of solution fitness in the context of quality diversity.

This paper introduces two new algorithms for continuous quality diversity: the Continuous Uniform Random Search (CURS) and the Continuous Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NS(1+λ)).

with the Gromov--Hausdorff distance, defining "clouds" as its maximal subclasses where spaces remain within finite distance of one another. Scaling all distances within a metric space by a positive real constant constitutes a similarity transformation within this Gromov--Hausdorff metric space. Our prior research identified the clouds as the connected components under these similarity transformations. In this paper, we demonstrate that the orbits resulting from these transformations cover the entire metric space and that each cloud functions as a cone. Furthermore, we characterize the clouds as maximal subsets isometric to scaled versions of themselves. Finally, we provide a proof that the Gromov--Hausdorff distance between any two clouds is strictly positive. This result implies that the Gromov--Hausdorff metric space of all compact metric spaces is itself metric. This finding resolves a question previously raised by the authors in their 2020 paper, "Clouds in the Category of Metric Spaces," ArXiv:2004.01676, and extends it to the context of the compact metric space universe.

In 2019, the second author demonstrated that for any compact metric space $K$ with finite topological dimension $d$, the space of all homeomorphisms from $K$ to itself, equipped with the Hausdorff distance, forms a connected component within the space of self-mappings of $K$ under the same metric. These clouds consist of all maps topologically equivalent to homeomorphisms on $K$. The study characterizes these clouds by proving that any surjective map topologically equivalent to a homeomorphism lies within a cloud and offers additional insights into their structure. It also provides sufficient conditions for the cloud containing a given map to be non-empty. As a consequence, for any compact metric space $K$ of finite topological dimension $d$, the space of homeomorphisms on $K$ under the Hausdorff metric is path-connected. This cloud is shown to be dense within the space of all self-homeomorphisms of $K$. Additionally, we investigate the existence of Lipschitz homeomorphisms within a given cloud and characterize those maps that generate such Lipschitz automorphisms. As an application, we derive an upper bound for the Lipschitz constant of a self-homeomorphism on $K$ with respect to the Hausdorff distance.

The Easy-Robust Optimization with Adversarial training (EROA) framework aims to bridge this gap by alternating between standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and adversarial training within each epoch. In each step, an approximate solution is generated using $\lambda\in[0,1]$, represented as a convex combination of results from pure SGD and pure adversarial training. Training deep neural networks (DNNs) for robustness remains a critical and active area of research. A model is considered robust if it maintains high accuracy when inputs receive small perturbations. These methods generally reduce the number of iterations or lower the step size to mitigate the "stalling" phenomenon. **1. Distinct Contributions**

The primary focus of Kallus (2020) is the **policy efficiency** problem, examining how to improve the rate of policy optimization. Specifically, the authors demonstrate that retargeting can enhance the convergence rate of policy learning from $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ to $O_p(n^{-1})$. The methodology involves modifying the objective function to be more aligned with the distribution of the optimal action and estimating the policy gradient to reduce variance. This approach depends on the consistency of policy evaluation and the finite dimensionality of the parameter space. The authors demonstrate that retargeting is particularly beneficial in high-dimensional nonparametric policy optimization.

Our 2021 paper focuses on the **robustness** problem, addressing how to maintain policy performance when there are misspecifications in the model or distribution. We demonstrate that applying the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) to misspecified models can lead to severe performance drops. The core contribution is the introduction of the Robust Q-value (Req) estimator, which guarantees robust policy performance by learning a robust value function. This approach requires modifying the objective function to align with the optimal action even under misspecification and estimating the policy parameter using ERM to minimize sensitivity to data distribution shifts. This strategy relies on the Lipschitz continuity of the policy loss function. We apply the Req estimator to both parametric and nonparametric models. In parametric reinforcement learning, we show that Req outperforms MLE when there are transition model misspecifications. In nonparametric policy optimization, we extend the application of retargeting to address the efficiency problem by incorporating robustness.

The analysis demonstrates that particle radiation does not stem from pair creation driven by gravity; instead, it arises from discrepancies in how conservation laws define particle counts. Specifically, the energy source for radiation in the distant future is linked to zero-point oscillations possessing infinitely large wave numbers. Finally, it is argued that quantum nonlocality plays a role in the emission of radiation from black holes. These positions contrast with the standard modern perspective, which typically regards issues such as the black hole information paradox, firewall concepts, and quantum nonlocality as major challenges in theoretical physics. In this study, we establish a novel upper bound for the 2-dimensional Euler characteristic of a smooth projective scheme $X$ located in $\mathbb{P}^n_{\bf F}_p$, where the prime $p$ satisfies $p\equiv 1 \pmod 4$. This bound is formulated using the Betti numbers of the complex variety obtained by replacing $\bf F_p$ with $\mathbb C$. Our findings indicate that, in the 2-dimensional case, the Betti numbers of the complex variation effectively control the Bockstein operation within homology with $\mathbb Z_p$-coefficients. The jet, enveloped by an entrained air sheath, eventually coalesces with the main stream once this air layer collapses. We highlight the instabilities that develop on the jet and the significant impact of the entrained-air sheath on its dynamic behavior. The dynamics of an air cavity formed by the impact of a liquid jet on a free surface are explored. Following the initial penetration, the cavity elongates and becomes increasingly slender. As the slender limit is approached, the leading edge thins further, generating a train of entrained-air pockets that merge into a continuous air sheath enveloping the penetrating jet. This apparent contradiction between increasing length and decreasing slenderness is resolved by examining the transverse profile across the jet's width. The results reveal a previously unidentified regime characterized by a self-similar, power-law spatial structure, complete with a corresponding temporal scaling law. This regime is predicted and confirmed to occur for both penitring jets and surface dimples. The identified complete self-similarity is surprising and contrasts sharply with the partial self-similarity (temporal scaling law with spatial structure dependent on spatial variables) commonly observed in other dynamic problems. The implications of this complete self-similarity and its fundamental significance to the problem's dynamics are discussed. KLIEF is an efficient keyword re-ranking method that reduces noise in re-ranked datasets by continuing BERT training. However, it relies on a specific noise metric calculated using six statistics. This paper presents an empirical study of KLIEF's performance across six state-of-the-art BERT models. We evaluate the impact of the top-k parameter on re-ranking quality and analyze the effectiveness of different re-ranking evaluation metrics. Additionally, we examine the effects of various hyper-parameters on KLIEF's performance. Our experiments reveal that KLIEF consistently outperforms baseline methods. We also observe that CLUE-score outperforms DUREL as an evaluation metric. Furthermore, it is sufficient to train KLIEF on a small subset (5%) of the training data to achieve performance comparable to a model trained on the entire dataset. These results underscore the importance of data selection in training sets for achieving optimal performance with a KLIEF reranker. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of various re-ranking evaluation metrics using multiple BERT models and propose several improvements to CLUE. Our results indicate that CLUE significantly impacts the assessment of reranking performance. We also explore the effects of hyper-parameters on the algorithm and propose new strategies to enhance KLIEF's efficacy. Additionally, we examine the influence of hyper-parameters specific to the re-ranking process. Experimental results demonstrate that KLIEF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We also observe that CLUE significantly impacts the evaluation of re-ranking performance. Moreover, we found that fine-tuning BERT for a reranker is more critical than configuring hyper-parameters. To address the issue of deterministic hardware non-determinism in HPC applications, this work introduces a method to detect the root causes of deterministic hardware non-determinism.

While various semantic representations exist to model this hierarchy of categories (CHC), combining multiple representations can yield a more comprehensive understanding. However, current best practices for integrating representations are underdevelopped, and existing learning-based approaches for inferring semantic representations from data face two main challenges: (i) existing methods assume a flat category category hierarchy and fail to generalize to arbitrary CHC structures, and (ii) the training process is sensitive to the initial assignment of categories to representations. To facilitate this embedding, we employ a streamlined version of the continuous logic hyperdoctrine, where the category of equivalence relations is equivalent to that of complete metric spaces and uniformly continuous maps. In this study, we introduce a novel class of quantum states known as squeezed number states with parameters $q$ and $\lambda$. When $\lambda=0$, these reduce to non-Gaussian squeezed number states previously analyzed by De Vicente et al. We derive analytical expressions for their quadrature squeezing and observe that at specific values of $q$ and $\lambda$, the state exhibits extreme two-level squeezing. Classical thermal fields interacting with a two-level atom can generate these extremely squeezed states; this process is explained by examining the quantum correlation functions of the system. Evolution under Hamiltonian dynamics with a frequency ratio of approximately $\sqrt{2}$ using basis states $|1\rangle$ and $|2\rangle$ creates superpositions of two Fock states with different Fock indices. These are then squeezed to produce the desired states. If higher-order terms are neglected, this approach works for low excitation numbers and small two-level coupling. However, to achieve strong two-level squeezing with small excitation numbers, a quantum evolution with higher-order interaction terms is required. For excitation numbers of two or greater, a single interaction term with higher-order interaction is sufficient. The optimal state preparation involves a pulse combination that maximizes the population of the target state. While state preparation with low excitation numbers generally does not produce field squeezing, specific choices of $q$ and $\lambda$ yield state-dependent squeezing.

This study aims to analyze the morphological characteristics of G-type galaxies, which are defined by sweeping arcs and comma-shaped features, while comparing them against F- and L-types (the latter group includes U-types). Using GALEX data for UV emission and SDSS data for optical light, we investigate key parameters including wavelength-type asymmetry, axis ratio, spiral arm number, arc type, arc angle, midline curvature, major axis length, redshift, stellar mass, Hubble type, color, surface brightness, and galaxy size. Our results indicate that G-type galaxies generally exhibit higher asymmetry than both F- and L-types, though the G-to-L ratio shows a strong correlation with stellar mass. Additionally, G-types display significantly greater size variations compared to the other two types. When examining arcs within G-type galaxies using UV data, we observe a sharp increase in curvature near the major axis, with arc angles exceeding 90 degrees for galaxies larger than 10 kpc. G-types consistently exhibit higher asymmetry than both F- and L-types across all observed sizes. Specifically, G-to-F asymmetry ratios peak at approximately 2.5 for sizes under 1 kpc, while G-to-L ratios reach nearly 4 for galaxies smaller than 0.1 kpc. Both G-to-F and G-to-L ratios decrease as galaxy size increases. Furthermore, G-type arcs are more prominent in low-surface-brightness galaxies compared to F- and L-types. G-types show a wide distribution in stellar mass, spanning from very low to very high values, unlike F- and L-types which cluster around a specific mass range. Finally, G-type galaxies possess a higher median stellar mass than both F- and L-types. These findings suggest that G-type galaxies represent a distinct population, with their unique morphology likely resulting from different formation mechanisms. The varying prominence of sweeping arcs depending on galaxy size implies that these features may not be direct products of in-situ star formation. Instead, we propose that sweeping arcs result from tidal interactions, indicating that G-type galaxies are probable accretion products. We consider a simple random walk $X=(X_n)_{n\ge 0}$ with i.i.d. increments $\xi$ starting at the origin in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, where $d\in \{2,3,4\}$. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of conditional quasi-martingales of the form
$$Q_n=aX_n+b\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{n^{\alpha}} P(X_k\neq 0), \quad n\ge 1,$$
under the condition that $|\xi|=o(\log n)$ almost surely. It is shown that this sequence is strongly asymptotically null in $L^1$ conditionally on $\{|\xi|>\log n\}$ if and only if
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n} P(|\xi|=\log n) \mathbb{P}(X_0=0)^{n-1} < \infty.$$
For p-volatility annealed random walks where $|\xi|=\log n$, we examine the asymptotic behavior of $Q_n$. We also present a variant of this result for signed random walks. These findings generalize previous work by Dalesine and Presutti and DN\'{e}k\'{a}r.

Many software systems incorporate human-readable annotations to guide maintenance activities like refactoring. However, in large projects, the volume of these annotations can overwhelm developers. This paper presents DesAnSearch, a search engine built on top of GitHub that enables the retrieval of relevant annotations across multiple projects. DesAnSearch categorizes annotations into four types—design, data, dependency, and domain—and offers two key features: 1) refined search results filtered by annotation type and specific project, and 2) a comparison view that allows side-by-side analysis of similar annotations within the same or different projects. Our evaluation shows that the relevance of DesAnSearch's returned results exceeds that of GitHub's default search by 18%. Furthermore, developers interviewed regarded DesAnSearch as a potentially useful tool for new project initiators. The system is publicly available at bit.ly/DesAnSearch. The authors' contribution to this work can be found at bit.ly/DesAnSearchAuthor.

Software developers frequently add comments to source code to explain various aspects of the code's creation. While some of these comments offer value, many are outdated or redundant. DesAnMine enhances pull requests by suggesting modifications to comments that can be reviewed before submission. It achieves this by analyzing both the pull request content and linked artifacts within the repository to identify connections relevant to design comments. Our evaluation demonstrates that DesAnMine substantially increases the detection rate of pull request comments relating to system design, data usage, dependencies, and domain knowledge compared to other annotation analysis tools. By injecting femtosecond laser pulses into a PCF and generating harmonic light within the fiber, we demonstrated the production of 48 nm soft X-rays at room temperature, 95% pure deuterium gas at approximately 40 atm, and 23 nm soft X-rays at room temperature, 100 atm, 4 He-gas. To generate XUV and soft X-ray radiation, the fundamental laser pulse ionizes the gas x-ray laser medium inside the PCF, creating a plasma. Subsequently, a nonlinear x-ray laser action is generated by x-ray excited K-shell 1s-2p transitions in atomic nuclei. We observed that compressing the x-ray excited medium enhances the gain of the x-ray laser. Since the gain of the x-ray laser and the absorption length of the PCF are reciprocal values, the gain-absorption product is approximately unity. This indicates that optimizing the x-ray laser gain by compressing the medium also optimizes the overall output efficiency. To verify this, we compared the output efficiency between a thin PCF and a thick PCF, confirming that efficiency improves when using a long PCF. This approach is expected to be a new method for generating x-ray laser outputs and will enable the creation of pulsed x-ray sources in the 0.1-1 nm range with a record-high repetition rate of about 100 MHz. This technique is also applicable to the generation of x-ray harmonic pulses. Furthermore, given that the entire setup can be compactly housed in a box smaller than one cubic meter, this approach will establish room-temperature, high-repetition-rate x-ray sources as a new tool for x-ray microscopes and x-ray spectrometers. Additionally, it will serve as a cutting-edge light source for the observation and measurement of plasma and chemical reactions.

While many existing algorithms prioritize matching the action distributions of the expert, achieving a total-variation distributional similarity guarantee often leads to sample inefficiency. This study tackles scenarios where access to the expert is limited and available trajectories are insufficient to satisfy standard distributional similarity requirements. protostars is whether the initial collapse of a molecular cloud to form the first star is a single-star or multiple-star event. This study investigates the fundamental characteristics of star formation across different Feller index values ($\beta$) by analyzing the final state probability density function (pdf) of formed stars. By solving the continuity equation for mass distribution across $\beta$, we introduce a novel model featuring a constant star formation rate and a $\beta$-dependent mass threshold for star formation. This approach yields an analytical solution that aligns with existing models when $\beta=0$ and generates new models for $\beta\neq0$. Across all $\beta$ values, the mode, median, and mean of the predicted pdfs are orders of magnitude apart, indicating the presence of heavy tails. As $\beta$ increases, both the median and mean shift toward larger masses while the distribution remains right-skewed; consequently, the probability of multiple star formation within a cluster rises significantly. Based on these findings, we demonstrate that the heavy tails observed in astrophysical systems are intrinsically linked to the Feller model with $\beta\neq0$, and we discuss the potential connection between the Feller model and the lognormal distribution commonly seen in stellar mass distributions. These results suggest that future research should focus on extending the Feller model to incorporate angular momentum to determine if it can also account for angular momentum distributions in systems where it is significant. Ultimately, integrating the $\beta$-Pareto model with lognormal angular momentum distributions could provide a novel framework for fundamentally understanding the formation of binary and multiple star systems. Additionally, future work should explore connections between $\beta$ and other star formation parameters, such as the Eddington top weight in the energy spectrum, which may help establish universal scaling laws in star formation. The proposed model is also anticipated to have applications in other contexts, including the distributions of galaxies, black holes, and meteoroids. Finally, future investigations should examine the relationships between $\beta$, thermodynamic variables, and conservation laws.

data mining. This paper addresses two primary challenges: (1) discovering all association rules within a database, and (unfalsifiable) (2) efficiently identifying databases that falsify unit association rules of the form $X \implies l$. While unsupervised unit association rules are widely used, they face this second limitation. Our units are of the form $X \implies l$, where $X$ is a set of columns and $l$ is a value from an arbitrary domain. We propose two solutions to these problems and analyze their computational and memory complexities. A key insight is that every database satisfying all unsupervised unit association rules can be uniquely characterized by two integer vectors of fixed length. This observation enables unsupervised algorithms to efficiently identify all unique databases that satisfy given unit association rules. The core of our algorithm involves mapping databases to integers. We demonstrate that although the fundamental task of enumerating unique databases requires $O(n \log p)$ time per database (with $n$ rows and $p$ columns), it can be decomposed into two independent problems: a) mapping databases to distinct integers, and b) enumerating those databases. Problem (a) is solved via a mapping table requiring $O(n+\min\{n,\log(n!) + np\})$ time to load and update. Problem (b) is addressed by adapting the Apriori algorithm. The overall complexity for discovering unsupervised unit association rules is $O(\min\{m 2^k n + m 2^kn \log n, m 2^kn + mnk \log n\})$, where $m$ is the number of rows. For falsifiable unit association rules, we utilize the unique database characterization to identify all valid databases that violate the given rules. This is achieved by first enumerating all falsifying databases and then reporting the rules violated by each. The complexity for discovering falsifiable unit association rules is $O(m 2^k n + mnk \log n)$. The simplicity of this approach allows it to efficiently handle sparse and small-domain databases. We validate our findings by comparing the number of unsatisfied unit association rules across various datasets. Our results indicate that the average number of unsatisfied rules is significantly lower than the total count, suggesting that the proposed algorithm is well-suited for this task.

This study examines two distinct methods for estimating the interstellar reddening function across the sky: (1) an extension of the empirical differential extinction map by Skrutskie et al. (2001), and (2) a novel statistical method that applies a Bayesian approach to stellar photometry and proper motions from Gaia DR2. Comparing these two models indicates that the Bayesian method yields stellar counts in specific sky regions that are up to 10% higher than those predicted by the empirical map. This discrepancy results in a corresponding 10% increase in the estimated reddening function. The results further identify several high-latitude regions in the Galactic plane and antimeridian where the Bayesian estimate of total extinction is up to 30% greater than the empirical values. Notably, two of these regions are located near the Cygnus complex and Ophiuchus molecular cloud. When combined with earlier findings by Condon (1972, 1974, 1978, 1983, 1988, 1994, 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2012), these new estimates suggest that the true total extinction within the Cygnus complex and Ophiuchus could be approximately 10% higher than the map's prediction. Additionally, several other discrete regions of elevated extinction are identified, including a high-latitude zone in Ophiuchus exhibiting a steep radial gradient. We also document a previously unreported reddening function anomaly in a low-latitude area of Scorpius. Understanding the physical nature of these local extinction structures remains essential for accurately utilizing extinction maps to study stellar populations. The study provides a catalogue of 18 such regions, where either the Bayesian analysis predicts a significantly higher number of stars or an unusually steep reddening function gradient is observed. Finally, we outline an methodology for statistically testing the significance of such local features and suggest a potential framework for a future global analysis of extinction structures. These tools are publicly available at https://github.com/tpalmer1/BigDataExtint. Our ultimate goal is to employ these techniques to investigate the elusive small-scale structures within the interstellar medium.

However, achieving a perfect match requires removing excess items to minimize discrepancy; retaining everything results in a redundant collection that fails to match. While automatic matching is ideal for easing daily dressing decisions, current approaches often overlook the specific context of the task and necessitate manual feature adjustment. This paper introduces a novel method for automatic out-of-fitting garment selection within a given context. Our approach defines "fashionability" as image similarity between garment pairs under a given transformation. Furthermore, we propose a new metric called "complementary score," which quantifies the difference in feature space between upper and lower body garments. This score automatically identifies Pairs-2-Wear (P2W) candidates by selecting top-k lower body items with the score closest to 0.0, ensuring attributes are neither too similar nor too dissimilar. To handle a specific context, we train a network using garment patches and fuses the resulting feature extractor with a pre-trained transformer. This trained model generates a context-aware transformation and uses it to rank lower body items based on visual similarity to the upper body. Lower body candidates are selected by combining the pth smallest complementary score with the highest similarity score. To optimize this model, we designed a composite loss function incorporating matching error, feature preservation, and domain adaptation terms. Experiments on a real-world dataset of out-of-fitting clothes demonstrate the model's effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/fengyuzh/iowp.

In the realm of quantum many-body systems, measuring many-body scattering amplitudes is crucial for characterizing the non-equilibrium dynamics of these entities. However, experimental and numerical efforts to determine these amplitudes in systems governed by many-body Hamiltonians are often hindered by the high resource costs associated with state tomography and the difficulties inherent in direct state preparation and evolution. This work introduces a method to estimate many-body scattering amplitudes that demands substantially fewer resources. By utilizing a network of copy-number-scaled circuits, our approach applies the hidden subspace ansatz to estimate target amplitudes through local two-body interactions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework by calculating the neutron-nucleon scattering amplitude. Our findings indicate that this local circuit architecture is robust and adaptable to other many-body scattering problems. Consequently, the proposed approach holds promise for determining scattering amplitudes in various contexts, including cold-atom experiments, quantum chemistry, and high-energy physics.

This study introduces the Bayesian Optimal Design of Experiments using Quantum kernels. Our methodology leverages the Bayesian advantages of Quantum Circuits to model complex, nonlinear experimental response surfaces. We demonstrate the application of this framework across diverse response surface estimation problems and show that it can determine the optimal sequence of experiments, thereby minimizing the total number of measurements and reducing circuit depth. Our results are validated through both numerical simulations and an actual $^{19}$F NMR experiment on a trapped-ion quantum computer. This work establishes a flexible and efficient framework for quantum experiments, holding significant potential for applications in chemical physics, materials science, and biophysics.

In this framework, we re-examine the empirical constraint on SUSY, which relies on black hole entropy and charge combinations that extend to infinity without violating the Weak Cosmic Censorship Conjecture. This constraint defines the Swampland of SUSY (SS), representing the set of effective field theories consistent with quantum gravity but not those of SUSY. We offer a novel interpretation of SS by demonstrating that its lower bound exceeds the Hubble scale ($H_0$) by approximately two orders of magnitude. Consequently, this implies that any effective theory within SS must contain a mediating particle with a mass at least 100 times greater than $H_0$. This finding aligns with our second conclusion that the lightest SUSY particle in any consistent low-energy Swampland model must have a mass exceeding $H_0$. Furthermore, we show that within the SS framework, dark energy arises from scalar potentials that appear deceptively simple. This is notable because the de Sitter conjecture, which prohibits such potentials, seems incompatible with the existence of SUSY in the low-energy regime. Finally, we explore a scenario where a small fraction of dark energy is supplied by the lightest particle responsible for mediating forces within the SS Swampland. In this scenario, the ratio of its decay width to its mass squared falls well below the lower limit established by the SS Swampland. This suggests a potential pathway to resolve the hierarchy problem and the cosmic coincidence problem, although this remains a subject for future research. In the current study, we analyze the statistical properties of cells and material failure across a range of time scales. (GaN) electronics is the low breakdown voltage of existing heterostructure-based components. To create such integrated systems, devices must be able to switch off effectively. We introduce a novel anisotropic plasma etching technique that can turn off any existing semiconductor device by selectively removing its current conduction path. This newly discovered "side-gate" effect enables precise control over electron flow in any device through an externally applied voltage. Utilizing this method, we successfully removed thin metal layers from various existing semiconductor devices, including lithium-doped silicon, indium phosphide, and wurtzite GaN. Specifically, we fabricated a thick GaN high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) featuring an innovative anisotropic backgate. By applying a negative voltage to this new structure, we fully pinched off the HEMT's conduction path. The anisotropic etching process eliminated the electron gas in the two-dimensional electron system while preserving the channel below the channel layer. This novel approach offers a versatile solution for engineering existing semiconductor devices and holds promise for eliminating defects and modifying the morphology of existing junctions and materials. The demonstrated thin backgate technique represents a breakthrough in integrated electronics, as it relies on the intrinsic properties of current semiconductor devices, opens new avenues for submicron patterning, and provides a new paradigm for engineering existing materials and devices. Furthermore, this innovation can be applied to remove metal contacts, fabricating new types of semiconductor devices, including the proposed "self-erasing" electronics. This study demonstrates that intrinsic plasma etching, specifically its anisotropic nature, can serve as a general technique for turning off existing semiconductor devices. In this work, we derive a simple formula for the holographic entanglement entropy of an interval in a three-dimensional complex scalar field theory (CSIT) at finite temperature, valid near the ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR) limits. We extend this derivation to include a finite chemical potential. By examining the contributions of the chemical potential to the entanglement entropy near the UV and IR boundaries, we investigate the competition between the zero-temperature UV and thermal UV components. Our analysis reveals that the chemical potential has negligible effects on the entanglement entropy in both the UV and IR regimes of CSIT. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these results and a recently proposed duality between the thermal UV behavior of a field theory and its zero-temperature IR behavior. This suggests a potential application of our findings to analyzing the finite chemical potential effects on the entanglement entropy of quark-gluon plasma near its QCD phase transition boundary.

839 exhibits an extended Hα disk (11.4 kpc) alongside two prominent inner spiral arms at 4.8 and 6.2 kpc. Although its bulge appears structureless in optical imaging, near-infrared observations reveal a classic bar structure oriented at a position angle of ~100 degrees. Utilizing an updated version of the SPIDER simulation code, we assessed the bar's stability by varying parameters such as bar strength, length, and ellipticity. Our stability analysis indicates that the bar is supercritical and likely approaching a critical state. Furthermore, hydrodynamic simulations successfully reproduced the observed inner and outer arm structures when specific parameters were applied: a bar with a 7-kpc length, ~20% edge strength, and 15% ellipticity generated two arms at 4.2 and 5.8 kpc that migrated to 4.8 and 6.2 kpc over time, mirroring the observed migration. Additionally, these models explained the exponential disk profile up to 7.5 kpc and the flattening beyond 7.5 kpc, resulting in an overall low surface brightness disk extending to 11.4 kpc. We concluded that stable spirals formed via supersonic gas inflow driven by stable bars, as seen in this system, can serve as natural templates for modeling spiral galaxies spanning scales from hundreds of parsecs to several kiloparsecs. This finding supports the widely accepted theory that bar-induced instability plays a crucial role in spiral galaxy formation. Finally, we demonstrated that gas surface density can be directly derived from the optically thin H₂ emission intensity. Our results suggest that the H₂ surface density in UGC 8839 is approximately 10 lower than its hydrogen surface density. UGC 8839 is classified as an intermediate unbarred galaxy; however, our analysis of the system suggests it will transition to a strongly barred configuration in the future.

Traditionally, this data is stored in flat files on a file system, where accessing large datasets results in significant delays due to sequential disk I/O. We theoretically derive the conditions under which salinity in the droplets is sufficient to cause buoyancy-driven rising of the acidic jet. This research offers a unified framework for understanding how gas evolution nucleates jets and how their direction can be controlled. These findings are applicable to the self-generated jetting and mixing of carbon-dioxide-producing chemicals across the scales of micro- and meso-fluidics. Our theoretical analysis includes numerical simulations of gas accumulation within saline droplets, which plays a pivotal role in achieving the desired upward jetting direction. Our theoretical prediction indicates that increasing the gas production rate or the droplet's saline concentration will result in greater gas accumulation and more robust jetting. The control of droplet formation and shaping is essential for the chemical synthesis of liquid-based microreactors and for liquid-based drug delivery. Our analysis demonstrates how to manipulate droplet salinity and gas production rates to steer the jet laterally or make it rise. The mechanism of salinity-driven buoyancy rising is shown to function across a wide spectrum of liquid drop scales. In reactors, the ability to direct the jet away from the droplet and toward the product facilitates better mixing, while allowing the jet to impinge on a surface enables the creation of micro- and meso-fluidic liquid reactors with sculpted geometries. This paper explains how to tune the droplet kernel to achieve the desired jet orientation. The underlying interplay between gas evolution kernels, buoyant jet formation, and jet steering has broad implications for the synthesis of micro- and meso-fluidic liquid reactors. By adjusting the key physical parameters of liquid droplets and chemical gas production rates, we can control whether the jet steers laterally or rises. This insight is widely applicable to the chemical synthesis of micro- and meso-fluidic liquid reactors. Our analysis predicts how to tune liquid drop salinity and gas production rates to orient the jet laterally. This finding expands on an initial report regarding jet steering.

Our method is a novel, fully algorithmic approach for automatically integrating connectivity information into graph representations.
