Over the past decade, deep learning on graphs has emerged as a dominant technique for analyzing structured data. However, the primary limitation of most current graph neural networks (GNNs) is their reliance on fixed aggregation functions for neighbor information, which restricts their ability to adapt to varying neighbor importance. Although existing methods attempt to mitigate this by learning aggregation functions, they typically offer a global design applicable to all nodes or local design at the edge level, failing to account for hierarchical structures. Our work introduces an innovative approach to automatically incorporate connectivity patterns at a global scale by learning a connectivity adjacency matrix. We evaluate the learned patterns across multiple datasets and tasks, showing that this technique is both scalable and effective. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach is complementary to local designs and can be easily integrated into popular GNN architectures. Experimental results on classification tasks with human interpretability indicate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with improvements of up to 14.5% on some datasets. We also prove that our method can automatically discover connectivity patterns that are interpretable by humans.

We evaluate the technique on classification tasks with human interpretability, showing that it surpasses baseline performances by up to 14.5% on certain datasets. The method is scalable, capable of handling large-scale datasets, and offers a global design perspective to complement existing local approaches. All experiments are reproducible through the use of standard datasets and open-source code. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/justinfiorelli/CITAG. Clinical radiology reports contain crucial details concerning a patient's condition and are vital for subsequent diagnostic and treatment decisions. While numerous studies have explored automated methods for radiology report generation and information extraction in recent years, a comprehensive review of the current state of research in this domain has not yet been published. The findings across three sections—report summarization, entity extraction, and relation extraction—demonstrate that neural network-based methods have significantly outperformed traditional models. This article offers an extensive overview of current research in this field. Along the way, we address three key questions: (a) Can every hyperbolic 3-manifold admit a taut foliation? (b) Can the norm of every hyperbolic Euler class be realized? (c) Can the norm of every hyperbolic Euler class with first Betti number zero be realized? Our analysis reveals that the answers to these problems are largely dependent on the solutions provided in this very paper. Additionally, we examine the significant open problem regarding the existence of plane fields whose Euler classes exhibit a norm exceeding one. Furthermore, we discuss the intricate problem of determining which plane fields on 3-spheres can be represented by Morse functions. Finally, we explore a broad family of open problems concerning the Eisinger-McMullen plane field. All of these issues stem from their deep connection to fundamental problems in the general theory of hyperbolic 3-manifolds. This work is dedicated to the memory of Cliff Gordon. Keywords: hyperbolic 3-manifolds, plane fields, foliations, Euler classes, Morse functions. Math. Subj. Class. No.: 57M50.

Analyzing 11 major cryptocurrencies across 11 major global currencies from August 2011 to May 2022, we examined the long-term relationships and dynamic structure within their price systems. We extend weak noise theory, which translates large deviations into a non-linear hydrodynamic framework, by demonstrating its full solvability via a link to the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Free electron lasers (FELs) capable producing ultra-short pulses in the few hundred attosecond range have been anticipated in prior studies. However, existing schemes generally depend on external drivers or face constraints related to the coherence time. This study proposes a revised chirp-taper scheme that overcomes the reliance on external drivers and expands the temporal bandwidth of attosecond pulses beyond the radiation's coherence time. By implementing a chirp-matching condition at the FEL instability threshold and applying a linear slope to the seeding curve, attosecond pulses can be continuously stretched. Utilizing numerical simulations for the XUV and soft X-ray FEL facility FLASH, we predict the generation of pulses with peak powers exceeding 100 MW at several hundred attoseconds long. This represents a significant step toward next-generation attosecond science facilities. Keywords: Free electron laser; Chirp-taper scheme; Attosecond pulse; FLASH; XUV and soft X-ray FEL.

Within Einstein gravity, the sufficient condition for this implies an upper bound on the Bondi mass $m$, specifically $|\dot{m}|\leqslant 0.3810~c^3/G$. This bound corresponds to the rate of change of the mass of a maximally massive black hole, equivalent to the maximum power output of a Hawking process. Conversely, within Hořava gravity, the sufficient condition places no restrictions on $\dot{m}$, allowing black holes to be effectively invisible. Consequently, black hole quasi-stars of the Hořava type could radiate energy for an arbitrarily long duration, a mechanism that in the late universe could accelerate their expansion to the speed of light. This scenario could be observed in early cosmic quasar light if gravitational waves from massive black holes were intense enough to cause significant dimming of the light en route to us. In this framework, a black hole of mass $M$ could radiate a quantity of energy up to ${\cal O}(Mc^2)$. This suggests that in Hořava gravity, the Hawking temperature need not be positive, and black holes with a higher Hawking coefficient $\lambda>0$ could grow by absorbing radiation. Furthermore, this theory offers a mechanism for the trans-Planckian problem, addressing the question of how gravity can remain weak at high energies without violating quantum mechanics. In this context, gravity weakens at high energies because energy is not conserved, as dictated by the non-zero curvature of the Fierz-Pauli equation for massive gravity. This energy loss manifests as gravitational radiation. Additionally, gravitational waves in this framework possess a longitudinal component of degree 5, rather than the tensorial component (degree 2) found in Einstein gravity. The emission of gravitational radiation causes energy to decrease, causing matter to fragment into black holes of the Hořava type during the densest stages of the Big Bang. This indicates that the theory supports private sector black holes. In this scenario, private black holes could constitute the majority of dark matter in the universe. If gravitational radiation from private black holes is intense, it will cause a noticeable dimming of light traveling through space to us. This effect could be tested by comparing the luminosity of early quasar light with modern observations. This paper investigates the existence, uniqueness, and the time-decay behavior of global-in-time solutions for a class of nonhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations set in the torus $(\mathbb{T})^n$. Our work extends the global well-posedness theory to nonhomogeneous equations by relaxing constraints on initial and forcing data, thereby providing the first extension of Schrödinger theory to scenarios involving low-regularity data in both homogeneous and nonhomogeneous settings. The primary motivation for selecting the MEM in this analysis stems from the extensive amount of event information offered by final states resulting from heavy particle decays. The numerical computation of resonances in this study is accomplished through an extended maximum likelihood technique, which enhances the traditional maximum likelihood approach by enabling parameter estimation even when event reconstruction is imperfect. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to estimate the mass of a neutral scalar resonance decaying to two Higgs bosons, using simulated events to emulate the experimental environment. For each generated event, we intentionally introduced uncertainties in the momentum measurement, the number of associated photons or hadrons, and the misidentification of the final state to assess the impact of these factors on the statistical results. As an proof-of-concept, we computed two possible final states: the SUSY $t\bar{t}$ channel and a non-SUSY three-jet plus missing energy signature. In both scenarios, the estimated mass parameters showed satisfactory agreement with the input mass values. Furthermore, we calculated the $\chi^2$ values for each fitted parameter. For the specific case of the SUSY $t\bar{t}$ final state, we also computed various systematic uncertainties. Given that the MEM provides numerous kinematic variables, we conclude that employing this technique for experimental searches of new physics is promising. Additionally, the technique for estimating the mass parameter, based on the MEM, is applicable to other relevant physics scenarios at the LHC. Finally, as the MEM remains underutilized in current LHC experiments, incorporating it into search procedures for new physics could lead to improvements in both sensitivity and discovery potential. A future publication will provide a comprehensive comparison between the traditional maximum likelihood method and the extended version. Current public health guidelines often depend on unpredictable future variables, such as the emergence of new viral variants and the potential availability of effective treatments. This study utilizes a non-linear programming model to explore how these factors influence the optimal allocation of vaccine doses. By quantifying the impact of case reduction through vaccination, the model determines the optimal number of doses and the fraction of the population that should be vaccinated to minimize total infections, hospitalizations, deaths, and the cumulative sum of these metrics. Results indicate that, in the absence of other control measures, a person with a severe underlying condition should receive up to 95% of the available vaccines, followed by children, followed by the elderly. Furthermore, to achieve an R value of 0.5 within 100 days, the model requires that 65% of administered vaccines target the elderly, 25% target those with underlying conditions, and 10% target children. These findings offer a quantitative basis for future policy decisions. However, the model is applicable only in scenarios where COVID-19 transmission occurs directly from infected individuals. Given that most COVID-19 variants are believed to be non-aerosol transmissible, the results remain invalid when air-borne transmission is a primary factor. Finally, the model does not support variants that cause mild symptoms. These limitations should be considered as we move toward the end of the first year of the pandemic. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for learning on large, dense graphs by leveraging data parallelism. While current distributed training techniques, such as data partitioning, fail to account for intra-partition connectivity, resulting in unnecessary communication overhead, this work introduces a novel approach called D-PGNN. GNNs are ideally suited for partitioning due to their reliance on local neighborhood data; however, the aggregation operation necessitates synchronization after each layer, which is hindered by the need to merge outputs across partitions. D-PGNN overcomes this by partitioning both nodes and edges to create independent subgraphs that can be processed and synchronized without direct communication. Instead, outcomes are written to shared storage for reading during synchronization. Empirical results on diverse graph datasets show that D-PGNN improves communication efficiency by 50x to 750x and accelerates training by 1.25x to 3x on larger graphs compared to standard data parallelism. Although this introduces increased memory overhead, it can be mitigated for wide graphs by optimizing model storage. Furthermore, we introduce a new technique for executing node partitioning operations on shared storage using GPU-accelerated bulk-symmetric exchange. This approach reduces CPU-to-CPU communication latencies and eliminates unnecessary network interactions. The source code is available at https://github.com/UT-AHLI/D-GNN.

is to identify terrestrial worlds within the habitable zones of nearby stars. While ground-based telescopes have successfully detected numerous exoplanets, most of these objects possess high masses or long orbital periods. Consequently, ground-based radial velocity surveys must be complemented by highly sensitive, precise infrared instruments capable of detecting Earth-mass planets, particularly those with short orbital periods. The ground-based Hot Jupiter Search (HJS) survey exemplifies this approach; it aims to identify short-period giant planets by employing a strategy of continuous, short-exposure monitoring of bright stars, followed by ground-based adaptive-optics (AO) follow-up for targets exhibiting short-period radial velocity variations. This combination of sparse cadence and short exposures allows the initial survey phase to rely on existing telescopes without additional equipment. Targets identified as having short orbital periods then serve as ideal candidates for ground-based AO assisted by natural guide stars. In this framework, AO enables high adaptive mirror blade counts and efficient use of exposure time. The HJS survey has already yielded 16 new giant planet candidates, 8 of which are suitable for AO follow-up using natural guide stars. Future efforts will seek to determine the obliquities and eccentric obits of these candidates. Establishing the ratio of giant planets with and without aligned spin-orbit angles will help refine current planet formation and migration models. Approximately 20 similar giant planet candidates are currently being assessed for AO observability. If observational conditions remain favorable, these targets will soon contribute to the study of orbital alignment. Ultimately, understanding orbital alignment and obliquity is essential for determining the final architecture of multi-planet systems. Data supporting the statistical evaluation of obliquet alignment can be found at https://doi.org/10.1184/R7/5F3493. The paper utilizes the term "candidate" to denote objects with short periods derived from radial velocity data that have not yet been confirmed or validated.

a graph $G$ is a mapping of colors to the edges of $G$ such that any vertex $v$ is surrounded by $\varphi$-distinct colors on the edges of its closed neighborhood $N[v]$. The minimum number of colors needed for such a strong edge-coloring is termed the strong edge-coloring number, denoted by $sech(G)$. In 2000, Faudree and Leclerc conjectured that $sech(G) \leq 5ex(G)$, where $5ex(G)$ represents the edge-covering number, defined as the smallest count of five edges whose removal leaves the graph disconnected. While M. Didinger proved this for planar graphs in 2004, the general case remained unproven. This note presents a counterexample, demonstrating that the conjecture does not hold. Specifically, we exhibit a graph $G$ with $5ex(G) = 10$ and $sech(G) = 149$, thereby showing that the ratio $sech(G) / 5ex(G)$ can be arbitrarily large. A similar counterexample was independently created by S. Suresh and R. Sankar in 2022. Additionally, we provide constructive methods for generating $5ex(G) = 7$ and $5ex(G) = 9$ counterexamples, achieving the minimal possible values for these parameters. Finally, we formulate a conjecture regarding the maximum value of $5ex(G)$ when $G$ contains a bridge. Keywords: Strong edge-coloring; Edge-covering number; Disconnected graph; Bridge; Counterexample. [End] [arXiv]

These findings indicate that jets originating from high-scalar-transverse-momentum (p$_\perp$) particles exhibit significant two-flavor flavor dependence on interactions with the quark-gluon plasma. Specifically, the ratio of charged-pion to $\pi^0$ fragmentation functions is suppressed by a factor of approximately 2 in Pb-Pb collisions relative to pp collisions for low p$_\perp$, a trend that aligns with predictions from perturbative QCD jet Monte Carlo simulations combined with nuclear modification factors derived from parton transport theory. Notably, the ratio of charged-pion to $\pi^0$ fragmentation functions recovers toward unity for both pp and Pb-Pb data as p$_\perp$ rises to approximately 50 GeV/c, consistent with parton-scale scale evolution predictions. These findings confirm that high-energy partons experience minimal color charge interactions with the quark-gluon plasma at the highest energies examined. The analysis also reveals a systematic trend of flavor ordering in the nuclear modification factor (R$_{AA}$) for charged hadrons with varying p$_\iperp$, further supporting predicted flavor dependence on parton energy loss. Overall, the results indicate a systematic reduction in the nuclear modification factor for charged hadrons as energy loss grows. Finally, the collaboration observed a broad increase in jet p$_\perp$ and an elevation in the nuclear modification factor for $\pi^0$ in Pb-Pb collisions compared to pp collisions for p$_\perp$ between approximately 20 and 50 GeV/c. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results in the context of existing experimental data. This method yields a unique approximate solution that defies intuition. While the solution adheres to the maximum principle, its time-dependent behavior collapses for all positive times, rendering it highly irregular and non-smooth; consequently, the frequently used traveling wave approximation is invalidated. Although the solution starts smoothly at $t=0$, it becomes increasingly non-smooth as the parameter $\varepsilon$ approaches zero. This outcome is driven by a resonant interaction between different spatial frequencies. Although the solution remains bounded, it exhibits Logarithmic divergence of the Laplacian at specific space-time points. These findings offer insights into the "shattering phenomenon" reported in computational fluid dynamics. Furthermore, the analysis extends to the approximation $\mathcal A_{\infty}$, which converges to a weak solution as $\varepsilon \to 0$. This solution satisfies the traveling wave approximation and also emerges from the Fisher-KPP equation found in the mathematics of the COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, these methods are applied to derive an explicit approximation for the heat equation within the COVID-19 context. This approach yields a very accurate long-time asymptotic solution that is initially incorrect and counterintuitive, yet it corrects itself as time approaches zero. Unlike the Fisher-KPP case, this asymptotic solution is monotone in both space and time, does not violate the maximum principle, and allows for the explicit determination of optimal spatial and temporal smoothing. The corresponding traveling wave profile is also explicitly calculated. Similar to the Fisher-KPP equation, the optimal spatial smoothing corresponds to the "critical slope" mentioned in the COVID-19 context. Additionally, the approximate solution displays a logarithmic divergence at specific spatial points as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Finally, the $\mathcal A_{\infty}$ approximation for the heat equation yields a precise long-time asymptotic solution for the Laplace transform of the heat equation's fundamental solution. Since Laplace transforms are extensively utilized to analyze nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations like the Fisher-KPP and Burgers' equation, this result holds significant importance. This approach offers a fresh perspective on solving these equations. This study investigates the impact of false negatives on occupancy models by analyzing data from 32 cameras at a temperate forest research station in New Hampshire. We examined the presence of white-tailed deer (*Odocoileus virginianus*) across varying light conditions, including bright days, dark nights, and dark overcast days. Our results indicate that occupancy estimates are unbiased when false negatives are independent and constant, or when they increase with rare detection events but remain below 50%. Bias becomes significant only when the probability of false negatives drops below 50% and varies substantially with environmental conditions. Although occupancy models appear robust to false negatives at high light levels, this finding is counterintuitive. We conclude that researchers should be cautious when interpreting occupancy model results, particularly when detection probabilities are low, and should consider these limitations in their final reports. Furthermore, we encourage the continuous development and application of alternative methods that do not rely on the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption. Finally, we recommend integrating multiple data sources to enhance both the number of detection events and ecological understanding.

This paper presents the findings from a challenge designed to identify missing data imputation methods and classification models suited for dermatology. The competition took place alongside the Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention conference and included three tracks: 2D-222, circular-90, and circular-180. The study demonstrates that 2D k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) effectively handles the 2D-222 task, while Support Vector Machine (SVM) is highly suitable for both the circular-90 and circular-180 tasks. Gaining missing data can significantly boost classification performance; however, applying this technique in real-world scenarios presents practical difficulties. The best overall performance achieved a area under the curve of 0.9749 in the circular-180 task. While the entry-level category was won by 12 teams, the leading performances across all tracks still fall short of an ideal area under the curve value of 1.0. Furthermore, despite 35 submissions, the current state of the art remains inconsistent regarding missing data imputation and classification in dermatology. This is largely due to the use of diverse datasets featuring various imaging angles and gaps, alongside applications of numerous algorithms and performance metrics. Consequently, there is a need for future benchmarking in this domain. Additionally, a significant challenge lies in accounting for clinical context, as factors such as lesion age and morphology are as critical to diagnosis as image data. Finally, the prevalence of benchmark studies evaluated solely by accuracy is concerning, prompting a call for the adoption of more rigorous metrics like the F1 score or area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. These factors collectively indicate that substantial improvements are still required in dermatology machine learning. Additionally, we show that the model can generate realistic synthetic data, which may be valuable for training other models or simulations. This research facilitates the discovery of temporal hierarchical structures within high-dimensional datasets and their applications. Key words: Machine Learning; Neural Networks; Data Analysis; Generalized Additive Models; Time Series; Solar and Heliospheric Physics; Heliospheric Magnetic Field; Heliospheric Transport of Magnetic Flux; Heliospheric Alfvén Wave.

While most prior research assumes a homogeneous population with uniform connectivity to justify mean-field approximations, this study examines heterogenous contact graphs where nodes represent a mixed population of susceptible and infected individuals, maintaining consistent homophily between susceptible-susceptible and infected-infected pairs. Our approach leverages a randomized algorithm derived from the Petersen graph (which features 50% edge expansion) to construct a universal decoder graph. Furthermore, we propose an efficient variant of this algorithm that achieves the same performance with significantly improved per-node computational and communication complexities. We also provide experimental validation on synthetic contact graphs with varying homophily levels, as well as real-world graphs derived from university campuses and high schools. Across all datasets, our algorithm is approximately an order of magnitude faster than competing methods while delivering more accurate results. the correctness of multi-agent systems. Typically expressed in Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), the verification process involves translating an LTL specification into an automaton and subsequently searching for accepting runs within the system model. However, for large-scale systems, this translation can result in automata that are excessively large and inefficient to construct. Consequently, researchers have proposed methods that directly convert specifications into more compact automata. To our knowledge, no previous work has addressed the inverse challenge: given a fixed system model, how can one efficiently derive an automaton tailored specifically to that model? We answer this question by introducing the notion of the system-specific deterministic Rabin automaton (DRRA) for an agent system or property pair. We present an algorithm with a linear complexity relative to the system model and quadratic complexity relative to the DRRA's size. Furthermore, our approach represents the first method to achieve optimal complexity—linear with respect to both the system model and the DRRA size. This technique is broadly applicable to any method capable of converting formulas into finite-state automata. To demonstrate its efficacy, we apply the approach to systems modeled by Kripke structures, with formulas represented either in LTL or Computation Tree Logic (CTL*). Our primary contributions include: (i) a direct construction of the DRRA from fairness-free words with linear complexity relative to the input word and automaton; (ii) an extension of this direct construction to fairness-aware scenarios; and (iii) an alternative construction that leverages existing techniques for mapping words and automata. We also experimentally validate our findings, comparing our methods against those previously presented in the literature.

boasting over 1.6 billion active users globally. Owing to its user-friendly interface and extensive features, it has become the primary avenue for interpersonal and business communications. However, this widespread adoption has also turned the platform into a prevalent vector for malware and malicious activities. These threats range from phishing attacks and spam to malicious links and secretive apps designed to function as keyloggers, keyboard capturers, and covert data spies. Given the critical nature of messages on WhatsApp, particularly those unfilled with irretrievable media, effectively detecting and tracing malicious agents is essential. While some solutions exist for detecting malicious apps and links, there is a significant gap in the ability to trace the specific agents sharing these harmful messages once the malware spreads. To address this lack of traceability, this paper introduces MalWhat, a novel approach designed to identify and backtrack the agents disseminating malicious content on WhatsApp. MalWhat relies on a specialized file format capable of decoding encrypted messages. This technique was developed by exploiting vulnerabilities within the WhatsApp server's encryption protocol. The method has been validated on Android apps using the application programming interfaces of an Android emulator. Furthermore, a web-based interface has been built to facilitate easy data input via the website or file upload through API endpoints. This interface allows for the analysis of messages across various media types supported by WhatsApp, including text, voice messages, audio files, images, videos, and links. Ultimately, MalWhat enables the precise detection of malicious messages, along with their content and sender, whether the messages are encrypted or decrypted. The following sections will detail MalWhat's architecture, capabilities, and provide use cases. Furthermore, the potential for extending MalWhat's functionality beyond WhatsApp is limited only by the similarities in encryption protocols shared by other messaging platforms. However, due to policy and privacy constraints, those explorations will be deferred for future work. Additionally, malicious apps can utilize MalWhat to analyze the messages they receive. Therefore, incorporating safeguards to prevent unauthorized access to user messages is crucial for the ethical deployment of this technology. Finally, the limitations of MalWhat's current implementation include its reliance on a pre-defined dictionary for text and a link repository. Expanding these components is left for future research.

This study investigates the consistency of parameter estimation when accounting for the probability of misclassification. Specifically, under the assumption of correct classification, Dumbalski and Dickman (2020) demonstrated that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) of the parent distribution is inconsistent in finite dimensions unless the process is balanced. In this work, assuming the true distribution belongs to a finite-dimensional family, we introduce a de-biased estimator that achieves asymptotic normality and converges in probability to the MLE. Additionally, we propose an estimator for the minimal distance between the true distribution and the finite-dimensional family, proving its consistency and asymptotic normality. A crucial insight is that, despite data misclassification, the underlying assumption of independence in the branching process allows us to leverage results from dimension identification (from our 2021 paper) to implement an approximate de-biasing strategy. This approach is shown to be optimal, and we establish lower bounds for the convergence rate of any consistent estimator. Finally, all proposed estimators are evaluated through simulations.

To accomplish this, we propose integrating an attentive activation function, specifically the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU), into an end-to-end spoofing countermeasure framework. Because AReLU utilizes the attention mechanism to enhance the influence of pertinent input features while filtering out irrelevant ones, its inclusion enables the system to concentrate on artifact-related features. When evaluated on the Logical Access (LA) task of the ASVSpoof2019 dataset, the proposed framework surpassed systems employing standard non-learnable activation functions. Furthermore, we assessed the impact of using a learnable activation function for AReLU itself; however, results indicated that the default, non-learnable version yields superior performance. Additional analysis explored the relationship between AReLU and input speech variability. The system's performance was also examined in relation to the secondary information inherent in acoustical features. To address this, we developed a static-dynamic separation module that partitions the secondary information into static and dynamic components. La input speech features were split into static and dynamic components. La static features capture the vocabulary and style of the synthetic voice, whereas dynamic features reflect speaker-specific characteristics. Experiments demonstrated that the proposed framework benefits significantly from this static-dynamic separation module. This is evident in tasks involving language or style classification, as the system can more effectively leverage the style-specific secondary information contained in the static component of the synthetic speech. To assess robustness, we evaluated the system using test sets with hidden classes not present in the training data. Under these conditions, the system achieved an equal error rate of 18.5% on the ASVSpoof2019-La task. We also analyzed how the system handles varying degrees of data contamination within the training set. With 0% contamination, the system achieved an equal error rate (EER) of 6.8% and maintained a performance delta under 10% compared to the baseline. As contamination increased, both the EER and the performance delta rose. With 50% contamination, the EER reached 20.6%, and the performance delta exceeded 10%. These findings indicate that while the proposed system outperforms the baseline across all scenarios, it performs most effectively in environments with no training data contamination. Index Terms: speech synthesis, spoofing countermeasure, attention mechanism, static-dynamic separation.

involves identifying the application layer protocol to facilitate timely and accurate protocol-specific deep packet inspection. This challenge is significant because relying solely on isolated features, such as port numbers, is insufficient for reliably distinguishing application layer protocols. Consequently, dynamic detection methods have emerged. This paper examines the dynamic protocol detection mechanisms implemented within 14 prominent open-source network monitoring tools. The analysis evaluates the strengths and limitations of these mechanisms across two key dimensions: trigger strategies and state machine design. Using the protocol HTTP as a case study, the study details how these strategies and state machines are configured. Findings indicate that while most tools offer reasonable defaults, they suffer from two main issues: (1) a lack of support for hybrid trigger strategies that combine multiple methods, and (2) design flaws including a scarcity of transitions based on field values and the failure to account for redirects and HTTP/2, which could lead to detection failures. To address these issues, we propose a set of recommendations to guide future tools toward incorporating arbitrary and hybrid trigger strategies. Furthermore, we introduce protocol detection v2 (Pd2), an extension to the current Protocol State Machine Abstract (PSMA) designed to support hybrid protocol detection and automatic rule synthesis from protocol samples. Pd2 also resolves issues related to tool maintenance and complexity. A protocol database built on Pd2 using 10,000 samples is provided in the experiment package. Finally, we outline the process for integrating protocol detection v2 into existing tools. Experiment results show that the average detection success rate drops to 70.53% when using current open-source tools compared to protocol-aware analysis engines. However, the proposed method achieves a 98.68% average detection success rate. These outcomes demonstrate that protocol v2 offers a practical solution for automatically detecting applications, thereby alleviating the heavy manual burden of maintaining detection rules while ensuring high accuracy. Additionally, Pd2 enables automatic rule synthesis, significantly reducing the manual effort required for maintaining both individual tools and the monitoring ecosystem at large. The experimental package can be accessed at: https://github.com/whu-monde-watching/DeMon. As of now, no existing tools support protocol v2; therefore, we are actively collaborating with the monitoring tools community to integrate it into the industry's monitoring ecosystem. To our knowledge, this work represents the first systematic analysis of open-source protocol detection mechanisms. It offers a comprehensive solution that enhances monitoring capabilities without increasing complexity or maintenance burdens, all while ensuring accurate detection. This study presents the discovery of stable zero-dimensional nanowires for both hole- and electron-type conduction in monolayer CoTe₂. We observed that these nanowires exhibit strong strain sensitivity; specifically, applying tensile strain to 0D nanowires derived from 2D sheets suppresses carrier transport. The paper introduces a fast algorithm to generate Dirichlet Beta random variables, derived from a generalization of the Gamma distribution. This approach leverages the relationship between the Dirichlet Beta distribution and exponential variables. We demonstrate a $O(d)$ method for sampling a Dirichlet Beta random variable and extend this to obtain a $O(Nd)$ algorithm for Dirichlet random variables, where $N$ represents the number of samples. These algorithms are particularly suited for applications requiring the sampling of a large volume of random variables. Furthermore, we analyze the runtime performance of our proposed approach. We address the challenge of extracting a single representative instance from each class in a high-dimensional dataset. We frame this as a constrained optimization problem and develop a novel algorithm to solve it. We provide a theoretical analysis of the approach, proving both its convergence and time complexity. Experimental results validate our claims, demonstrating that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, across various applications, our approach yields more consistent and coherent prototypes.

We examine the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP), a critical attribute for compressed sensing matrices. While traditional analysis assumes entries are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), we extend this to weakly dependent scenarios. Specifically, we analyze matrices where rows are $\epsilon$-correlated Gaussian processes. We derive a new upper bound for the RIP, showing that for matrices with sufficient dimensions, the bound approaches 1. This indicates that such matrices are highly probable to satisfy the RIP. Additionally, we prove a concentration inequality for quadratic forms involving sub-Gaussian random matrices with dependent rows. Our approach relies on established techniques from graph theory. Numerical experiments support these theoretical findings.

To probe the limits of such generalization in machine learning, this study investigates how well models can simultaneously learn to predict continuous values ($y_{c}$) and their corresponding rank ($y_r$) within a group. The results indicate that models struggle to generate solutions that are both accurate and ranked correctly, a challenge that becomes more pronounced as the difference in actual values grows. This phenomenon is characterized as "generalization interference." Drawing on principles from human cognitive development, we propose that this issue arises because neural networks are trained to treat ranking and regression as mutually reinforcing tasks. During training, the gradient information received by the network consistently pushes the models to increase the gap between values with different ranks. While this behavior is observed as accurate on the training set, it leads to significant errors when the model encounters new, unseen inputs. Furthermore, we find that gradient descent inherently creates a solution where the representation and scoring functions amplify each other: one component ensures inputs with distinct Ranks of Interest are separated sufficiently, while the other ensures the scoring function heavily weights this separation. We validate these findings using both simulated datasets and neural networks. Additionally, we introduce an extension of the Permutation Function Loss that directly enforces separation at specific Ranks of Interest. This approach successfully prevents generalization interference, allows for decoupling the two objectives, and results in a solution with lower overall loss, even without altering the gradient descent optimization process. In conclusion, this work highlights a novel form of multi-task generalization interference in machine learning and introduces associated challenges for creating models that effectively solve dual ranking and regression problems.

ptune exoplanets have revealed a distinct "radius valley" in the brown-dwarf-to-terrestrial planet transition, separating dwarf-gas-planets from rocky worlds. This gap is thought to result from the atmospheric mass-loss evolution of gaseous planets, leaving rocky bodies as mass loss ceases. As observations of substellar mass planets gain momentum, evolving our understanding of this phenomenon is critical for the broader community. This study theoretically investigates mass loss in sub-Neptune planets with masses between 10 and 100 Earth masses ($M_{\oplus}$) and radii between 1.5 and 3 ($R_{\oplus}$), located at semi-major axes from 0.02 to 0.5 AU. We assess how initial conditions and high-energy (HE) stellar flux influence the temperature evolution, radius over time, final radius, and fractional core mass of these planets. Additionally, we explore how HE stellar flux varies with the distance between the star and the HE source. Our results indicate that HE flux significantly impacts the evolution and final radius, particularly for close-in planets around active stars or distant planets around inactive stars. The final radius is heavily dependent on the heating timescale relative to the stellar HE flux timescale and the initial flux timescale. Generally, planets orbiting active stars or situated very close to their host stars tend to be larger and more gaseous, explaining the absence of large planets very close to stars. Conversely, large planets can exist further out, consistent with the "radius inflation" effect at larger semi-major axes. Furthermore, larger planets retain higher fractional core masses compared to smaller ones. The primary driver for this variation in final radius and fractional core mass is the final mean density, which correlates with final radius and core mass. This work contributes to refining the current comprehension of the radius valley for substellar planets and predicts final properties for a specific planet population. Ultimately, this model serves as a foundation for future research on HE flux effects on sub-Neptune planets and can be utilized to generate synthetic data for upcoming radial velocity and transit surveys. This system, characterised by two mirror separations and the input rate of atoms passing through the cavity, generates multiple standing wave patterns within the cavity mode. Surprisingly, we observe that the standing wave intensity can exceed the unenhanced standing wave intensity by a factor of two. Surprisingly again, for specific intermediate values of the intermediate parameter, the intensity at certain standing wave locations can drop to approximately 0.25 of the unenhanced intensity. Our findings investigate how optical enhancement depends on both mirror separation and atomic flux. These findings hold potential applications for quantum information processing and the study of atoms interacting with standing waves.

Furthermore, we explore the theoretical framework concerning multiple scattering and coherent backscattering (CBS) in two-dimensional (2D) stacks of 2D colloidal crystals. We begin by reviewing the coherent addition of multiple scattering paths, which leads to the coherent backscattering phenomenon—a frequency-dependent increase in the backscattering cross-section and the formation of a cone-shaped distribution when an incoherent wave traverses a multiple-scattering medium. Next, we examine the effects of random deformations in a pristine 2D colloidal crystal stack on the coherent backscattering cone and the standing wave pattern caused by coherent interference of multiple scattering paths. Wesurprisingly find that for small random deformations with an exponential height distribution, the standing wave intensity can be nearly doubled. Finally, through numerical simulations, we analyse how the standing wave pattern is affected by the incoherent interference of multiple scattering paths for varying numbers of 2D colloidal crystal layers. While these results were initially derived for a square lattice, they are expected to be general applicable to other common 2D colloidal crystal lattices.

In summary, this work introduces and experimentally demonstrates a novel approach to controlling standing wave enhancement in both atomic gases and multiple-scattering media by manipulating the intermediate parameter, thereby offering new perspectives on standing wave enhancement. These findings are anticipated to have significant implications for optical enhancement and related quantum information processing applications.

We introduce Selective Labeling, which streamlines the annotation process by generating "yes/no" labels for document elements based on a single model's predictions. Specifically, elements predicted with high confidence are marked for verification, while those with low confidence are marked and subsequently re-predicted by a model fine-tuned on the verified set. ## 1.1 Background and Motivation

Ratcheting costs, characterized by convexity and nondegeneracy, are increasingly common in operational decision-making. These costs, also known as aversion to reversals, arise when decision variables represent actions like investment or effort that can only move in one direction. For instance, a venture capital firm may increase but not decrease investment in a startup between funding rounds, while employees can raise but not lower their work effort. Literature on ratcheting effects spans control theory, contract theory, and mechanism design. Within control theory, problems featuring both state and control ratcheting costs are prevalent in operations management, as our focus here will demonstrate.

Focusing on state ratcheting costs, a standard approach for solving stochastic control problems involves minimizing the expected infinite-horizon average cost. This technique, referred to as RHO, approximates the optimal policy by solving a finite-horizon deterministic optimization problem. Although various solution methods exist for this finite-horizon problem, this paper adopts the approach described in \cite{bertsekas2005rhc}. Specifically, we employ an adaptive policy iteration method that begins with a recursive policy approximation to generate a suboptimal parametric policy, bounding the suboptimality. Utilizing thermodynamic modeling of Bayesian systems, we derive the system's dual formulation and demonstrate the calculation of dual variables via the inverse Hessian of the energy function. By applying the Legendre transform, we establish the primal-dual relationship and prove that both formulations share identical free energy. A key analytical challenge is identifying patterns in these vectors by examining rows, columns, specific index subsets, or quadrant subsets. Standard approach involves computing pairwise distances between indicator vectors using metrics like Jaccard, symmetric profile, or simple matching coefficients. However, these measures often fail to capture essential dissimilarities; for instance, they assign a distance of 0.5 to both (0,1) and (1,1,1,0), despite their significantly different nature. Similarly, they produce identical distances for (0,1,0,1) and (1,0,1,0), masking their distinct characteristics. To address this, we propose a new family of metrics grounded in the Euclidean geometry of the data. These metrics are easily calculated and effectively reveal data structure, as demonstrated by a simulation. Furthermore, we apply these metrics to identify structures within various data sets where the symmetric profile distance and Jaccard distance failed to detect them. Additionally, we demonstrate the advantages of these metrics when clustering is performed and explore their utility as similarity measures for constructing neighbor-based multiway partitionings of presence-absence data. While prior studies in this domain have explored various applications of such architectures, this paper presents a solution drawn from Nash equilibrium theory within game theory. Drawing an analogy between an image and a polygon, the research examines the behavior of its edges under transformations like rotation and reflection. It observes that while no single edge represents the salient object, the collective sum of all edges does. This insight underscores two key factors: (1) equidistance between adjacent edges, and (2) the uniform contribution of every edge to the total sum. These observations lead to the conception of a circular game, where players are positioned at equal intervals around the circle's perimeter. A significant contribution is the derivation of an exact expression for the Shapley value of a specific game characterized by a specific permutation. This formula demonstrates that when the value of a circular game $v$ represents a symmetric permutation of a set $S$, the $i$-th player's share ($i$-sh) equals $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j,i}$, provided the players are numbered $1$ through $n$. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of this game-theoretic approach for SOD. Furthermore, a new, simple, and highly effective value function is introduced to measure a salient object detector's performance. The method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the SOD2014 and SOD2015 benchmark datasets. Additionally, a novel salient object map is proposed, illustrating how circular game theory can be extended to cooperative games. In this context, circular games assess the individual contributions of coalition members to the overall value, whereas circular theory in general game theory estimates the average contribution of each player relative to others. However, this approach risks overcomplicating OOP syntax to a degree that undermines its core programming model. In this paper, we introduce SecPar, an object-oriented concurrent programming language designed to ensure runtime resource isolation and controlled mutual exclusion. SecPar is fully concurrent and leverages the C++ standard library to simplify the expression of concurrency and parallelism. It minimally extends C++ and employs well-known concurrency constructs to maximize code efficiency while reducing semantic complexity. The language supports multiple threads per object to facilitate fine-grained concurrent object access, thereby increasing object granularity and allowing larger chunks of sequential code to execute concurrently. We have implemented a compiler for SecPar as a frontend that translates SecPar code into equivalent C++ programs, which we have validated using a concurrency module from the C++ standard library. Additionally, we will release an open-source explorer and simulator to demonstrate SecPar at the runtime level and verify isolated and controlled behavior. Our experimental evaluations present a novel approach to concurrent object access that simultaneously achieves high performance, increased granularity, and computational resource isolation and control. These capabilities enable the development of computationally intensive applications, such as data and image processing tasks, with greater efficiency than previously possible using object-oriented languages. Developers can find a detailed user guide at secpar.purdue.edu, while the complete project, including the compiler and runtime, is available on GitHub. The code also allows for easy extension to support additional features. Looking ahead, we plan to extend the runtime to integrate caching and calibrate concurrency levels and thresholds. We believe that extending SecPar to translate into Java, Scala, or other object-oriented languages will be straightforward, as our framework operates at the concurrency unit level rather than the class level. At its core, SecPar provides a controlled method for concurrent object access that can be seamlessly integrated into object-oriented programs. This includes an expression for increasing concurrency in code blocks while ensuring isolated and controlled resource usage.

**I. INTRODUCTION**

The standard cosmological model, $\Lambda$CDM, aligns well with various observational datasets, yet it introduces several unexplained issues and numerous free parameters. Simple solutions, such as the existence of dark matter and/or dark radiation, would significantly advance our comprehension of the cosmos and stellar evolution. However, despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, a confirmed candidate for dark matter or dark radiation remains elusive. Consequently, we are forced to consider more intricate interactions and structures to achieve a more robust explanation of dark matter and dark energy.

We begin by examining a well-established mechanism: the kinetic mixing between standard model $U(1)_Y$ and a hypothetical $U(1)_D$ gauge group. In this context, a standard dark photon can mediate interactions for standard dark matter and radiative components. When these residual charges differ between the standard model and the dark sector, new portal couplings emerge through products of the corresponding currents. These result in smaller mixing angles and more complex scenarios, as cosmological observations impose stringent limits on kinetic mixing.

Galactic Center (GC) is home to a supermassive black hole and a dense collection of stars within a limited area. Due to the strong tidal forces near the GC, these stars follow highly eccentric orbits around the black hole, some of which infrared surveys have identified as potential stars orbiting the Sun more tightly than any other. This study employs a novel approach to identify promising candidates for such orbits by integrating high-precision astrometric data from Gaia DR2 with information from the Near Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer (NIRCAM) on JCNT. By selecting sources with photometric quality greater than 3 to ensure accurate proper motions and parallax, we determined that the majority of the approximately 1,300 identified candidates are background stars. These background objects exhibit tenuous correlations between their tidal acceleration estimates and squared proper motion anomalies, aligning well with Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, most of these sources display high tangential velocity anomalies compared to the low radial anomalies expected for stars orbiting the GC. Only two sources, S0499-005 and S0528+602, are positioned sufficiently close to the GC to be considered candidates for a GC orbit. These two sources are estimated to complete one orbital period in approximately 4.5 and 3.9 years, respectively. Our findings suggest that there is at least one GC candidate with an orbital period exceeding 4.5 years, which is consistent with the known population of GC stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the current sample of candidates with a photometric quality score of 4 is too sparse to serve as a effective alternative to the traditional GC candidate sample. This highlights the need for more precise astrometric data in future surveys to properly characterize the GC population. Finally, we propose that S0499-005 may be a new GC candidate, although it cannot be confirmed without utilizing next-generation high-precision astrometric data. In this regard, we suggest that data from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will be essential for the definitive identification of GC candidates. When x-ray pulses excite plasmon resonances in nanometer-scale metal nanoparticles, they generate localized electromagnetic (EM) near-field hot spots capable of influencing second harmonic generation (SHG) from embedded semiconductor quantum dots (QDs). This study investigates the interaction dynamics and spatial distribution of these EM hot spots using time-resolved x-ray SHG imaging at the K-line of Si QDs embedded in a gold nanoring, tracked across single electron dwell times of approximately 10^8 x-rays per second. The resulting two-dimensional (2D) imaging data provides direct access to EM field hot spots at the 50 nm scale. By analyzing time-resolved imaging sequences, we establish a causal link between the excitation of localized surface plasmon resonances and the modulation of the plasmonic field. This imaging capability offers a new window into the interaction between localized EM field hot spots and QDs, enabling the control of X-ray pump-probe experiments with higher precision. Such insights are essential for x-ray nanophotonics and will support future XFEL experiments designed to explore the coupling of strong EM field hot spots with x-ray probing of QDs. By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slip, rough, and sticky. These regimes are defined by an inverse dependence of shear stress on the average roughness scale and are mediated by the plastic viscosity of the foam. Transition points between these regimes occur at stress values matching the foam's yield stress, while the variation of friction stress with velocity follows a power law whose exponent is dictated by the plastic-to-elastic viscosity ratio. The ISIC-2019 challenge comprises two tasks: task 1 focuses on diagnosing skin cancer using color images, while task 2 expands on this by incorporating metadata alongside images. This competition continues a series initiated in 2017 by the Medical Image Analysis group at the University of Sydney, which has consistently aimed to test and compare various machine learning techniques. Our primary objective was to explore how graph theory and metadata can be leveraged for diagnostic tasks, building on our previous experience with a similar diabetes-related challenge that utilized metadata and benefited from deep learning and clustering on image data.

Our proposed approach involves training a deep convolutional network to extract features from input images, followed by applying graph-based clustering to construct a similarity graph. The similarity between nodes is defined by the graph's adjacency matrix. We then utilize labeled nodes and the graph Laplacian to learn vertex labels through multi-label classification. An optimization function is designed to simultaneously perform graph clustering and multi-label classification, leveraging labeled data to guide label predictions for remaining nodes and ensuring classes are well-distributed on the graph. Finally, vertex labels are determined by taking the most frequent class among adjacent nodes.

While these models accept various modal inputs such as images, audio, and sequences, they typically struggle to effectively utilize sequence data due to their heavy dependence on external visual or auditory cues. This limitation necessitates substantial scaling of audio artifacts or visual imagery during training. In this work, we introduce Sound2Sequence, a novel approach for unsupervised sequence-to-sequence translation between sequential representations. We demonstrate that combining these models accelerates the learning process for new languages or sequences using unsupervised, text-to-sequence diffusion models. Specifically, we apply this methodology to learn a musical pitch sequence-to-sequence generator. Aligning with established unsupervised methods, Sound2Sequence achieves state-of-the-art quality within a single-day learning period and reaches perceptual indistinguishability from human recordings after approximately three days. Furthermore, we show that incorporating these models allows for per-language adaptation requiring only around 200 samples, reaching human-level quality in roughly two weeks—approximately 40 times faster than previously reported methods. To facilitate broader research, we make our code and pre-trained models publicly available. The method achieves these results without relying on musical annotations. Our approach consists of two components: first, we employ a novel spectral-based generator to produce pitch sequences, and second, we utilize a novel multi-step automatic feature extractor that converts spectrograms into pitch representations. We validate that this configuration optimally balances sample efficiency with computational cost. Our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art results by more than 50% in most evaluations while offering a two-fold improvement in computational efficiency. Additionally, our approach enables the creation of synthetic datasets that are indistinguishable from real ones. These acquisitions are traditionally treated as linear, physical projections that can be mathematically modeled; however, recent research has introduced nonlinear models for spectroscopic data, particularly in fields like chemistry where nonlinear behavior is well-documented. This study investigates whether applying deep learning to radiometric data should adopt similar nonlinear approaches. By comparing results from deep learning and spectroscopy across over 100 datasets from diverse scientific and industrial applications, we determine that a deep learning spectrum encoder should not be designed as a nonlinear function. Instead, the spectral dimension must be engineered for interpretability, and the system should be optimized for information-theoretic entropy maximization rather than raw information content maximization. Furthermore, our work establishes a direct link between spectral entropy and acquisition time, demonstrating that a spectrum encoder focused on maximizing entropy is more effective at filtering noise than one aimed solely at maximizing information content. Full-Disk Brightness Temperature (FDBT) maps revealed temperature variations corresponding to active regions across the observed wavelength band. Future dosALMA observations will enable us to investigate small-scale dynamical processes within solar active regions, specifically energy deposition and convection. This new capability will significantly advance our understanding of solar magnetism, supporting the project's ultimate objective of contributing to our understanding of stellar magnetic activity. **Keywords:** Sun: atmosphere – Sun: observations – Sun: active regions – Sun: disk – Sun: resolution – Sun: bands.

In these frameworks, magnetic monopoles originating from a broken dark $U(1)$ manifest within our sector as magnetic charges within a Maxwell term for electromagnetism. While such dual electric and magnetic charges typically signify confinement via the Nielsen-Olesen mechanism, we demonstrate that these charges can remain screened and move freely if they possess a large mass. This screening occurs within a plasma exerting a Debye mass, which is also experienced by any residual force carried by the dual photon. We outline a framework to derive this result from an analytic Coulomb patch calculation and support it with numerical simulations of the system in three spatial dimensions. These findings have significant implications for detecting heavy magnetic charged particles in experiments such as LHC run 3, FCC, SHiP, LHCf, FASER, and DUNE. Furthermore, we discuss the relevance of this phenomenon to dark sector models featuring non-Abelian gauge symmetries and spontaneously broken global $U(1)$ factors. Although global symmetries generally forbid magnetic charges, we show that they can appear effectively if a heavy electric charge undergoes a Nielsen-Olesen confinement transition. This is pertinent to models involving a heavy charged scalar interacting via a dark $U(1)$, a scenario commonly encountered in broken global symmetries. Consequently, these particles represent a viable and testable magnetic sector for standard model plasma environments. Finally, we illustrate the movement of heavy magnetic charges in our sector within a specific dark sector model designed to extend dark photon mass generation through Yukawa interactions. In this context, we propose that these heavy magnetic charged particles constitute a viable dark matter candidate. Estimating their production cross sections and interaction rates within plasma is essential for determining their detectability across various experimental facilities. We present a new stochastic model for the transport of these objects, governed by a probability density function that depends on spatial coordinates, time, and the objects' orientation angles. By employing the method of moments, we derive a system of conservation equations for the population moments. Our findings indicate that the zeroth moment, representing the total number of objects, converges to both a deterministic solution, which aligns with existing models ignoring orientation, and a stochastic solution that reaches statistical equilibrium. For the first moment, which accounts for object orientation, we also demonstrate convergence to deterministic and stochastic equilibria. Numerical solutions of this conservation system reveal that the zeroth moment is unaffected by orientation diffusion but influenced by translational diffusion. In contrast, the first moment depends on all three diffusion types: translational, orientational, position-orientational coupling, and angular velocity-translation; however, only the former two significantly impact it. We conclude that our proposed model extends current theoretical frameworks. Furthermore, we propose using the moment closure version of this model to investigate general neuron development and to calculate the average position of synaptic mitochondria.

Using the quantum hydrodynamic equations, we model the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet to simulate the binary system's evolution. During periastron passage, the white dwarf sheds a small amount of mass; this material falling into the black hole generates intense electromagnetic and gravitational radiation. Each periastron passage triggers bursts of ultraluminous radiation, a phenomenon resembling the recurrent X-ray flares recently identified by Irwin et al. Gravitational energy bursts are primarily emitted at very low frequencies. Additionally, the accretion disc formed from the stripped white dwarf material eventually begins to contribute continuously to both electromagnetic and gravitational radiation. Parameter analyses indicate that both electromagnetic and gravitational luminosities increase as the white dwarf's mass decreases. The electromagnetic luminosity peaks when the white dwarf's semi-major axis is approximately three times the black hole's Schwarzschild radius. Furthermore, total electromagnetic energy emission reaches its maximum for a white dwarf mass of roughly $3\times10^{-6}M_{\odot}$, whereas gravitational energy emission peaks at approximately $10^{-8}M_{\odustar}$. Our findings suggest that if such systems exist in nature, future observations with next-generation telescopes could detect both electromagnetic and gravitational wave signals.

This study analyzes the algebraic properties of their core operator—the binary XOR operator—derived from Boolean algebra. We demonstrate that these properties cause the search space to degenerate into subspaces, causing algorithm performance to collapse within these lower-dimensional environments. To address this degeneracy, we propose a family of improved algorithms that utilize Boolean rings to overcome the limitations of Boolean algebra. The resulting binary particle swarm optimizers exhibit robust search capabilities and consistent performance across various applications. Experimental results on several binary constraint satisfaction problems, including Sudoku and 2- SAT problems, confirm the effectiveness of our methodology. This success rate was achieved without relying on problem-specific preprocessing techniques.

However, this strategy is heavily dependent on the quality of synthetic data, which must be generated without any blur kernel to avoid relying on kernel knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we propose an end-to-end motion deblurring framework utilizing a training approach analogous to self-supervised semantic segmentation. In this segmentation-based deblurring, synthetic blurry and sharp images are replaced by a single blurry image; kernel knowledge is replaced by labels identifying boundary pixels; and classification is replaced by generation. Specifically, we propose a novel "boundary boundary" loss function that allows current supervised deblurring models to train on labeled blurry images with varying degrees of blur. Abstract: A novel approach to generating and designing entangled atomic states for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry is presented. While standard approaches to writing these states rely on technical limitations of the writing device, this work leverages them. Using spin-exchange collisions in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates (BEC) as a prototype, we show that a technical limitation of the entangling device, specifically a finite detector resolution, can be turned to its advantage: by adjusting the detector's sensitivity, these limitations produce a classically correlated seed that, once activated, writes an optimized entangled atomic state for interferometry. This process also enables the control and reduction of the state's entanglement. We extend this method to write more general quantum sequences and calculate the quantum noise achievable at the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we prove that the writing device's technical limitations can facilitate the realization of quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry using less valuable entanglement. This represents a new pathway to writing quantum sequences that improves on previous approaches regarding the security and robustness of the quantum input state, as well as the writer apparatus. These findings hold broad implications for all quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry protocols. Additionally, they provide a framework to write quantum sequences for the quantum simulation of many-body Hamiltonians and the quantum control of spatially delocalized atoms

This study introduces a GCNN-based approach designed to interpolate regularized Toeplitz matrices, offering a potentially superior solution for seismic data interpolation. To enhance both computational efficiency and interpolation quality, the proposed method employs learning-based sparse convolution. This technique substitutes standard sparse convolutions with a combination of sparse Hopfield networks and dense convolutions. The approach was assessed on synthetic 2D data across various missing patterns, on real 3D data using different down-sampling rates, and was also compared against a regular sparse convolutional encoder-decoder structure. Results indicate that sparse encodings reduce the number of operations by at least 60%. Furthermore, the proposed sparse GCNN achieved 10% higher Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) on both synthetic and 3D datasets compared to the standard sparse encoder-decoder architecture. To further improve performance, the method was also compared against the Wavenumber Domain Interpolation (K-DOMAIN) technique, though this comparison is not exhaustive. While the proposed sparse GCNN performed competitively against K-DOMAIN in terms of PSNR, its greatest advantage lies in its ability to adapt to a wider range of down-sampling rates. These findings suggest that sparse GCNNs present a promising direction for future seismic data interpolation research. The code will be made available for download at the time of publication. Yang-Mills theories featuring an $\mathfrak{so}(4N)$ algebra and specific global structures exhibit non-invertible symmetries. By identifying the holographically dual branes associated with these symmetries, we derive their fusion rules based on the branes' worldvolume dynamics. These non-invariant operators possess anomalous dimensions that vary with the theory's coupling constant. We demonstrate that these dimensions can be determined through the OPEs of quark bilinears and by examining the discrepancy between the branes' worldvolume actions and those predicted by holographic duals of simpler theories. Additionally, we relate these anomalous dimensions to the non-invertible 1-morphisms within the category of long-range operators. Finally, we suggest that the $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory's global structure can be probed by inserting point defects corresponding to singularities in the dual gauge theory. Through the holographic dictionary, these point defects map to D0-branes, whose dynamics are governed by Dirac monopole instantons. We show that fusing specific point defects yields the same set of non-invertible symmetries. Furthermore, by applying the non-invertible 1-morphisms to these point defects, we generate even more complex 2-morphisms, whose properties can also be investigated using holography. This process reveals that long-range instantons on the branes' worldvolume are dual to quark flavor instantons in the bulk. These 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms are constructed using long-range instantons, providing a pathway to determine their properties via the holographic approach. This methodology can be extended to other theories that exhibit both long-range instantons and non-invertible symmetries. As a concrete example, we propose that $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM with $\mathfrak{so}(8)$ global symmetry on a 3+1D long-range instanton possesses 1-morphisms associated with Nielsen-Obolev instantons. We verify that the dimensions of the operators carrying the representations generated by these 1-morphisms can be determined via the holographic technique. On the field theory side, these dimension analyses can be cross-checked using the technique of long-range instantons. This methodology is also applicable to other long-range instantons by employing the corresponding supersymmetric saturation identities.

We introduce a new result in finite combinatorics invariants with CPT within the embedded canonical evaluation context, establishing a unified polynomial-time characterization of the (non-)existence of uniform gaps in the generalized (non-)canonical property. Specifically, for any uniform generalized Ramsey sentence $\Phi$, the CPT of a structure $\mathcal{A}$ determining a uniform $\Phi$-gap exists if and only if $\Phi$ holds in $\mathcal{A}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CPT can identify not only uniform gaps in the (generalized) Ramsey property but also uniform gaps in the (uniform) canonical property, providing a fresh polychromatic proof of the long-standing conjecture that every uniform canonical partition sentence admits a long homogeneous sequence. Additionally, our findings in polychromatic context reveal that every uniform canonical partition sentence is equivalent to a weakly non-canonical one, offering another independent proof of this established conclusion. In the context of non-embedded canonical evaluation, we prove that uniform gaps in the uniform canonical property emerge precisely when choosing color copies instead of substructures, a finding that also yields a novel polychromatic proof of the conventional uniform canonical property (selecting color copies). Finally, by combining results from both settings, we extend the polychromatic proof of the uniform canonical property (on uniform generalized Ramsey sentences) by a factor of four. These results hold for structures of general finite width, including those of infinite width, such as general finite graphs on natural numbers. Any of these findings could be converted into a traditional (non-polychromatic) proof of the uniform canonical property (on uniform generalized Ramsey sentences) for a specific family of finite structures $\mathcal{F}$. We show that, starting from a vacuum-field condition, Rabi oscillations in the cavity mode during anti-Jaynes-Cummings interactions proceed in the opposite direction compared to standard Jaynes-Cummings interactions, yet the temporal evolution of entanglement follows an identical pattern. Consequently, the formation of maximally entangled qubit states at specific durations remains unchanged. This same technique can be applied to achieve entanglement swapping within the anti-Jaynes-Cummings setup. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach is equally applicable to other scenarios involving the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction. These results have significant implications for the future development of quantum technologies relying on the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction. # 1. Introduction

The Internet has profoundly transformed how people interact with information. With the continuous growth of online content, users face challenges in navigating and evaluating the overwhelming volume of data. To manage this complexity, collaborative filtering systems have been developed to filter and rank relevant items for individual users. These systems analyze user-item interaction patterns to forecast future activities, enhancing the quality of user responses. Despite their advantages, CF models manage massive interaction matrices that demand high computational power. Consequently, there is a critical need to enhance CF performance through the integration of advanced computational techniques. This study proposes a solution by constructing a Deep Learning model for Collaborative Filtering.

Deep learning has emerged as a powerful approach for handling various interactions within machine learning. It offers computational benefits through specific architectural properties, making it well-suited for collaborative filtering. By applying deep learning, the complexity of large interaction matrices can be reduced. Specifically, this work employs Deep Learning to factorize user-item patterns. Additionally, the approach utilizes Additional Information to refine predictions. Specifically, the proposed solution is a deep neural network factorization model designed to predict user-item interactions. This model is a deep neural network optimized to generate factorizations that maximize the likelihood of interactions. During prediction, additional features are incorporated to further boost accuracy. The core contribution of this paper is a refined neural network factorization model for collaborative filtering. Consequently, confirming the absence of such activity is essential to validate that a observed flux dip is indeed caused by the transit of a true planet. This study examines stellar activity in the system HD 22488, where four transit candidates have been identified. Although the candidate with the shortest period (0.84 days) has been observed across six cycles, it produces an implausibly small transit depth. In contrast, three other candidates—with periods of 2.33, 3.53, and 4.63 days—have been detected in at least two cycles each; the most frequent of these occurs every 2.33 days. We present new photometric data derived from archival sources, indicating that HD 22488 exhibits strong flare-like behavior. Given this significant stellar activity, we conclude that all detected transit signals are likely artifacts of the activity rather than evidence of transiting planets. Furthermore, we propose strategies for future follow-up observations to definitively rule out or verify any bona fide transiting objects. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the broader population of short-period transit candidates around active stars.
