This study addresses the fundamental challenge of locomotion on compliant surfaces by developing a snake that traverses sand using a single simple gaits. Unlike previous approaches relying on complex actuation and sensing systems, our approach utilizes a novel mapping between snake shapes and actuation patterns. Specifically, the snake moves by shifting guidance points in a continuous loop; this shifts the guidance point loop across the body in both directions, generating motion through a combination of sliding and non-sliding (waving) behaviors. Non-sliding waves are surprisingly efficient in sliding over sand, matching sliding waves in efficiency and significantly extending their activation range. Optimal wave shapes correspond to Gaussian distributions, with optimal parameters determined analytically and independent of wave speed. We validate these sliding snakes experimentally on sand, confirming consistent traversal, uniform wave usage, and the superior performance of Gaussian wave shapes compared to square waves. Furthermore, we show how these sliding snakes relate to control strategies for multi-link animals and robots. Our work demonstrates that a snake can move across sand despite being extremely simple, featuring a uniform wave distribution during movement, an efficient design independent of speed, and an ability to traverse and self-recharge on a single battery. These findings suggest that sliding waves may represent a universal solution for multi-link locomotion on compliant terrain. We envision this approach will enable new robotic applications, offering an advantage over prior strategies that require high actuation and sensing complexity to navigate sand. Additionally, our insights suggest that animals of all sizes and compositions—whether in air or over ground—may achieve compliance by non-sliding (slipping) waves. This could enable new bio-inspired designs for multi-link mobile robots and sensors that are cheaper and more power-efficient. Finally, we propose that our results will inspire new mathematical theories connecting actuation and sensing to performance.

We analyze the self-similar solutions in detail, focusing particularly on the similarity exponent that governs the acceleration of the shock, across both cylindrical and spherical geometries and a broad spectrum of adiabatic and spatial density exponents. Furthermore, we show how these analytical solutions can be replicated within Lagrangian hydrodynamic codes, thereby establishing their utility as a benchmark for code verification and validation. Finally, we derive an analytic approximation applicable to the most physically significant scenario: a cylindrical geometry with a centrally depleted density distribution (negative spatial density exponent), a setup frequently employed in nuclear fusion research and inertial confinement fusion. In this specific case, our findings indicate that the main cycle of fusions of two one-dimensional laser-plasma jets can achieve an on-average energy conversion efficiency of approximately one third, with the ability to both intensify and accelerate ions to multi-MeV energies. We also explore the inertially confined fusion of two plasmas and describe a method to enhance the ion yield in this context. This approach relies and benefits from a secondary process: the generation of additional ion-spikes during the main acceleration phase, whose number and characteristics are determined during an initial pre-compression stage. The proposed strategy is shown to simultaneously increase the ion flux while preserving a high energy conversion efficiency. This mechanism of secondary spike production is fundamentally analogous to the jet-tail interaction observed in laboratory experiments involving ultra-intense laser-plasma interactions. A key distinction is that, unlike that phenomenon, the effect is constructive rather than destructive. We demonstrate that this mechanism is robust and can be generalized to a wide range of plasma parameters, including applications in nuclear fusion. This is achieved by selecting appropriate geometries and initial density distributions, a strategy that is also relevant to the acceleration and fusion of heavy ion beams. This capability is essential for creating bright sources of charged particles in the tens of MeV range, capable of producing bright neutron sources and achieving a laboratory-scale deuterium-tritium ignition. The proposed strategy to generate ion-spikes is generally and universally applicable, as it does not depend on any specific physical mechanism. It holds promise for future applications in various fields, such as inertial fusion, nuclear astrophysics, and nuclear physics. quantum many-body systems that can reveal significant thermalization and prethermal phenomena. In this work, we determine the long-time asymptotic two-point correlation functions and their temporal broadening for the non-interacting Fermi-Hubbard and spin-1/2 Heisenberg chains. We then investigate how these quantities are influenced by interactions and boundary conditions. Our findings indicate that interactions cause only minor perturbations to the asymptotic values and time scales, with the most notable effect being interaction-driven dephasing affecting higher-order moments. Under open boundary conditions, we find that the leading-order correlation functions remain largely unchanged, but the distribution of temporal scales is altered, highlighting a competition between transport and dephasing effects. Finally, by comparing results across different systems and boundary conditions, we discuss potential extensions to interacting systems in the thermodynamic limit. These methods and observations are expected to be valuable for studying the real-time dynamics of cold-atom experiments. The supplementary material contains additional data on higher moments, interaction effects, and finite-size scaling behaviors. Additionally, we provide experimentalists with code to fit their data. This study introduces a clinical application that leverages the intrinsic edges of vertebrae to overcome low contrast and artifact issues while enhancing speed and scalability. The asymptotic statistics of these observables are fully described by their cumulants, which can be calculated via generating functions and scaled cumulants derived through the Markovian master equation. These equations account for both linear and nonlinear dynamics and can be extended based on the transition probability kernels. Consequently, Gaussian statistics with Poissonian counting statistics naturally arise only in specific limiting cases. Our framework precisely identifies these regimes and within them distinguishes between quantum and classical behaviors. This approach is universally applicable and has been successfully applied to various quantum quantum master equations and multiple quantum open systems. As a demonstration of its broad utility, we apply the theory to classical quantum flip-flop dynamics governed by the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equation, a model commonly used to describe energy relaxation in artificial atoms and quantum dots. We outline the flip-flop model and solve the resulting equations. Furthermore, we examine the quantum-to-classical transition, the low-temperature regime, and the specific characteristics of relaxation processes. Finally, we discuss how this method can be extended to even more complex many-body systems. Energy relaxation in quantum devices holds significant practical importance in the field of quantum technology. Therefore, a rigorous statistical framework capable of consistently characterizing the transition from classical to quantum regimes is essential for a proper understanding of these systems. The approach not only clarifies the nature of relaxation in quantum technology but also establishes a clear distinction between a universal quantum diffusive regime and a truly quantum regime. This represents a substantial challenge in quantum thermodynamics, where heat and work operators are ill-defined at the microscopic scale due to their operator nature. The theory successfully quantifies the characteristics of these two regimes as properties of jump observables and current fluctuation-dissipation relations. These findings open new avenues for future theoretical and experimental investigations. In particular, measuring noise characteristics and scaled jump observables in quantum systems could serve as a tool for quantifying the transition from a universal thermal quantum-particle-like regime to a purely quantum regime. Such measurements would be meaningful for many emerging quantum technologies. Additionally, the theory can be readily extended to stochastic non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. Key experimental candidates for testing these methods include cold-atom systems, circuit quantum electrodynamics, and quantum dots.

2 b exhibits periodic and stochastic transits, with the latter suggesting the presence of an extended comet-like tail for the first time in a disintegrating exoplanet. Our 2.5-meter telescope observations captured three stochastic transits lasting 15–30 minutes and detected four X-ray sources associated with K2-222: K2-22 A, K2-22 B, K2-22 C, and K2-22 D, recorded 2, 53, 53, and 56 days after their initial detections by the Kepler mission. Analysis of our light curves reveals that the average particle radii for these stochastic transits do not significantly differ from previous findings, but the particle mass increases by at least one order of magnitude. Our results indicate that the dust particles are roughly spherical with a minimum radius of $r_{min} \approx 0.8~\mu$m, with a median radius of $<r> \approx 8~\mu$m and a maximum radius of $r_{max} \approx 10^4~\mu$m; the largest particles are twice as massive as those previously reported. By fitting the transit light curves of these new stochastic events, we determined the positions of the centers of mass for their trajectories: $R_0 = 13.6 \pm 0.1$, $R_0 = 15.6 \pm 0.1$, $R_0 = 15.6 \pm 0.1$, and $R_0 = 16.6 \pm 0.1$ for K2-22 C, K2-22 D, K2-22 B, and K2-22 A, respectively. Additionally, the stochastic transit depth is $d = 0.041 \pm 0.003$, which is over 20 times deeper than the regular transit depth of $d_{reg} = 0.0017 \pm 0.0004$. These findings support a physical model in which the extended comet-like tail of K2-22 b originates from the continuous sublimation and erosion of the surface due to high-temperature stellar irradiation on the highly eccentric exoplanet.

Specifically, his mathematical and spatial skills appear to have constrained his experimental program, leading to a publication strategy focused on advanced optics. In this context, his experimental work on such topics as free fall, motion on inclined planes, collisions, and pneumatics probably predated his writings on advanced mathematics and optics. Consequently, the personal character of Galileo—defined by his mathematical and spatial competencies and priorities—may have influenced not only his individual career but also the broader progression of scientific knowledge. More generally, this argument highlights how a scientist's specific competencies can serve as a historical variable explaining divergent paths of scientific development. Finally, I contend that our own competence in mathematics significantly affects our perception of Galileo's legacy, and we should strive to cultivate alternative mathematical competencies to foster alternative visions of his contributions.

This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of two processes: the rolling-down dynamics of balls bearing simultaneously random initial positions and velocities on a tilted, slowly expanding 1D sawtooth see-saw, and the multiplication sequence of random variables defined by $x_{n+1}=x_n \circ r_n$ with $\langle r_n\rangle =b>1$ and $P(r_n)=\frac{1}{r_{\rm m}^2}\left[\frac{r_{\rm m}^2+b^2}{2b}\left|r_{m} \frac{1}{r_n}-\frac{r_n}{r_{\rm m}}\right|\right]$. In the large $n$ limit, both systems yield a $q$-exponential distribution for their respective first exit times and distributions of averages, characterized by the parameter $q=\frac{1+1/b}{2}$. These findings extend to confined versions of the problems, where the see-saw and multiplication sequences are confined via a reflecting barrier. While the multiplication sequence strictly follows an $q$-exponential distribution, the see-saw system, while asymptotically seeing a $q$-exponential form, distinctly approaches the $q$-Gaussian distribution in the large $n$ limit. This convergence demonstrates the weak consistency between the two processes in the strict large $n$ limit. Furthermore, a weak consistency between the see-saw and confined multiplication processes is established based on their respective $q$-variance values. The paper also provides exact expressions for the average position $\langle x_n\rangle$ and the root-mean-square width $\langle x^2\rangle^{1/2}$; while the ratio $\frac{\langle x^2\rangle^{1/2}}{\langle x_n\rangle}$ does not vanish as $n$ increases, the ratio of the standard variance to the square of the average remains non-zero. These results, which are analytically exact, can be effectively approximated by simple analytic expressions. Additionally, a finite-size scaling form for the distribution of averages of the see-saw process is derived, confirming its weak consistency with the Doyne-Jones consistency relation.

This study employs the MHD-AEPIC framework to examine the interaction between magnetic antiparallel flux tubes. We compare results from kinetic simulations against those from pure MHD, noting that the kinetic model generates smaller separation distances and larger, more complex separation and reconnection sites. Furthermore, MHD simulations fail to capture the production of whistler waves and electrostatic potentials, suggesting these are suppressed by early reconnection in the kinetic scenario. Additional findings indicate that the small separation width and complex geometry of the reconnection region hinder magnetic field line tracking, causing some separatrix surfaces to appear as planes rather than cones. These complex separation zones arise from whistler-mediated reconnection, which is more than an order of magnitude faster than reconnection driven by magnetic tension in pure M simulations. Our results corroborate earlier reports of rapid reconnection and upstream whistler activity in collisionless environments, confirming that kinetic effects can decouple the separation rate from the Alfvén speed and that magnetic field lines can bend due to whistler propagation even when upstream whistler mediation is absent. Finally, our work offers an alternative explanation for observations of rapid reconnection in young stellar objects that does not rely on pre-existing thin separation regions.

While general neuroscience provides essential context for these technologies, it is presented with a focus on machine and computational systems. The primary teaching methodology consists of lecture-demonstrations, where each session pairs a theoretical lecture with a subsequent demo. These demonstrations cover various cognitive and computing systems, including human and animal brains, robotic systems, and software or neural network models. The course is structured into three sections: Computing Machines, Biological Systems, and Conclusions. A detailed description of each topic is provided through course notes. Additionally, the accompanying website features video recordings of all lecture-demonstrations; while the demos are integrated into the lecture flow, the notes serve as a summary of their content. Finally, it is important to note that this course is distinct from Neuroscience and Computing (CSC221A), which was offered in the following Spring semester.
